definitions.definition: Abetment, as used in Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to the act of instigating, aiding, counselling, or facilitating another person in knowingly infringing the copyright in a work or any other right conferred by the Act. It encompasses any direct or indirect assistance, encouragement, or support rendered to a person who commits copyright infringement, thereby making the abettor equally liable for the offence.
definitions.plain_english: Abetment means helping, encouraging, or assisting someone else to illegally copy or use someone's protected creative work without permission. If you knowingly help another person pirate a book, film, song, or software, you are guilty of abetment even if you did not do the copying yourself. The law treats the helper as equally guilty as the person who actually committed the infringement.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based printing press owner knowingly prints thousands of unauthorised copies of a bestselling Hindi novel for a publisher who lacks the copyright licence, thereby abetting the infringement of the author's copyright.

A Hyderabad shop owner allows a vendor to use his premises and equipment to duplicate and sell pirated Tollywood DVD collections, knowing fully well that no licence has been obtained from the film producers.

An IT professional in Bengaluru provides a cracked software activation key generator to a colleague, knowingly enabling the colleague to install and distribute unlicensed copies of a proprietary software program, thereby abetting infringement of the software company's copyright.

A Delhi-based social media influencer shares a direct download link to an unauthorised free PDF of a textbook published by a major educational publisher, knowingly assisting thousands of followers in accessing infringing copies, thereby abetting mass copyright infringement.

A Chennai recording studio engineer secretly provides unreleased master audio tracks of a popular music album to a third party who then distributes them online without the record label's permission, constituting abetment of infringement of the broadcast reproduction right and sound recording copyright.
what_it_covers: Knowingly providing equipment, tools, or infrastructure (such as duplicating machines or servers) used to reproduce or distribute infringing copies of a copyrighted work.
Actively encouraging, instructing, or financing another person to carry out copyright infringement, such as commissioning a pirate publisher to reproduce a copyrighted literary or artistic work.
Distributing or sharing access credentials, links, or decryption tools that enable another person to access, reproduce, or communicate a copyrighted work without authorisation.
Allowing one's premises, platforms, or business channels to be knowingly used by an infringer to manufacture or sell infringing copies of films, music, software, or books.
Providing logistical support such as transportation, storage, or online hosting for infringing copies while being aware of their infringing nature.
what_it_excludes: Innocent or unknowing assistance where the person had no knowledge that the act being facilitated constituted copyright infringement, as the provision expressly requires the infringement to be 'knowing'.
Construction of a building or other structure that infringes or would infringe copyright in another work, which is explicitly carved out from criminal liability under Section 63 itself.
Acts that constitute independent infringement by the person themselves rather than facilitation of another's infringement, which fall under direct infringement rather than abetment.
Infringement of the right conferred by Section 53A of the Act, which is expressly excluded from the ambit of Section 63 and therefore cannot give rise to abetment liability under this section.
Mere failure to prevent infringement by a third party in the absence of any positive act of instigation, aid, or facilitation directed toward the infringing act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's conduct qualifies as abetment under Section 63 determines whether they face mandatory criminal prosecution with imprisonment of not less than six months extendable to three years and a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees extendable to two lakh rupees; without this classification applying, the same person could avoid criminal liability entirely even if they knowingly assisted in large-scale piracy. It extends the penal reach of copyright law beyond the direct infringer to all those in the chain of infringement, serving as a critical deterrent against organised copyright piracy networks.

definitions.definition: An 'accessible format' means a format that gives a person with disability access to the work, including such access to the work which is as feasible and comfortable as the access available to a person without such disability. It includes any format which is capable of being used by a person with a print or reading disability, such as Braille, large print, audio recording, digital text or any other format that enables such persons to access the copyrighted work.
definitions.plain_english: An accessible format is a specially adapted version of a copyrighted work that makes it usable by people with disabilities, such as blindness, visual impairment, or other print disabilities. For example, a book converted into Braille, an audio recording of a text, or a digitally formatted e-book readable by screen readers would all qualify as accessible formats. The idea is that the person with disability can access and enjoy the work as comfortably as a person without any disability.
real_world_examples: A blind student at Delhi University needs a textbook converted into Braille script by the National Institute for the Visually Handicapped, Dehradun — this Braille edition is an accessible format under Section 52.

An NGO in Mumbai converts a Hindi novel into an audio recording using text-to-speech software and distributes it free of charge to visually impaired readers registered with the National Association for the Blind — this audio version qualifies as an accessible format.

The Daisy Forum of India produces a DAISY (Digital Accessible Information System) formatted version of a medical textbook for students with dyslexia enrolled in AIIMS — the DAISY file is an accessible format enabling screen-reader compatibility.

A Kolkata-based disability rights organisation converts a copyrighted law report into large-print format for persons with low vision — this large-print edition constitutes an accessible format permissible under the copyright exception.

A charitable trust in Chennai creates a sign-language video interpretation of a published dramatic work for deaf students — this sign-language version is an accessible format tailored to persons with hearing and communication disabilities.
what_it_covers: Braille transcriptions of literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works prepared for visually impaired persons
Audio recordings or text-to-speech conversions of published books made for persons with visual impairment or dyslexia
DAISY (Digital Accessible Information System) formatted e-books designed for use with screen readers or assistive devices
Large-print editions of copyrighted works produced for persons with low vision
Sign-language video renditions of literary or dramatic works made for persons with hearing or communication disabilities
what_it_excludes: Standard commercial reproductions or adaptations of a work that are not specifically designed to address a disability-related access barrier
Formats that merely change the aesthetic presentation of a work without enabling access by a person with disability, such as a foreign-language translation or a colourised film version
Digital copies made for general public distribution or commercial profit, even if incidentally usable by some persons with disabilities
Adaptations or modifications made for technological compatibility purposes unrelated to disability access, such as converting a file format for device interoperability
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a reproduction or adaptation qualifies as an 'accessible format' determines whether it falls within the Section 52 exception to copyright infringement, allowing organisations, NGOs, educational institutions, and individuals to reproduce copyrighted works without the author's permission and without payment of royalties for the benefit of persons with disabilities. If the format does not meet this definition, creating or distributing such copies could constitute copyright infringement under the Act, exposing the person responsible to civil and criminal liability.

definitions.definition: "adaptation" means, in relation to a dramatic work, the conversion of the work into a non-dramatic work; in relation to a literary work or an artistic work, the conversion of the work into a dramatic work by way of performance in public or otherwise; in relation to a literary or dramatic work, any abridgement of the work or any version of the work in which the story or action is conveyed wholly or mainly by means of pictures in a form suitable for reproduction in a book, or in a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical; in relation to a musical work, any arrangement or transcription of the work; and in relation to any work, any use of such work involving its rearrangement or alteration.
definitions.plain_english: An adaptation is when you take someone's original creative work and transform it into a different form or format. For example, turning a novel into a stage play, converting a play into a story book, or rearranging a song into a new musical version all count as adaptations. Even making a picture-book version of a story or an abridged summary of a book is an adaptation under copyright law.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood production house converts R.K. Narayan's novel 'Malgudi Days' into a television drama serial — this is an adaptation of a literary work into a dramatic work.

A Mumbai-based publisher creates a comic book (Amar Chitra Katha style) retelling the story of a Hindi play by Mohan Rakesh, conveying the plot mainly through pictures suitable for magazine reproduction — this constitutes an adaptation of a dramatic work.
A classical musician in Chennai rearranges a Carnatic composition by a contemporary composer into a Western orchestral transcription — this is an adaptation of a musical work.
A Delhi theatre group converts a published stage play into a prose short story to be published in a literary magazine — this is an adaptation of a dramatic work into a non-dramatic work.

An educational publisher in Pune creates an abridged version of a full-length Hindi novel for school children, condensing the plot while retaining the essential story — this qualifies as an adaptation of a literary work.
A streaming platform converts a Bengali short story into a web series script for public performance — this is an adaptation of a literary work into a dramatic work.
what_it_covers: Converting a Hindi novel into a stage play or screenplay for public performance in India.
Rearranging or transcribing a copyrighted Indian classical or film song into a new musical format, such as an orchestral or jazz version.
Creating an abridged or picture-based retelling of a literary or dramatic work suitable for publication in a magazine, newspaper, or book.
Turning a published stage play into a prose narrative or short story (dramatic to non-dramatic conversion).
Making a comic strip or graphic novel version of a literary work where the story is conveyed mainly through pictures.
what_it_excludes: A straight reproduction or verbatim copy of a work without any transformation, rearrangement, or conversion — this constitutes reproduction, not adaptation.
A translation of a literary work from one language to another (e.g., Hindi to Tamil) — translation is separately treated under the Act and is not classified as adaptation.
A cinematograph film based on a literary work — while adaptation rights may be involved in the underlying creation, a cinematograph film itself is a distinct category of work under the Act.
Mere performance of a dramatic or musical work without any conversion, alteration, or rearrangement of the underlying work.
Independent original works that are inspired by or thematically similar to an existing work but do not involve actual conversion, abridgement, or rearrangement of that work.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as an adaptation is critical because the Copyright Act grants the original copyright owner the exclusive right to make or authorise adaptations of their work under Section 14; any unauthorised adaptation constitutes infringement under the Act, exposing the infringer to civil remedies and criminal penalties. Conversely, establishing that an act is an adaptation (rather than an independent creation or a mere reproduction) determines which rights — including moral rights under Section 57 and rights of performers and assignees under Sections 24 and 14 — are engaged and who must seek a licence.

definitions.definition: An anonymous work is a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work in which the identity of the author is not disclosed publicly by both the author and the publisher, and has not been otherwise established to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board by that author. In the context of joint authorship, a work qualifies as an anonymous work of joint authorship where the identity of any of the authors remains undisclosed.
definitions.plain_english: An anonymous work is a creative work — such as a book, song, painting, or play — where the real name of the person who created it has not been made public. The author's identity is either hidden entirely or has not been officially confirmed. Copyright law treats such works differently because the normal rules (which tie copyright duration to the author's lifespan) cannot easily apply when the creator is unknown.
real_world_examples: A Hindi novel published in Mumbai in 1985 under no author name — the publisher releases it simply as 'A True Story' with no attribution — qualifies as an anonymous work, and copyright runs for 60 years from the year of publication.

A collection of folk poems compiled and published by a Delhi publishing house without crediting any individual author, where neither the compiler nor the original poets are identified publicly, constitutes an anonymous work under the Act.

An editorial cartoon published in a Kolkata newspaper in 1970 without any artist's signature or byline, where the newspaper has never publicly attributed it to any artist and no Appellate Board determination has been made, is treated as an anonymous artistic work.

A piece of classical Carnatic music notation published by a Chennai music academy in 1960 under the title 'Traditional Composition' with no composer named — and the academy has never disclosed or confirmed the composer's identity — is an anonymous musical work for copyright purposes.

A jointly authored legal commentary published in Pune under pseudonyms, where all authors use pen names and none of their real identities have been publicly disclosed by either author or publisher, is treated as an anonymous work of joint authorship under Section 54 for the purpose of determining the copyright owner.
what_it_covers: A literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work published without any author name where neither the author nor publisher has publicly disclosed the author's identity.
A work of joint authorship published without disclosing the identity of any of the authors, either by the authors and publisher jointly or through an Appellate Board determination.
A work where an author's name was never attached at publication and no subsequent public or official disclosure of identity has been made within the copyright period.
Artistic or literary works published under a blank attribution where the publisher alone holds the rights as 'owner of copyright' under Section 54 due to non-disclosure of authorship.
what_it_excludes: Works published under a pseudonym (pen name) where a false or assumed name is used — such works are classified as pseudonymous works, not anonymous works, though similar rules may apply.
Works where the author's identity has been publicly disclosed by both the author and the publisher, even if the work was originally published without attribution.

Works whose authorship has been established to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board, as such establishment removes the work from the anonymous category and activates the standard life-plus-60-years copyright term.
Government works or works by bodies corporate, which have their own copyright provisions and do not depend on individual author identity for term calculation.
Photographs, which are explicitly excluded from the scope of Section 23's special provisions for anonymous and pseudonymous works.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as an anonymous work determines both the duration of copyright protection (60 years from publication rather than 60 years from the author's death) and who holds the rights — under Section 54, the publisher steps into the role of 'owner of copyright' until authorship is publicly disclosed, which directly affects who may grant licences, sue for infringement, or collect royalties.

definitions.definition: "Appellate Board" means the Appellate Board referred to in section 11.
definitions.plain_english: The Appellate Board is a special judicial body established under the Copyright Act to hear and decide appeals and disputes related to copyright matters in India. It acts as a higher authority where parties can challenge decisions made by the Registrar of Copyrights or seek resolution of specific copyright disputes such as compulsory licensing. It functions like a tribunal with the power to hear cases, review decisions, and grant remedies in copyright-related matters.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music composer whose application for a compulsory licence was rejected by the Registrar of Copyrights appeals to the Appellate Board under Section 31 seeking a licence to republish the work.

A Mumbai-based publishing house challenges a copyright society's refusal to grant a licence for reprinting a literary anthology, and the matter is referred to the Appellate Board for adjudication under Section 33A.

A radio broadcasting company in Chennai disputes the royalty rates set under a statutory licence for sound recordings broadcast over FM radio and approaches the Appellate Board under Section 31D for a determination.

A disability-rights NGO in Delhi applies to the Appellate Board under Section 31B seeking a compulsory licence to convert a copyrighted textbook into an accessible format for visually impaired students after the copyright owner refuses permission.
A Kolkata-based film producer contests the cancellation of their copyright registration by the Registrar of Copyrights and files an appeal before the Appellate Board under Section 72.
what_it_covers: Appeals against orders or decisions of the Registrar of Copyrights under Section 72 of the Act.
Applications for compulsory licences in works withheld from the public, cover versions, and broadcasting of literary and musical works under Sections 31, 31A, 31C, and 31D.
Disputes relating to the registration, functioning, or tariff schemes of copyright societies under Sections 33 and 33A.
Appeals concerning rectification or cancellation of entries in the Register of Copyrights.
Determination of disputes arising from assignment of copyright where the assignee fails to exercise rights under Section 19A.
what_it_excludes: Civil courts of ordinary jurisdiction, which have no original jurisdiction over matters exclusively vested in the Appellate Board under the Copyright Act.
The Copyright Office and the Registrar of Copyrights, which are administrative bodies with first-instance jurisdiction, not appellate bodies.
Criminal courts dealing with copyright infringement offences under Sections 63–68A, which fall outside the Appellate Board's jurisdiction.
The High Courts and Supreme Court of India in their original writ jurisdiction, which are constitutionally distinct from the statutory Appellate Board.
Arbitration tribunals or private dispute resolution bodies, which are not constituted under Section 11 and thus do not qualify as the Appellate Board.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of the Appellate Board is critical because it is the sole statutory forum empowered to grant compulsory licences, adjudicate copyright society disputes, and hear appeals against the Registrar's decisions — filing before any other body would be without jurisdiction and void. Whether a forum qualifies as the Appellate Board determines whether its orders on royalty rates, licence grants, and registration cancellations carry binding legal force under the Copyright Act.

definitions.definition: A contract of apprenticeship, as used in Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to a formal arrangement under which a person is engaged to learn a trade, craft, or profession under the supervision and direction of an employer, and in the course of which any literary, dramatic, or artistic work created by such apprentice is treated on par with work created under a contract of service for the purposes of determining first ownership of copyright.
definitions.plain_english: An apprenticeship is a learning arrangement where a person works for an employer to acquire skills or training in a particular trade or profession. Under copyright law, if an apprentice creates a work (like an article or artwork) as part of their apprenticeship duties, the employer — not the apprentice — is generally the first owner of the copyright in that work. This is the same rule that applies to regular employees under a contract of service.
real_world_examples: A trainee journalist apprenticed at a leading Mumbai newspaper writes news articles and features as part of their apprenticeship training; the newspaper proprietor becomes the first owner of copyright in those articles published in the newspaper.

A graphic design apprentice at a Delhi-based advertising agency creates artistic illustrations for a client campaign during their apprenticeship period; the agency, as employer, is the first owner of copyright in those illustrations.

A film production apprentice at a Bollywood studio in Mumbai produces written scene breakdowns and dramatic scripts as part of their training; the studio holds the first copyright ownership over those dramatic works.

A software coding apprentice at a Bengaluru tech firm writes computer programmes and documentation under an apprenticeship contract registered under the Apprentices Act, 1961; the firm is the first owner of copyright in the resulting literary works.

A young artist apprenticed to a master painter in Chennai creates original paintings as directed by the master under an apprenticeship agreement; the master, as the proprietor-employer, is presumed to be the first owner of copyright in those artistic works absent any contrary agreement.
what_it_covers: A formally registered apprentice under the Apprentices Act, 1961 who creates copyrightable works as part of their prescribed duties for a media or publishing employer.

Literary, dramatic, or artistic works created by an apprentice at a newspaper, magazine, or periodical in the course of their apprenticeship, where the proprietor becomes the first owner for publication purposes.

Works made by an apprentice in the course of any other employment arrangement under a contract of apprenticeship not covered by clauses (a) or (b) of the proviso to Section 17, where the employer becomes the first owner of copyright.
Any work produced by an apprentice as a direct task or assignment forming part of their apprenticeship training duties under the employer's supervision and direction.
what_it_excludes: Freelance or independent contractors engaged on a project-by-project basis without a formal contract of apprenticeship or service, who retain first ownership of copyright in their created works.
Works created by an apprentice entirely on their own time and outside the scope of their apprenticeship duties, which are not connected to the employer's trade or publication purposes.
Internships or casual observation-based training arrangements that do not constitute a formal contract of apprenticeship or service under law.
Works created after the apprenticeship period has formally concluded, even if the skills were acquired during the apprenticeship.
Addresses or speeches delivered in public by an apprentice, which are governed separately under the proviso to Section 17 regardless of employment or apprenticeship status.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work is created under a contract of apprenticeship directly determines who holds first ownership of copyright under Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — the apprentice-author or the employer — which in turn governs who may license, assign, or enforce copyright and who may sue for infringement. If the apprenticeship relationship is established, the employer obtains copyright ownership by default absent a contrary agreement, stripping the creator-apprentice of first ownership rights.

definitions.definition: 'Artistic work' means a painting, a sculpture, a drawing (including a diagram, map, chart or plan), an engraving or a photograph, whether or not any such work possesses artistic quality; a work of architecture; and any other work of artistic craftsmanship.
definitions.plain_english: An artistic work is any visual or three-dimensional creative work such as a painting, drawing, sculpture, photograph, map, or an architecturally designed building. Importantly, the law does not require the work to have any particular artistic merit or quality — even a simple technical diagram qualifies. It also covers handcrafted objects that display skill and artistry, such as jewellery or pottery.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based painter creates an oil painting of the Gateway of India — the painting is an artistic work protected under the Copyright Act, giving the painter exclusive rights to reproduce or sell prints of it.

A Bengaluru architect designs the blueprint and model for a new commercial complex — both the architectural drawings and the constructed building qualify as artistic works, protecting the architect's design from copying.

A Delhi photographer takes a photograph of a cricket match at Wankhede Stadium — the photograph is an artistic work regardless of whether it is considered aesthetically excellent, and the photographer holds the copyright.

A Rajasthani artisan hand-crafts an intricately decorated silver jewellery piece using traditional filigree techniques — this constitutes a work of artistic craftsmanship and is protected as an artistic work.

A Chennai-based graphic designer creates a detailed map of Tamil Nadu's road network for a travel publication — the map, being a drawing, qualifies as an artistic work even though it serves a functional, non-decorative purpose.

A Kolkata sculptor creates a bronze statue of Rabindranath Tagore for a public park — the sculpture is an artistic work, and reproducing it without authorisation would amount to copyright infringement.
what_it_covers: Paintings, sketches, and illustrations regardless of the medium used (oil, watercolour, digital)
Photographs taken by any means, whether film-based or digital, without any requirement of aesthetic quality
Sculptures, including carved, cast, or moulded three-dimensional works
Drawings including technical diagrams, maps, charts, plans, and engineering drawings
Engravings including etchings, lithographs, wood-cuts and similar works
Works of architecture — both the constructed building or structure and architectural models
Works of artistic craftsmanship such as hand-made jewellery, pottery, or embroidered textiles displaying artistic skill
what_it_excludes: Purely functional industrial articles manufactured through an industrial process that do not qualify as works of artistic craftsmanship
Cinematograph films and video recordings, which are separately defined and governed as a distinct category of work under the Act
Literary, dramatic, and musical works, even if presented in a visually appealing format, as these fall under their own separate definitions
Typefaces or fonts in isolation, which are not expressly included within the enumerated categories of artistic work
A raw idea or concept for a painting or design that has not been reduced to a tangible visual or physical form
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as an 'artistic work' determines whether copyright subsists in it under Section 13, who the first owner is under Section 17, the duration of protection under Section 22, and what acts constitute infringement under Section 51 — including unauthorised reproduction, communication to the public, or issuance of copies. Misclassification can strip a creator of all statutory protections and remedies, including injunctions and damages under Section 55.

definitions.definition: In the context of assignment of copyright, 'assignee' means the person to whom the copyright in an existing or future work is assigned, either wholly or partially, and who thereby becomes entitled to the rights so assigned and is treated as the owner of copyright to that extent. In respect of the assignment of copyright in any future work, the expression 'assignee' includes the legal representatives of the assignee, if the assignee dies before the work comes into existence.
definitions.plain_english: An assignee is the person who receives copyright ownership — or a part of it — from the original copyright owner through a formal written agreement called an assignment. Once the assignment takes effect, the assignee steps into the shoes of the copyright owner for all the rights that were transferred. If the assignment was for a future work and the assignee dies before that work is created, the assignee's legal heirs take their place.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based film production house (e.g., Dharma Productions) pays a novelist from Delhi to acquire the copyright in her upcoming novel so it can be adapted into a Hindi film; the production house becomes the assignee of those adaptation rights.

A music composer assigns the copyright in a newly composed background score to a Bengaluru-based music streaming company for digital exploitation in India; the streaming company is the assignee and is treated as the copyright owner for that exploitation.

A Hyderabad software firm assigns the copyright in a proprietary computer programme it developed to a US-based parent corporation; the parent corporation becomes the assignee and can enforce the copyright against infringers in India.

A Pune-based literary author assigns the translation rights of her Marathi novel to a Chennai publisher for Tamil adaptation; the Chennai publisher is the assignee and holds ownership over the translation copyright for the agreed term and territory.

A deceased lyricist had assigned copyright in future lyrics to a record label before completing the songs; upon the lyricist's death before completion, the lyricist's legal heirs step in as assignees by operation of the statutory provision under Section 18.
what_it_covers: A natural person or legal entity who receives copyright in an existing work through a written assignment agreement signed by the assignor.
A company or individual who receives partial copyright — such as only distribution rights or only digital streaming rights — for a limited territory or duration.
The legal representatives (heirs or executors) of an originally named assignee who dies before a future work comes into existence, who step in automatically under Section 18.
A film production company that acquires rights in a literary or musical work to include it in a cinematograph film, thereby becoming the assignee subject to the author's retained royalty rights.
An assignee who, after failing to exercise the assigned rights within one year, still holds the original assignment until it lapses by operation of Section 19(4).
what_it_excludes: A licensee who is granted only a licence (exclusive or non-exclusive) to use the copyright without ownership being transferred; a licensee is not an assignee.
The original author or first owner of copyright who created the work and never transferred ownership; they are the assignor, not the assignee.
A person who receives only a bequest of physical property (e.g., a manuscript) without any accompanying transfer of the underlying copyright.
A copyright society authorised to collect and distribute royalties on behalf of authors; such a society acts as a collecting agent and not as an assignee of the copyright itself.
An employer who owns copyright in a work made by an employee under a contract of service; such ownership arises by statute as first owner, not through assignment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an assignee determines whether they are treated as the 'owner of copyright' under the Act and thus have standing to sue for infringement, grant sub-licences, and claim statutory remedies. It also triggers the royalty-sharing obligation under Sections 18 and 19, whereby the assignee must share royalties on an equal basis with the author for exploitation beyond cinema-hall communication, and subjects the assignee to potential revocation proceedings before the Appellate Board under Section 19A if assigned rights are not sufficiently exercised.

definitions.definition: Assignment of copyright means the transfer by the owner of copyright in an existing work, or the prospective owner in a future work, of the copyright either wholly or partially, either generally or subject to limitations, and either for the whole term of the copyright or any part thereof, to any person; such assignment must be in writing signed by the assignor or his duly authorised agent, and shall identify the work, specify the rights assigned, the duration, territorial extent, royalty and other consideration payable.
definitions.plain_english: An assignment of copyright is when the person who owns a copyright formally transfers some or all of their ownership rights to another person or organisation, by signing a written agreement. It is like selling or partially selling your ownership of a creative work, such as a book, song, or film. The transfer can be for all uses or limited to specific uses, for all territories or just some, and for the entire copyright period or just a portion of it.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based novelist signs a written agreement transferring the copyright in her debut Hindi novel to a major publishing house like Penguin Random House India for a period of ten years and within Indian territory only, in exchange for an advance and royalty share.

A Bollywood music composer assigns the copyright in musical compositions created for a film to the film production company (e.g., Dharma Productions), but retains the right to receive an equal share of royalties whenever those songs are used on streaming platforms like Spotify or JioSaavn outside cinema hall screenings.

A freelance software developer in Bengaluru assigns the copyright in a custom-built mobile application wholly and globally to a startup client, with the assignment specifying a lump-sum payment and a one-year duration after which the rights revert if the startup does not exploit the software.

A Punjabi folk singer assigns the copyright in an album of sound recordings partially to a regional music label for distribution in Punjab and Haryana only, while retaining rights for international distribution and digital streaming outside those states.

A visual artist based in Delhi assigns the copyright in a series of digital artworks to an advertising agency for use in a specific marketing campaign for two years, with the assignment clearly stating it does not cover use in mediums or modes of exploitation not commercially existing at the time of signing.
what_it_covers: Complete transfer of all copyright rights in an existing literary, musical, dramatic, or artistic work from the author to a publisher, studio, or other entity.
Partial assignment of specific rights comprised in copyright, such as only the right of reproduction or only the right of communication to the public, for a defined period and territory.
Assignment of copyright in a future work that has not yet come into existence, with the assignment taking effect automatically once the work is created.
Assignment by the legal representatives of a deceased assignee where the assignee died before a future work came into existence.
Assignment of rights subject to conditions, including revision, extension, or termination clauses mutually agreed upon by both parties.
what_it_excludes: Oral or unwritten transfers of copyright, which are not valid assignments under the Act and have no legal effect.
Exclusive licences, which grant permission to exercise copyright rights without transferring ownership, and are governed separately under the Act.

Assignment of an author's right to receive royalties on equal basis with the assignee for utilisation of literary or musical works in cinematograph films (other than cinema hall screenings), which cannot be assigned away except to legal heirs or a copyright society.

Assignments that purport to cover mediums or modes of exploitation not in existence or not in commercial use at the time of assignment, unless the assignment specifically refers to such future mediums.
Assignments made contrary to the terms and conditions of rights already assigned to a copyright society of which the author is a member, which are void.

Assignments of copyright in a work for making a cinematograph film or sound recording that purport to extinguish the author's statutory right to an equal share of royalties for utilisation of the work in other forms.

definitions.definition: The assignor is the owner of copyright in an existing work, or the prospective owner of copyright in a future work, who assigns such copyright wholly or partially to another person (the assignee). As respects the rights not assigned, the assignor shall be treated as the owner of copyright for the purposes of the Act. In the context of Section 19A, the assignor is specifically the party who has transferred copyright rights and who may file a complaint before the Appellate Board seeking revocation of the assignment.
definitions.plain_english: An assignor is the person who originally owns a copyright and transfers it (or a part of it) to someone else through an assignment agreement. Think of them as the seller or giver of copyright rights. Even after the transfer, the assignor retains ownership over any rights that were not part of the assignment. If the person who received the rights (the assignee) fails to properly use them, the assignor can approach the Copyright Board to get those rights back.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood lyricist in Mumbai assigns the copyright in his song lyrics to a music production company for use in a film; the lyricist is the assignor and can approach the Appellate Board if the production company fails to release or exploit the song within a reasonable period.

A Bengaluru-based software developer assigns the copyright in her mobile application code to a tech startup; she is the assignor and retains the right to complain to the Appellate Board if the startup never deploys or commercialises the application.

A Chennai publisher holds copyright in a Tamil novel and assigns it to a national publishing house for distribution across India; the original publisher is the assignor and may seek revocation if the national house fails to publish or distribute the work adequately.

A Pune-based graphic novelist assigns his copyright in an illustrated series to an animation studio for adaptation into a web series; he is the assignor and, being also the author, can seek revocation before the Appellate Board if the assignment terms are found harsh.

A Delhi composer assigns copyright in a background score to a streaming platform for online use; the composer is the assignor and retains rights over any medium of exploitation not specifically mentioned in the assignment agreement.

A Kolkata photographer assigns copyright in a collection of photographs to an advertising agency for use in print campaigns; the photographer is the assignor and may dispute the scope of the assignment before the Appellate Board if the agency uses the images beyond the agreed territorial extent.
what_it_covers: The original author of a literary, musical, dramatic, or artistic work who transfers copyright to a publisher, producer, or other entity.
A non-author first owner of copyright (such as an employer who owns copyright in a work made during the course of employment) who assigns those rights to a third party.
A prospective owner of copyright in a future work who enters into an assignment agreement before the work comes into existence, once that work comes into existence and the assignment takes effect.
An author who is simultaneously the assignor and retains the special statutory protection under the proviso to Section 19A(2) against harsh assignment terms.
A legal entity (such as a company or firm) that holds copyright and assigns it wholly or partially to another person or organisation.
what_it_excludes: The assignee — the person who receives the assigned rights — is explicitly distinguished from the assignor and cannot simultaneously hold the same assigned rights in the capacity of assignor.
A licensee who grants a licence (rather than an assignment) of copyright is not an assignor, as a licence does not transfer ownership of the underlying copyright.
Legal heirs or legal representatives who receive copyright by inheritance or succession rather than by a voluntary act of assignment are not assignors in relation to that inherited copyright.

A copyright society that collects and distributes royalties on behalf of authors does not act as an assignor in its administrative capacity, even though authors may assign rights to it for collection purposes.
A person who merely authorises performance or communication to the public without executing a formal written assignment signed in accordance with Section 19 is not an assignor under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The legal status of 'assignor' determines who has standing to file a complaint before the Appellate Board under Section 19A for revocation of assignment on grounds of the assignee's failure to exercise the assigned rights or due to harsh terms, and who retains ownership (and associated remedies for infringement) over copyright in rights not included in the assignment. Misidentifying the assignor could result in a complaint being dismissed for lack of locus standi or in erroneous attribution of ownership rights and royalty entitlements.

definitions.definition: "author" means,— in relation to a literary or dramatic work, the author of the work; in relation to a musical work, the composer; in relation to an artistic work other than a photograph, the artist; in relation to a photograph, the person taking the photograph; in relation to a cinematograph film or sound recording, the producer; and in relation to any literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work which is computer-generated, the person who causes the work to be created.
definitions.plain_english: The 'author' is the person who creates a work, but who exactly counts as the author depends on the type of work involved. For books or plays, it is the writer; for music, it is the composer; for paintings or sculptures, it is the artist; for photos, it is the photographer; and for films or sound recordings, it is the producer. For works created entirely by a computer without direct human creative input, the person who set up or caused the computer to generate the work is treated as the author.
real_world_examples: A novelist from Jaipur who writes an original Hindi fiction novel is the 'author' of that literary work and holds the initial copyright in it under the Copyright Act, 1957.
A Bollywood music composer like A.R. Rahman who composes the background score for a film is the 'author' of the musical work, distinct from the lyricist who writes the accompanying words.

A photographer who takes photographs at a wedding in Mumbai is the 'author' of those photographs, meaning she owns copyright in those images unless she was employed to do so under a contract of service.
A production house in Chennai that produces a Tamil feature film is the 'author' (as producer) of that cinematograph film and is therefore treated as the first owner of copyright in the film.

A software company in Bengaluru that runs an AI tool to auto-generate background illustrations for a mobile app is considered the 'author' of those computer-generated artistic works, as it is the entity that caused the works to be created.
A sculptor in Kolkata who creates a bronze statue for a public park is the 'author' of that artistic work, and retains moral rights under Section 57 even if ownership is later transferred.
what_it_covers: The writer or poet who personally creates a literary or dramatic work, including the author of a novel, screenplay, or choreographic piece fixed in writing.
The composer who creates the musical notes and arrangements of a song, regardless of whether he records it in any graphical notation.
The producer of a cinematograph film or sound recording, who bears responsibility for making the work, is treated as its author for copyright purposes.
The artist who paints, sculpts, draws, or crafts an artistic work (other than a photograph), including painters, sculptors, and graphic designers.
The person who takes a photograph, i.e., the individual who operates the camera and captures the image.
The person who causes a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work to be created, where no human author exists in the traditional sense.
what_it_excludes: A lyricist is not the 'author' of the musical work itself; they are the author of the literary work (the lyrics), while the composer is the author of the music.
A publisher or distributor who merely reproduces or circulates a work does not qualify as an 'author' under this definition.
An employer who commissions a work from an independent contractor is not automatically the 'author', though ownership rules under Section 17 may differ; authorship remains with the creator.
A film director, despite their creative contribution to a cinematograph film, is not recognised as the 'author' of the film under the Act — the producer holds that designation.
A person who merely finances or funds the creation of a work without causing or directing its creation is not considered an 'author' of the resulting work.
A performer who acts in or performs a dramatic or musical work is not the 'author' of that underlying work, even though they may have performer's rights under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of the 'author' is foundational to determining first ownership of copyright under Section 17, duration of copyright under Sections 22–23, and the vesting of moral rights under Section 57; an incorrect identification of the author can nullify a copyright claim or a moral rights action. It also determines eligibility for special rights such as the right to relinquish copyright under Section 21 and the right to receive royalties under assignments and licences governed by Sections 19 and 34–35.

definitions.definition: "Authority" is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957. As used in Section 68, it refers to the governmental or regulatory body empowered to grant permission or sanction for the performance of a work in public, particularly in the context of dramatic or musical works where approval of a competent authority is required before performance rights can be exercised or enforced.
definitions.plain_english: An 'authority' in this context means an official government body or regulatory entity that has the legal power to grant or withhold permission for certain acts under the Copyright Act. In Section 68, it refers to the body whose approval is needed before a work (like a play or musical performance) can be performed in public. Think of it as a licensing or approval body that controls whether a performance can legally go ahead.
real_world_examples: A theatre group in Mumbai seeks permission from the competent authority under Section 68 to perform a dramatic adaptation of a protected literary work, and the authority grants sanction after reviewing the application.

A music festival organiser in Delhi applies to the relevant authority for clearance to publicly perform copyrighted musical compositions, with the authority determining whether conditions imposed on performance are met before granting approval.

An educational institution in Chennai wishes to stage a public performance of a copyrighted play; the authority examines whether the performance qualifies under any permitted use and issues or denies the requisite sanction.

A regional broadcaster in Kolkata seeks authority approval before broadcasting a live performance of a protected musical work, ensuring compliance with Section 68 requirements before transmission to the public.

A cultural organisation in Hyderabad applies to the designated authority for permission to perform a protected choreographic work at a public event, and the authority imposes conditions such as payment of royalties prior to granting sanction.
what_it_covers: A government-designated regulatory body empowered under the Copyright Act to grant or refuse permission for public performance of protected works.
Any official authority whose sanction is a prerequisite under Section 68 before a dramatic, musical, or other protected work may be performed in public.
Statutory bodies or tribunals vested with jurisdiction to oversee compliance with conditions for performance, including royalty payment or licensing requirements under the Act.
Bodies such as the Copyright Board or Appellate Board when acting in the capacity of adjudicating or sanctioning performance-related matters under Section 68.
what_it_excludes: Private organisations or collecting societies such as copyright societies, which are not governmental or statutory authorities empowered to sanction performances under Section 68.
Individual copyright owners or exclusive licensees who may grant licences privately but do not constitute an 'authority' in the statutory sense used in Section 68.
Courts of law when exercising civil or criminal jurisdiction over copyright disputes, as they adjudicate rather than grant prior administrative sanction for performances.
Broadcasting organisations or performing rights societies acting in a commercial capacity, which manage licensing but are not authoritative bodies under Section 68.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a body qualifies as an 'authority' under Section 68 determines whether its approval is legally sufficient to permit the public performance of a copyrighted work, thereby either enabling or blocking that performance without liability for infringement. Failure to obtain requisite authority sanction before performing a protected work can expose the performer or organiser to civil and criminal liability for copyright infringement under the Act.

definitions.definition: A bequest, as used in Section 20 of the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to a testamentary disposition by which a person (testator) leaves the manuscript of a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work to another person through a Will or codicil. Where such a bequest is made and the work was not published before the testator's death, the bequest is construed as including the copyright in the work to the extent the testator was the copyright owner immediately before death, unless a contrary intention is indicated in the Will or codicil.
definitions.plain_english: A bequest is when someone leaves property to another person through their Will. In copyright law, if a writer, artist, or composer leaves their original unpublished manuscript or artwork to someone in their Will, that gift automatically includes the copyright as well — unless the Will specifically says otherwise. So the person who receives the manuscript also gets the right to publish, reproduce, and control the work.
real_world_examples: A Hindi novelist based in Mumbai dies leaving an unpublished manuscript of a novel to his daughter through his Will. Under Section 20, the daughter automatically receives both the physical manuscript and the copyright to publish or adapt the novel, even if the Will does not explicitly mention copyright.

A classical Carnatic music composer in Chennai bequeaths his handwritten musical scores of unpublished compositions to his student through a Will. The student thereby acquires copyright in those compositions and can commercially release recordings or grant licences to music labels.

A Kolkata-based painter dies testate, leaving a collection of original unpublished paintings to a charitable art foundation via Will. The foundation receives not just the physical artworks but also the copyright, enabling it to reproduce prints, sell merchandise, or license the images.

A playwright in Delhi leaves the typed but unpublished script of a play to a theatre academy through a codicil to his Will, with an express clause that copyright remains with his legal heirs. In this case, the academy receives only the physical manuscript and not the copyright, as the contrary intention was clearly indicated.

A software developer in Bengaluru dies leaving an unpublished technical manual (a literary work) to his business partner through a Will without any restriction. The partner inherits both the document and the copyright, allowing him to publish, translate, or license the manual commercially.
what_it_covers: A bequest of an original handwritten or typed manuscript of an unpublished literary work, such as a novel or poem, where copyright passes to the legatee along with the physical document.
A testamentary disposition of an unpublished artistic work, such as a painting or sculpture, where the legatee acquires copyright in addition to physical ownership of the artwork.
A bequest of an unpublished musical score or dramatic script through a Will or codicil, automatically transferring copyright to the beneficiary unless the Will expressly provides otherwise.
Situations where the testator was the copyright owner immediately before death, ensuring only the portion of copyright actually owned by the testator passes through the bequest.
what_it_excludes: Works that were already published before the testator's death — Section 20 applies only to unpublished works, so a bequest of a published book's manuscript does not carry copyright under this section.
Bequests where the testator's Will or codicil expressly indicates a contrary intention, meaning copyright is explicitly retained by the estate or directed to a different beneficiary.
Transfers of copyright during the testator's lifetime, such as assignments or licences executed before death — these are governed by assignment or licence provisions, not Section 20.
Intestate succession (dying without a Will), where the transmission of copyright is governed by general succession law and not by the bequest provision under Section 20.
Portions of copyright that the testator did not own at the time of death, such as copyright already assigned to a publisher or co-owned with a joint author — only the testator's actual share passes.

definitions.definition: A body corporate shall be deemed to be domiciled in India if it is incorporated under any law in force in India. In the context of Section 69, 'company' means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of persons, indicating that a body corporate is an entity with a legal personality distinct from its members, capable of holding rights and incurring liabilities under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'body corporate' is any organisation that has been given a separate legal identity by law — meaning it can own property, enter contracts, and be sued in its own name, just like a person. This includes companies registered under Indian company law, statutory corporations, and similar entities created by legislation. Under the Copyright Act, such entities can own copyrights, be held liable for copyright offences, and be treated as domiciled in India if they are incorporated here.
real_world_examples: A private limited company such as Infosys Ltd., registered under the Companies Act 2013, is a body corporate and can be the first owner of copyright in software developed by its employees in the course of their employment.

Doordarshan, established as a statutory body under the Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) Act 1990, is a body corporate and holds broadcast reproduction rights in its programmes under the Copyright Act.

Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd., a publicly listed company incorporated in India, qualifies as a body corporate and can be prosecuted under Section 69 of the Copyright Act if it commits a copyright offence, with its directors and officers also being held liable.

The Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), a society registered under the Societies Registration Act and functioning as a body corporate, can hold copyright in the cinematograph films produced under its direction.

A publishing house such as Oxford University Press India Pvt. Ltd., incorporated in India, is a body corporate deemed domiciled in India under Section 8 and can enforce copyright in literary works it publishes.

An international organisation such as the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), even if lacking the legal capacity of a body corporate in its home jurisdiction, is deemed to have such capacity under Section 41 for the purposes of holding and enforcing copyright in India.
what_it_covers: Companies incorporated under the Companies Act 2013 or its predecessors, such as private limited companies, public limited companies, and one-person companies registered in India.
Statutory corporations and public sector undertakings established by Central or State legislation, such as the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) or All India Radio.

Foreign companies that are incorporated under the laws of a foreign country but operate in India, which may hold copyright in works published in India (though they are not deemed domiciled in India under Section 8 unless incorporated here).
International organisations declared by the Central Government under Section 41, which are deemed to have the legal capacity of a body corporate for copyright purposes.
Any body corporate named as a defendant or complainant in copyright infringement proceedings, including corporate collecting societies registered under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Natural persons (individual human beings), such as independent authors, composers, or artists, who are covered by separate provisions relating to authorship and ownership.

Unregistered partnerships or informal associations of individuals that do not have a distinct legal personality separate from their members, unless they fall within the extended definition of 'company' under Section 69.
Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), which are recognised entities for tax purposes in India but are not incorporated bodies and do not possess the legal characteristics of a body corporate.
Sole proprietorships, which carry on business in a trade name but remain legally indistinguishable from the individual proprietor and thus are not body corporates.
Trusts created under the Indian Trusts Act 1882, which are not incorporated entities and do not possess separate legal personality in the same manner as a body corporate.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a body corporate determines whether it can be deemed domiciled in India under Section 8, thereby affecting its entitlement to copyright protection and its ability to enforce rights in Indian courts. Under Section 69, it directly triggers corporate criminal liability for copyright offences, making the company itself — along with its directors, managers, and officers — liable to prosecution and punishment.

definitions.definition: The term 'bona fide' is not formally defined in the Copyright Act, 1957, but as used in Section 39, it denotes an act carried out in genuine good faith, with honest intent, and without any fraudulent, commercial, or collateral purpose — particularly in the context of teaching or research that is sincere and not a pretext for infringement. An act is bona fide when it is undertaken with an authentic, legitimate purpose corresponding to the stated activity, free from deception or ulterior motive.
definitions.plain_english: Bona fide simply means 'in good faith' or 'genuine.' When the law says something must be done for 'bona fide teaching or research,' it means the activity must truly and honestly be for teaching or research — not just claimed to be so in order to avoid copyright rules. If someone uses copyrighted material pretending it is for research but is actually using it for business or personal gain, that would not be bona fide.
real_world_examples: A professor at Delhi University records a live classical music performance broadcast on AIR (All India Radio) and plays it to her students in a music appreciation class — this is bona fide teaching because the intent is genuinely educational and non-commercial.

A PhD scholar at IIT Bombay makes a personal audio recording of a televised documentary broadcast to analyse its sound design as part of his doctoral thesis — this qualifies as bona fide research since the purpose is genuine academic inquiry.

A coaching institute in Kota records a broadcast of a science lecture and sells CDs of it to students for profit — this is NOT bona fide teaching because the commercial motive overrides any genuine educational claim.

A schoolteacher in a government school in Tamil Nadu records a broadcast performance of a folk dance to show students the regional art form as part of the cultural studies curriculum — this is bona fide teaching due to the genuine instructional purpose.

A journalist at NDTV uses a brief excerpt from a performer's live-streamed concert broadcast to report on a current event (the performer's charitable initiative) — this is bona fide review or reporting of current events under Section 39.

A university library in Pune allows students to access a recorded broadcast of a literary reading for academic review purposes under faculty supervision — this constitutes bona fide research within the meaning of the Act.
what_it_covers: A genuine academic researcher recording a broadcast performance solely to analyse it as part of a university-approved research project.
A schoolteacher making a sound recording of a broadcast for the exclusive purpose of classroom instruction at a recognised educational institution.
A university student recording a televised performance to use as primary data in a thesis, with no intent to distribute or commercialise it.
A peer-reviewed journal reviewer using a broadcast excerpt to critically evaluate and write an academic review of a performance.
A non-profit educational NGO in rural India recording a broadcast to train teachers, with no commercial distribution involved.
what_it_excludes: A private coaching centre that records broadcast performances and sells or rents them to students under the guise of 'educational use,' since the commercial purpose negates bona fide intent.
An individual who records a broadcast performance claiming it is for personal research but subsequently uploads it to a public platform for general consumption.

A corporate training firm that uses broadcast recordings in paid professional workshops and labels them as 'research,' since the commercial and non-academic context defeats the bona fide qualification.
Any act of recording or using broadcast material where the stated purpose of teaching or research is a pretext and the actual motive is financial gain or unauthorised dissemination.
Systematic bulk recording of broadcasts by an organisation for archival or commercial licensing purposes, even if nominally described as institutional research.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is 'bona fide' determines if it falls within the statutory exceptions under Section 39, thereby shielding the person from liability for infringement of broadcast reproduction rights or performer's rights; if the bona fide character is absent, the act loses its exempted status and the person becomes liable for infringement, potentially attracting civil remedies and criminal penalties under the Copyright Act, 1957.

definitions.definition: "broadcast" means communication to the public— by any means of wireless diffusion, whether in any one or more of the forms of signs, sounds or visual images; or by wire, and includes a re-broadcast.
definitions.plain_english: A broadcast is any transmission of signs, sounds, or images to the general public, either through wireless means (like radio or television signals sent through the air) or through wired systems (like cable television). It also covers re-broadcasts, which means retransmitting a broadcast that was originally made by someone else. Essentially, it is any technology-based communication directed at the public at large.
real_world_examples: Doordarshan transmitting a cricket match via satellite signals to television sets across India constitutes a wireless broadcast under this definition.
A local cable TV operator in Mumbai distributing a Bollywood film channel to subscribers through a cable network qualifies as a broadcast by wire.
All India Radio (AIR) transmitting a news programme over FM frequency to listeners in Delhi is a classic wireless broadcast covered by this definition.
A regional cable network in Chennai re-transmitting a Star Sports broadcast of an IPL match to its cable subscribers amounts to a re-broadcast and falls within this definition.
A DTH (Direct-to-Home) service provider like Tata Play transmitting a Hindi entertainment channel via satellite signals to dish-equipped homes across India is a wireless broadcast.

A streaming platform transmitting a live event simultaneously to all users over the internet may, depending on the technology used, engage the concept of broadcast if diffused by wire or wireless means to the public.
what_it_covers: Wireless transmission of audio-visual content via satellite or terrestrial signals to the general public, such as FM radio or satellite TV broadcasts.
Wired transmission of television or radio programmes through cable networks to subscribers, as done by cable operators under the Cable Television Networks Act.
Re-broadcasts, i.e., the act of retransmitting an already broadcast signal or programme to the public, whether by the same or a different entity.
Transmission of signs (such as teletext or data signals), sounds (audio), or visual images (video), individually or in combination, to the public.
DTH transmissions by licensed DTH operators transmitting channels to home receivers via satellite uplink and downlink.
what_it_excludes: Issuance of physical copies of a work (such as DVDs or CDs) to the public, which falls outside 'communication to the public' and therefore outside broadcast.
A private, point-to-point transmission between two specific individuals not directed at the public at large, such as a private video call.

On-demand streaming where an individual user selects and views content at a time of their own choosing, which may be governed by the broader 'communication to the public' concept rather than 'broadcast' specifically.
Performance of a work in a physical public place (such as a concert or cinema screening) without any wireless or wired diffusion to a remote audience.
Delivery of a lecture or speech in person to a live audience without any simultaneous wireless or wired transmission.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a transmission qualifies as a 'broadcast' directly determines the existence and enforceability of broadcast reproduction rights under Section 37, performer's rights under Section 38A, and statutory licensing obligations under Sections 31 and 31D, meaning broadcasters must obtain licences and pay royalties for works they broadcast, and broadcasting organisations acquire their own protectable rights in their broadcasts. Misuse or unauthorised reproduction of a broadcast can trigger liability under Section 65B relating to protection of technological measures and rights management information.

definitions.definition: The term 'broadcast reproduction right' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957, but is used in Sections 37 and 39 to denote the special right vested in a broadcasting organisation by virtue of Section 37, being the exclusive right to re-broadcast the broadcast, cause the broadcast to be heard or seen by the public on payment of charges, or make any sound recording or visual recording of the broadcast, or to make any reproduction of such sound recording or visual recording where such initial recording was done without licence or where it is used for purposes different from those for which the licence was given.
definitions.plain_english: A broadcast reproduction right is a special legal protection given to radio and television broadcasters in India that allows them to control how their broadcast content is reused by others. It means that if a broadcaster airs a programme, no one else can re-broadcast it, play it publicly for a paying audience, or make recordings of it without permission. This right is separate from the copyright in the actual songs, scripts, or films being broadcast — it protects the act of broadcasting itself.
real_world_examples: A regional FM radio station in Chennai broadcasts a live cricket commentary; another radio station cannot re-broadcast or record and replay that same commentary without the originating station's permission under its broadcast reproduction right.

Doordarshan telecasts a nationally televised Republic Day parade; a private cable operator in Mumbai who records the telecast and sells DVDs of it to the public would be infringing Doordarshan's broadcast reproduction right.

A private satellite TV channel like Star Sports broadcasts a live IPL match; a hotel in Bengaluru that records this broadcast and screens it on loop in its lobby for guests on a subscription basis would require a licence from the channel for its broadcast reproduction right.

All India Radio broadcasts an original musical performance; an ed-tech company that records this broadcast and uses the recording in its paid online courses without permission would be infringing AIR's broadcast reproduction right.

A news channel like NDTV broadcasts a live interview with a politician; another news channel that re-broadcasts the same interview in its own prime-time bulletin without consent would be violating NDTV's broadcast reproduction right.
what_it_covers: The right of a broadcasting organisation to prevent others from re-broadcasting its broadcast without authorisation.
The right to control any sound recording or visual recording made of a broadcast by a third party.
The right to prevent public performance or display of a broadcast to an audience that pays charges, such as screening in cinema halls or paid public venues.
The right to prevent reproduction of any recording of the broadcast that was either made without a licence or used beyond the scope of the original licence.
Any communication to the public of a broadcast in a manner that was not originally sanctioned by the broadcasting organisation.
what_it_excludes: The copyright subsisting in the underlying works being broadcast, such as the literary work, musical work, or cinematograph film — those rights remain with their respective authors or producers.
Acts done for private and domestic use, as Section 39 carves out exceptions for fair dealing with broadcasts for personal use.
Re-broadcasting or recording done for bona fide teaching or research purposes that falls within the fair dealing exceptions provided under Section 39.
Performer's rights, which are separately governed under the Act and protect the individual artists whose performances may be included in the broadcast.
Any act authorised by the broadcasting organisation itself through a valid licence or assignment of the broadcast reproduction right.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a broadcast reproduction right subsists determines if activities such as re-broadcasting, public screening, or recording of a broadcast constitute an actionable infringement under Section 37, exposing the offender to civil remedies and criminal liability under the Act; if the right applies, the broadcasting organisation can seek injunctions, damages, and seizure of infringing recordings, whereas acts falling outside its scope — such as fair dealing under Section 39 — attract no liability.

Why it matters: Whether a broadcast reproduction right subsists determines if activities such as re-broadcasting, public screening, or recording of a broadcast constitute an actionable infringement under Section 37, exposing the offender to civil remedies and criminal liability under the Act; if the right applies, the broadcasting organisation can seek injunctions, damages, and seizure of infringing recordings, whereas acts falling outside its scope — such as fair dealing under Section 39 — attract no liability.

definitions.definition: A 'broadcasting authority' means any authority empowered to apply to the Appellate Board for a licence to produce and publish the translation of a literary or dramatic work or any text incorporated in audio-visual fixations prepared and published solely for the purpose of systematic instructional activities, for broadcasting such translation for the purposes of teaching or for the dissemination of the results of specialized, technical or scientific research to experts in any particular field, as contemplated under Section 32(5) of the Copyright Act, 1957.
definitions.plain_english: A broadcasting authority is an organisation or body that has the legal standing to apply for a special government-granted licence to translate and broadcast copyrighted works — particularly for educational or research purposes. Think of it as a body (like a public broadcaster) that can seek permission from a tribunal to translate a foreign textbook or scientific work and broadcast it to students or researchers. It acts as an institutional applicant, not an individual, and its broadcasting must serve teaching or the spread of technical or scientific knowledge.
real_world_examples: Doordarshan (Prasar Bharati) applies to the Appellate Board for a licence to translate a French-language scientific documentary series into Hindi and broadcast it for students enrolled in distance-learning programmes under IGNOU.

All India Radio (AIR) seeks a compulsory translation licence under Section 32(5) to translate and broadcast a foreign-published agricultural research text in regional languages like Tamil and Marathi to disseminate findings to farming communities and rural experts.

A state-owned educational broadcasting service such as the Rajasthan government's educational TV channel applies to translate and broadcast chapters of a foreign-published engineering textbook in Rajasthani for use in systematic instructional activities at polytechnic colleges.

The national educational broadcaster CIET (Central Institute of Educational Technology), functioning under NCERT, applies as a broadcasting authority to produce a Hindi translation of a UNESCO-published audio-visual fixation on climate science and broadcast it for secondary school teachers across India.

A public university-affiliated broadcasting unit recognised by the government applies to the Appellate Board to translate a Spanish-language medical research compilation into English and broadcast it to post-graduate medical students and specialists in India under systematic instructional activities.
what_it_covers: Government-owned or state-recognised broadcast organisations such as Prasar Bharati (Doordarshan and All India Radio) that apply for translation licences for educational broadcasting.
Institutional broadcasting bodies associated with universities or public educational systems that broadcast translated works specifically for systematic instructional activities.

Any authority empowered to broadcast translations of foreign literary or dramatic works or audio-visual fixations for disseminating specialized technical or scientific research results to domain experts in India.
what_it_excludes: Private commercial broadcasters such as private FM radio stations or entertainment television channels, as their broadcasting does not serve the requisite teaching or scientific research dissemination purpose.
Individual persons or private companies seeking translation licences for commercial publication or retail distribution, who must apply under sub-sections (1) or (1A) rather than sub-section (5).

Streaming platforms or OTT services that translate and distribute content for entertainment or profit, even if they occasionally carry educational programming, since they lack the statutory character of a broadcasting authority acting for teaching or research purposes.

Non-broadcasting entities such as publishers, libraries, or educational institutions that may use translated works but do not broadcast them, and therefore cannot invoke the specific rights available to a broadcasting authority under Section 32(5).
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'broadcasting authority' determines whether it can invoke the special compulsory licence route under Section 32(5) to legally translate and broadcast copyrighted works for teaching or research without the copyright owner's prior consent, subject to royalty payment conditions. Entities that do not meet this classification cannot access this statutory privilege and would require a direct voluntary licence from the copyright owner, failing which any broadcast of a translated work would constitute infringement under the Copyright Act, 1957.
