definitions.definition: A broadcasting organisation is any entity that transmits broadcasts to the public, whether by radio or television, and which holds or seeks rights in respect of such broadcasts, including the broadcast reproduction right under Chapter VIII of the Copyright Act, 1957. The term encompasses both domestic organisations transmitting from India and foreign organisations whose headquarters or transmitters are situated in countries to which the Central Government has extended the provisions of Chapter VIII by order.
definitions.plain_english: A broadcasting organisation is any company, body, or entity that sends out radio or television programmes to the general public. In India, this includes organisations like All India Radio, Doordarshan, and private TV or radio channels. These organisations have special legal rights over the content they broadcast, and they must also follow certain rules when they want to use others' copyrighted music, literature, or recordings in their broadcasts.
real_world_examples: All India Radio (AIR), a public broadcaster operated by Prasar Bharati, broadcasting classical music programmes nationwide — it qualifies as a broadcasting organisation and holds broadcast reproduction rights over its transmissions for 25 years.

Star India Pvt. Ltd. (now Star India), a private television network, broadcasting a cricket match under a statutory licence — it must pay royalties to copyright owners of any literary or musical works used, as required under Section 31D.

Radio Mirchi (Entertainment Network India Ltd.), an FM radio station, wishing to play Bollywood songs on air — as a broadcasting organisation it must give prior notice and pay royalties at rates fixed by the Appellate Board before communicating the sound recordings to the public.

Sony LIV or Zee Entertainment, a satellite television broadcaster, re-running a popular drama series — any third party who re-broadcasts this content without a licence from the broadcasting organisation infringes its broadcast reproduction right under Section 37.

A foreign broadcaster such as BBC World Service, whose headquarters is in the UK, being extended protection under Section 40A if the Central Government issues an order recognising UK broadcasters — it would then be treated as if it were an Indian broadcasting organisation for the purposes of Chapter VIII.
what_it_covers: Doordarshan and All India Radio as public service broadcasters transmitting to the public over terrestrial, satellite, or cable networks.
Private FM radio stations and satellite TV channels such as Radio City, Sun TV, or Zee TV that transmit programmes commercially to audiences across India.

Foreign broadcasting organisations whose headquarters or transmitters are located in countries to which the Central Government has extended Chapter VIII protections via an Official Gazette order under Section 40A.
Any organisation that re-broadcasts or communicates literary, musical, or sound recording works to the public under a statutory licence obtained pursuant to Section 31D.
what_it_excludes: Individual performers, musicians, or authors who merely perform or create works but do not themselves transmit broadcasts to the public.
Online streaming platforms such as Netflix or Hotstar that deliver content on-demand over the internet, which may not constitute 'broadcasting' in the traditional transmission sense under the Act.
Cable operators or DTH distributors who merely re-transmit signals of broadcasting organisations without independently originating or owning the broadcast.
A copyright society or collecting society that administers royalties on behalf of rights holders but does not itself engage in transmitting broadcasts to the public.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a broadcasting organisation determines whether it holds the special broadcast reproduction right under Section 37, giving it the power to prevent unauthorised re-broadcasting, recording, or public performance of its broadcasts for 25 years. It also triggers obligations under Section 31D — such as prior notice, royalty payment, and record-keeping — when the organisation wishes to broadcast published literary, musical, or sound recording works without individually negotiating with each rights owner.

definitions.definition: "Cinematograph film" means any work of visual recording and includes a sound recording accompanying such visual recording and "cinematograph" shall be construed as including any work produced by any process analogous to cinematography including video films.
definitions.plain_english: A cinematograph film is any recorded visual content — such as a movie, documentary, or video — along with any sound that accompanies it. It covers not just traditional celluloid films shot in a cinema camera, but also video films and anything made by a similar recording process. Essentially, if it is a moving image recording meant to be seen (and possibly heard), it qualifies as a cinematograph film under copyright law.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood feature film like a Dharma Productions release shot on digital cameras and released in theatres across India qualifies as a cinematograph film, giving the producer copyright protection over the entire audio-visual work.

A regional-language web series produced by an OTT platform such as Hotstar or Netflix India and streamed online is a cinematograph film, entitling its producer to exclusive rights of communication to the public.
A documentary on the 2023 Chandrayaan-3 mission produced by a Delhi-based production house and broadcast on Doordarshan is protected as a cinematograph film under the Copyright Act.

A wedding video recorded by a professional videographer in Mumbai and delivered to the client on a USB drive constitutes a cinematograph film, meaning copying or redistributing it without permission can amount to infringement.

A short promotional video advertisement produced for a FMCG brand and aired on Indian television channels is a cinematograph film, and unauthorised reproduction of that advertisement by a competitor would be an infringing copy.

Home-recorded video content uploaded by an Indian creator on YouTube — provided it involves original visual recording — can qualify as a cinematograph film, attracting copyright protection in favour of the producer.
what_it_covers: Feature films, short films, and documentaries produced using any camera or digital recording device and intended for theatrical, television, or online release.
Video films, including those recorded on VHS, DVD, Blu-ray, or digital formats, explicitly included by the definition through the phrase 'any process analogous to cinematography'.
The accompanying sound recording (dialogue, music, background score) that is part of the film, treated as an integral component of the cinematograph film.
Web series, telefilms, and digital content produced for OTT platforms where a continuous or episodic visual recording exists.
Advertising films, corporate films, and promotional videos that involve visual recording with or without accompanying sound.
what_it_excludes: A purely audio work such as a music album, podcast, or radio broadcast, which constitutes a 'sound recording' rather than a cinematograph film since there is no visual recording component.
A live theatrical performance or stage play that is not recorded, as there is no 'work of visual recording' in existence — it falls under 'dramatic work' or 'performer's right' instead.
Still photographs, even if taken in rapid sequence, since they do not constitute a 'visual recording' in the sense of a moving-image work as contemplated by the definition.
A dramatic work defined under Section 2, which is explicitly carved out and treated as a separate category distinct from a cinematograph film.
Computer-generated animations or video games considered purely as computer programmes or artistic works, unless they constitute a work of visual recording in the cinematographic sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as a cinematograph film determines the scope of copyright — including the exclusive rights under Section 14(d) to make copies, sell, give on hire, and communicate the film to the public — and fixes the producer as the first owner under Section 17. It also governs the term of copyright (Section 26: 60 years from publication), triggers performer's right obligations (Section 38A), anti-camcording protections (Section 52A), and defines what constitutes an 'infringing copy' attracting civil remedies under Section 55 and criminal liability under Section 63.

definitions.definition: The term 'citizen' is not independently defined in the Act but is used in the context of 'Indian work' under Section 2, which specifies that a literary, dramatic or musical work qualifies as an Indian work if the author is a citizen of India, or, in the case of an unpublished work, was a citizen of India at the time of making the work. 'Citizen' in this context refers to a citizen of India as determined under the Citizenship Act, 1955, or the Constitution of India.
definitions.plain_english: A 'citizen' in copyright law refers to a person who holds Indian citizenship. This is important because if an author is an Indian citizen, their literary, dramatic, or musical work may automatically qualify as an 'Indian work,' giving it protection under Indian copyright law. This applies both when the work is published and when it remains unpublished, provided the author was a citizen at the time of creating it.
real_world_examples: A Hindi novelist holding an Indian passport who writes and publishes a novel in New York — since the author is a citizen of India, the work qualifies as an 'Indian work' and enjoys full copyright protection under the Copyright Act, 1957.

An Indian-born musician who has acquired foreign citizenship and writes a composition abroad — since he is no longer a citizen of India, his work does not qualify as an 'Indian work' on the basis of citizenship, though it may still qualify if first published in India.

A student at an Indian university who is an Indian citizen creates an unpublished screenplay for a film school project — even though it has never been published, the work is an 'Indian work' because the author was a citizen at the time of making it.

A person of Indian origin (PIO) holding an OCI card but not Indian citizenship writes a literary work outside India that is not first published in India — their work does not qualify as an 'Indian work' on the basis of citizenship under the Copyright Act.

An Indian journalist working as a foreign correspondent in London who writes articles for an international publication — since the author remains an Indian citizen, the literary works are classified as 'Indian works' regardless of the place of publication.
what_it_covers: A person holding Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955, who authors a literary, dramatic, or musical work.
An Indian citizen author of an unpublished work who was a citizen at the time the work was created, even if citizenship status changes later.
An Indian citizen residing abroad who creates a work outside India — the citizenship link is sufficient to classify the work as an 'Indian work'.
A naturalised Indian citizen who writes a work after acquiring Indian citizenship, thereby qualifying the work as an 'Indian work' under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Foreign nationals who are not Indian citizens, even if they reside in India permanently — their works do not qualify as 'Indian works' on the basis of citizenship.
Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) cardholders and Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) who have not acquired Indian citizenship — they do not satisfy the citizenship criterion under this Act.
An Indian citizen who renounced citizenship before creating the work — since they were not a citizen at the time of making the work, the citizenship criterion is not fulfilled.

Artistic works such as paintings, sculptures, or photographs — the citizenship-based 'Indian work' definition under Section 2 applies only to literary, dramatic, and musical works, not artistic works.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an author qualifies as a 'citizen of India' determines whether a work is classified as an 'Indian work' under Section 2, which in turn affects whether copyright subsists in that work under Section 13 and whether the work is entitled to protections under Section 7 governing works of foreign authorship and international copyright relations. Misclassification could result in denial of copyright protection or incorrect application of reciprocal rights under international conventions to which India is a party.

definitions.definition: A 'collecting society' means a society registered under the Copyright Act for the collection and distribution of royalties on behalf of authors of literary or musical works included in sound recordings (not forming part of any cinematograph film), to whom authors may validly assign their right to receive royalties, as distinct from any other assignee. The term is used in Section 18 to identify the only permissible non-heir assignee of an author's royalty rights in such sound recordings.
definitions.plain_english: A collecting society is an officially registered organisation that collects money (royalties) earned from the use of an author's literary or musical work in a sound recording, and then distributes that money to the authors. Under Indian copyright law, an author of such a work can only hand over their royalty rights to either their legal heirs or a collecting society — no one else. This protects authors from being forced to give away their income rights to record labels or other commercial parties.
real_world_examples: A Hindi film lyricist whose song is included in an album (not part of a film soundtrack) assigns his royalty collection rights to the Indian Performing Right Society (IPRS), a registered collecting society, which then collects royalties whenever the song is streamed on Spotify or played on radio and pays the lyricist his share.

A classical music composer based in Chennai records an independent album with a music label. Under Section 18, the composer cannot waive his royalty rights in favour of the label; instead, he assigns those rights to a collecting society such as IPRS, which ensures he continues to receive 50% of royalties from any digital or broadcast use of the recording.

A music production company attempts to include a clause in its contract with a Punjabi folk singer requiring the singer to assign all royalty rights from her sound recordings exclusively to the company. This assignment is void under Section 18 because the only permissible assignees of royalty rights (other than legal heirs) are collecting societies.

An independent music publisher in Mumbai wants to ensure that royalties from a poet's lyrics used in a non-film album are properly managed after the poet's death. The poet, before passing away, had assigned royalty collection rights to a registered collecting society, which continues to collect and distribute royalties to the poet's legal heirs.

A regional language music aggregator approaches a collecting society registered under the Copyright Act to obtain licences for streaming multiple non-film albums. The collecting society, acting on behalf of the authors who have assigned their royalty rights to it, negotiates and issues licences and distributes the collected fees back to the respective authors.
what_it_covers: A society registered under the Copyright Act that collects and distributes royalties for authors of literary or musical works included in non-film sound recordings.
An organisation such as IPRS (Indian Performing Right Society) that acts as the sole permissible non-heir entity to whom authors may assign their royalty rights under Section 18.
Any duly constituted body authorised under Indian copyright law to manage collective rights on behalf of multiple authors of qualifying works, ensuring equitable distribution of royalty income.
The function of issuing licences to users (broadcasters, streaming platforms, radio stations) on behalf of member authors and remitting collected royalties to them.
what_it_excludes: A private music label or production company, which cannot be treated as a collecting society and cannot receive a valid assignment of an author's royalty rights under Section 18.

definitions.definition: 'Commercial rental' does not include the rental, lease or lending of a lawfully acquired copy of a computer programme, sound recording, visual recording or cinematograph film for non-profit purposes by a non-profit library or non-profit educational institution.
definitions.plain_english: Commercial rental refers to any arrangement where a copy of a protected work — such as software, a music recording, a video, or a film — is rented out or leased to someone in exchange for money or commercial gain. The law defines it by exclusion: it is any rental or lending that is NOT done for non-profit purposes by a non-profit library or educational institution. In practical terms, if a business charges customers to rent or borrow a DVD, game, or software copy, that is a commercial rental.
real_world_examples: A video rental shop in Mumbai charges customers ₹50 per day to rent a Bollywood DVD — this is a commercial rental of a cinematograph film.
A software company in Bengaluru leases copies of its accounting software to small businesses on a monthly fee basis — this constitutes commercial rental of a computer programme.
A music CD lending shop in Chennai rents out audio CDs of film soundtracks to customers for a fee — this is a commercial rental of a sound recording.
An online platform in Delhi charges a subscription fee to allow users to access and stream downloaded copies of films on their devices — this qualifies as commercial rental of a visual recording.
A gaming café in Hyderabad purchases licensed video game software and charges customers hourly rates to use the games — this is a commercial rental of a computer programme.
what_it_covers: Renting out DVD or Blu-ray copies of films to customers by a commercial video rental store for a fee.
Leasing or licensing copies of software to businesses or individuals by a commercial entity in exchange for periodic payments.
Charging customers to borrow or hire audio CDs, sound recordings, or music albums on a for-profit basis.
Any lending or rental of visual recordings or cinematograph films by a commercial establishment where profit or commercial gain is the purpose.
Subscription-based lending services that distribute copies of computer programmes or sound recordings to paying subscribers.
what_it_excludes: Lending of a lawfully acquired copy of a computer programme, sound recording, visual recording or cinematograph film by a non-profit library for non-profit purposes.
Lending or lending-out of such works by a non-profit educational institution for non-profit educational purposes.
Personal, private, non-commercial sharing of a lawfully acquired copy between individuals without any fee or commercial motive.
Sale or permanent transfer of a lawfully acquired copy of a work, as opposed to temporary rental or lease.
Streaming or broadcasting of works communicated to the public, which falls under 'communication to the public' rather than rental of a physical or digital copy.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an activity qualifies as 'commercial rental' determines whether the performer's special right under Section 38A — the right to receive equal remuneration from commercial rental of sound recordings — is triggered, and whether the copyright owner's exclusive right to authorise commercial rental under Section 14 applies, thereby making unauthorised commercial rental an act of infringement. If an activity is excluded from 'commercial rental' (i.e., non-profit library or educational institution lending), no such right or restriction operates, and no infringement or royalty obligation arises.

definitions.definition: Communicating to the public means making any work or performance available for being seen or heard or otherwise enjoyed by the public directly or by any means of display or diffusion other than by issuing physical copies of it, whether simultaneously or at places and times chosen individually, regardless of whether any member of the public actually sees, hears or otherwise enjoys the work or performance so made available.
definitions.plain_english: Communicating to the public means sharing a creative work — like a song, film, book, or artwork — with an audience by any method that does not involve physically handing out copies. This includes broadcasting on TV or radio, streaming online, playing music in a public place, or making content accessible on the internet. It covers both live and on-demand delivery, whether the audience receives it all at the same time or each person accesses it individually at their own chosen time.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood song is streamed on JioSaavn or Spotify to listeners across India — this constitutes communicating the sound recording to the public over a computer network.

Doordarshan broadcasts a live cricket match on national television, making the audiovisual content available to millions of viewers simultaneously — this is a classic act of communicating to the public by broadcast.
A multiplex cinema in Mumbai plays a film for a ticketed audience — projecting the cinematograph film in a theatre constitutes communicating the work to the public by way of performance.
A hotel in Delhi pipes background music through speakers in its lobby and restaurant, making musical works audible to guests — this amounts to communicating those works to the public.

An e-learning platform like BYJU'S makes recorded lectures and literary content available on demand to registered students across India — this constitutes communicating literary and dramatic works to the public via the internet.

A radio station like Radio Mirchi broadcasts a published musical work over FM frequencies to listeners in a city — this is communicating the musical work and sound recording to the public by way of radio broadcast.
what_it_covers: Streaming a Bollywood film on an OTT platform like Netflix India, making it available to subscribers on demand at their chosen time and place.
A live FM radio broadcast of a musical composition or sound recording to listeners across a geographic zone.
Public performance of a musical work at a ticketed concert or in a commercial establishment such as a restaurant, mall, or hotel.
Transmission of literary or artistic content over a cable television network to cable subscribers.
Making a literary work available on an educational website where students can access it at any time through a computer network.
what_it_excludes: Sale or rental of physical copies of a work (such as selling DVDs or CDs), since distribution of copies is not a communication to the public.
A purely private showing of a film or playing of music within a household with no members of the public present, as it does not involve making the work available to the public.
Issuing copies of a book or magazine to the public, which constitutes publication by distribution of physical copies rather than communication to the public.
Internal business communication where a copyrighted work is shared only among employees within a closed intranet not accessible to the public.
A one-to-one private email or message containing a copyrighted work sent to a single specified individual, as it is not directed at the public.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'communicating to the public' determines if the exclusive right of the copyright owner under Section 14 has been exercised or infringed, and whether a broadcaster must obtain a licence or comply with the statutory licence regime under Section 31D, including paying royalties fixed by the Appellate Board. Unauthorised communication to the public constitutes copyright infringement under Section 51, exposing the infringer to civil remedies and criminal penalties under Sections 55 and 63.

A Kolkata-based music app like Gaana or Spotify India making a licensed album available for on-demand streaming — where each user can choose when to play any song — is a communication to the public even if some users never actually play those tracks.
A university in Chennai broadcasting a live lecture over its YouTube channel so that students and the general public can watch it in real time is a communication to the public.

A news channel such as NDTV airing a documentary film during its prime-time slot, transmitted via satellite to cable operators and ultimately to television sets across India, constitutes communication to the public.

definitions.definition: In the context of the Copyright Act, 1957, 'company' means any body corporate incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 or any other law for the time being in force in India or in any other country, and includes a firm or other association of individuals. This definition is operative particularly under Section 69 which governs offences by companies.
definitions.plain_english: A 'company' under the Copyright Act refers to any legally incorporated business entity, such as a private limited company, public limited company, or similar body corporate. It also covers partnerships and associations of individuals that carry on activities as a group. This definition becomes important when a company itself commits copyright infringement, since the law can hold both the company and its responsible officers personally liable.
real_world_examples: A Bengaluru-based private limited company running a music streaming platform reproduces copyrighted songs without a licence — both the company and its directors can be prosecuted under Section 69 of the Copyright Act.

A Mumbai publishing house (registered as a public limited company) prints and distributes pirated textbooks — the company as an entity and the officer in charge are jointly liable for copyright infringement.
A Delhi-based partnership firm selling pirated software CDs in bulk is treated as a 'company' for the purposes of Section 69, making the managing partners personally liable alongside the firm.

A Chennai-based OTT platform incorporated under the Companies Act streams copyrighted Tamil films without authorisation — the CEO and managing director of the company face prosecution as persons responsible for the company's conduct.

An association of individuals running an unregistered business in Kolkata that photocopies and sells copyrighted academic journals commercially can be proceeded against as a 'company' under Section 69 of the Act.
what_it_covers: Private limited companies and public limited companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 or Companies Act, 2013.
Partnership firms and limited liability partnerships that commit or authorise copyright infringement.
Associations of individuals, whether registered or unregistered, that carry on commercial activities involving copyrighted works.
Foreign companies incorporated outside India but operating within Indian territory in a manner that infringes copyright.
One Person Companies (OPCs) and other body corporates recognised under Indian law.
what_it_excludes: Individual natural persons acting in their purely personal capacity, who are separately liable under other provisions of the Act.
Government departments and statutory bodies acting under sovereign functions, which may fall under 'Government work' provisions rather than company liability.
Non-profit trusts and charitable societies that are not incorporated as body corporates and do not conduct commercial trade or business involving copyrighted works.
Courts, tribunals, and other judicial authorities, which are distinct legal entities governed by separate statutory frameworks.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'company' under Section 69 is critical because it determines which entities can be criminally prosecuted for copyright offences — when a company commits an infringement, every person in charge of and responsible for the company's conduct is deemed guilty and can be imprisoned or fined, unless they prove lack of knowledge or due diligence. Without this definition, corporate entities could shield their officers from personal criminal liability for large-scale copyright violations.

definitions.definition: "Composer", in relation to a musical work, means the person who composes the music regardless of whether he records it in any form of graphical notation.
definitions.plain_english: A composer is the person who creates or originates a piece of music. It does not matter whether they write the music down on paper, in notation software, or simply keep it in their head — what matters is that they are the one who actually composed the musical piece. Under the Copyright Act, the composer is treated as the 'author' of a musical work.
real_world_examples: A R Rahman composing the background score for a Bollywood film such as Lagaan, making him the composer and therefore the author of that musical work under the Act.
A classical Carnatic musician in Chennai who creates a new raga-based composition purely through oral tradition and never writes it down in staff notation is still the composer of that work.
A Bollywood music director like Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy collectively creating an original soundtrack for a film, making each of them joint composers of the musical works they co-create.

An independent musician in Bengaluru who composes an original melody using a digital audio workstation (DAW) and uploads it to a streaming platform without ever producing a written score — that person is still the composer under the Act.

A folk musician from Rajasthan who orally composes a new devotional tune performed at a local festival, with no written notation, qualifies as the composer and thereby the author of that musical work.
what_it_covers: A person who creates an original musical composition and records it digitally without any written graphical notation.
A classically trained musician who composes a new piece using traditional Indian notation (sargam) or Western staff notation.

definitions.definition: A compulsory licence under Section 31B is a licence directed by the Appellate Board, on application by any person working for the benefit of persons with disability on a profit basis or for business, to publish any work in which copyright subsists for the benefit of such persons, where clause (zb) of sub-section (1) of section 52 does not apply; such licence shall specify the means and format of publication, the period of exercise, the number of copies that may be issued, and the rate of royalty payable to the owner of rights in the work.
definitions.plain_english: A compulsory licence is a government-granted permission that allows a person or organisation — even without the copyright owner's consent — to publish a copyrighted work in a format accessible to people with disabilities, such as Braille or audio. The Copyright Board (Appellate Board) can issue this licence after verifying the applicant's credentials and giving the copyright owner a fair hearing. The licence comes with conditions such as how many copies can be made, in what format, for how long, and what royalty must be paid to the copyright owner.
real_world_examples: An NGO in Mumbai that runs on a commercial basis applies to the Appellate Board for a compulsory licence to convert a popular Hindi textbook into Braille for visually impaired students, after the publisher refuses to do so.

A Delhi-based ed-tech company seeking to produce audio recordings of law books for blind law students applies for a compulsory licence under Section 31B when the copyright holder declines to grant permission voluntarily.

A Chennai organisation that creates DAISY (Digital Accessible Information System) format books for persons with print disabilities on a business model seeks a compulsory licence for a Tamil literary classic whose author's estate refuses to cooperate.

A Kolkata-based social enterprise that sells accessible-format books at subsidised rates to deaf-blind individuals applies for a compulsory licence to publish a medical reference guide in tactile graphics format after the copyright owner withholds consent.

A Pune technology startup building assistive software that embeds copyrighted educational content in screen-reader-compatible formats for dyslexic users seeks a compulsory licence when the publisher demands prohibitively high licensing fees.
what_it_covers: Applications by persons or organisations working for the benefit of persons with disability on a profit or business basis to publish copyrighted works in accessible formats such as Braille, audio, or DAISY.
Works in which copyright subsists — including literary, artistic, dramatic, and musical works — where the copyright owner has not voluntarily permitted accessible-format publication.
Licences that specify the format of publication, the duration of the licence, the number of copies permitted, and the royalty rate payable to the copyright owner.

Situations where the benefit of Section 52(1)(zb) — which grants a free-use exception to non-profit entities — is unavailable, typically because the applicant operates on a commercial or business basis.
what_it_excludes: Organisations or persons working for the benefit of persons with disability on a purely non-profit, non-commercial basis, who are instead covered by the statutory exception under Section 52(1)(zb) and do not need a compulsory licence.
Works not protected by copyright, such as works in the public domain, government works excluded from copyright, or works whose copyright term has expired, as no licence is required for such works.

Compulsory licences sought for the general public or for commercial exploitation unrelated to disability access — such licences for withheld works or unpublished works are governed separately by Sections 31 and 31A respectively.
Applications made in bad faith or by applicants whose credentials cannot be established to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board upon inquiry under sub-section (2) of Section 31B.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a compulsory licence under Section 31B applies determines whether a business-oriented organisation can legally reproduce and distribute a copyrighted work for persons with disabilities without the copyright owner's consent; without such a licence, doing so would constitute copyright infringement under the Act, exposing the applicant to civil and criminal liability, whereas a granted licence authorises the activity subject to the specified royalty and conditions, creating enforceable rights and obligations on both the licensee and the copyright owner.

definitions.definition: "computer" includes any electronic or similar device having information processing capabilities.
definitions.plain_english: A computer, under the Copyright Act, is any electronic or similar device that can process information. This is a broad definition that goes beyond traditional desktop or laptop computers to include any device capable of handling and processing data. It is intentionally wide to cover evolving technologies that perform computing functions.
real_world_examples: A software developer in Bengaluru writing code on a laptop — the laptop qualifies as a 'computer' under the Act, making the software a 'computer programme' eligible for copyright protection.

A Mumbai production house using a digital audio workstation (DAW) on a dedicated hardware unit to compose music — the DAW hardware device qualifies as a computer since it processes digital audio information.

A Delhi e-commerce firm using servers in a data centre to host its website — those servers are computers under the Act, and any software running on them attracts copyright protection as a computer programme.

A student in Chennai using a smartphone to run an educational app — the smartphone, being an electronic device with information processing capabilities, qualifies as a computer, bringing app software within the ambit of copyright protection.

A manufacturing unit in Pune using a Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) to automate assembly lines — the PLC, as an electronic device capable of processing instructions, falls within the definition of a computer under the Act.
what_it_covers: Desktop computers, laptops, and workstations used for creating, storing, or processing copyrightable works.
Smartphones and tablets that run software or applications, as they are electronic devices with information processing capabilities.
Servers, mainframes, and cloud computing hardware used by businesses and institutions in India.
Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and embedded systems used in industrial or automated settings.
Digital audio workstations, video editing hardware consoles, and other specialised electronic devices that process information.
what_it_excludes: Purely mechanical devices without any electronic information processing capability, such as a traditional typewriter or mechanical printing press.
Analogue recording equipment that does not have any digital or electronic information processing component, such as a reel-to-reel tape recorder with no electronic processor.
Simple electrical appliances like a conventional electric fan or light switch that perform no information processing function.
Non-functional replicas or models of computers that contain no actual electronic processing components.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'computer' is foundational to the protection of 'computer programmes' and 'literary works' (which include computer programmes and databases) under the Act — if a device qualifies as a computer, software created to run on it attracts copyright protection, and unauthorised copying or use of such software constitutes infringement under the Act. It also determines the scope of offences such as software piracy and the applicability of provisions relating to 'commercial rental' of computer programmes.

definitions.definition: A 'computer network' means an interconnection of one or more computers or computer systems through the use of satellite, microwave, terrestrial line, wire, wireless or other communication media, and terminals or a complex consisting of two or more interconnected computers or computer systems, whether or not the interconnection is continuously maintained, used for the purpose of communication, storage, or transmission of data and information. In the context of Section 65A, it refers to any networked infrastructure over which digital content protected under this Act may be accessed, transmitted, or against which technological protection measures are applied.
definitions.plain_english: A computer network is a system where two or more computers or devices are connected to each other — through cables, Wi-Fi, the internet, or satellites — so they can share data and communicate. Think of it as a digital highway linking computers together, whether within a single office building or spanning the entire globe as the internet does. In copyright law, it is the infrastructure through which protected digital content is distributed or accessed, and over which security measures guarding such content operate.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood production house deploys digital rights management (DRM) locks on its OTT platform (e.g., Netflix India, Amazon Prime Video India) to prevent unauthorised downloading; the servers, CDN nodes, and subscriber devices form a computer network over which Section 65A protections apply.

An Indian university's campus intranet connects hundreds of student computers to a central library server hosting licensed e-books and journal articles; this intranet is a computer network, and circumventing access controls on that network to copy protected works triggers Section 65A liability.

A software company in Bengaluru distributes its proprietary application over a corporate VPN connecting offices across Mumbai, Delhi, and Chennai; this VPN constitutes a computer network, and bypassing the authentication layer to duplicate the software without authorisation would attract Section 65A.

A cybersecurity professional in Hyderabad is contracted by a fintech firm to test whether its internal payment-processing network (a computer network) has vulnerabilities in its technological protection measures; under Section 65A(2)(d), this authorised penetration testing is explicitly exempt from criminal liability.

An independent music producer in Chennai discovers that a torrent network — a peer-to-peer computer network — is being used to distribute his copyrighted album without authorisation by circumventing its encryption wrapper; he can pursue action under Section 65A against the circumventor.
what_it_covers: The internet as a global computer network over which Indian copyright-protected content is streamed or downloaded.
A private corporate intranet or VPN connecting multiple office locations in India, used to host and distribute licensed software or media.
A peer-to-peer (P2P) network infrastructure used to share files, including copyrighted music, films, or software, among connected devices.
A university or institutional LAN (Local Area Network) in India linking student and faculty computers to servers hosting protected academic content.
Cloud computing networks (such as AWS or Azure hosted in India) over which protected works are stored and access-controlled via technological measures.
what_it_excludes: A single standalone computer or computer system not connected to any other device or network, which would fall under 'computer system' rather than 'computer network'.
Physical storage media such as USB drives, DVDs, or hard disks used to transport data between computers that are not networked together.
Purely analogue communication infrastructure (e.g., traditional telephone landlines not carrying digital data) that does not interconnect computers or computer systems.
A human courier or postal system carrying physical copies of copyrighted works, which involves no digital networked transmission.
A single-user offline software environment where no network connection exists and no inter-computer communication is involved.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an infrastructure qualifies as a 'computer network' under Section 65A determines whether the criminal offence of circumventing technological protection measures applies to activities conducted over it, potentially exposing a person to up to two years' imprisonment and a fine; it also determines the scope of the lawful exemption for authorised security testing under Section 65A(2)(d), which specifically requires the owner's or operator's authorisation before testing a computer network's security measures.

definitions.definition: "computer programme" means a set of instructions expressed in words, codes, schemes or in any other form, including a machine readable medium, capable of causing a computer to perform a particular task or achieve a particular result.
definitions.plain_english: A computer programme is any set of instructions written in any form — whether in a programming language, coded format, or machine-readable form — that tells a computer what to do and how to do it. This includes everything from mobile apps and operating systems to scripts and embedded software. The instructions must be capable of making a computer perform a specific task or produce a specific outcome.
real_world_examples: A Bengaluru-based software company develops a payroll management application written in Java — the source code and compiled binary both constitute a computer programme protected under Indian copyright law.
An IIT student writes a Python script that automates data analysis for a research project; this script is a computer programme and its author holds copyright in it as a literary work.
A mobile gaming company in Pune releases an Android game; the underlying game engine code, level logic, and AI routines are all computer programmes attracting copyright protection under Section 14.
A fintech startup in Mumbai creates an algorithm for fraud detection deployed on bank servers; the algorithm expressed as executable code qualifies as a computer programme under the Copyright Act.

A firmware update distributed by a Noida electronics manufacturer for its smart TV remote control contains embedded machine-readable instructions — this firmware is a computer programme protected against unauthorised copying under Section 63B.
what_it_covers: Source code written in any programming language (C, Java, Python, etc.) that instructs a computer to perform operations.
Compiled binary or object code stored on any machine-readable medium such as a hard drive, ROM chip, or optical disc.
Embedded firmware programmed into hardware devices such as microcontrollers, routers, or medical equipment.
Mobile applications, operating systems, database management software, and utility programmes.
Scripts and automation tools expressed in interpreted languages that direct computers to execute specific workflows.
what_it_excludes: Mere ideas, algorithms, or mathematical concepts not expressed in any concrete instructional form — the unexpressed logic behind a programme does not qualify.
Data files, databases, or raw data sets that do not themselves instruct a computer to perform a task (though databases may separately qualify as compilations).
Hardware or electronic circuits that physically implement logic, as these are devices rather than sets of instructions.
User manuals, technical documentation, or flowcharts that describe a programme's function but are not themselves capable of causing a computer to perform a task.
A cinematograph film or sound recording that may be stored digitally but whose primary character is audiovisual rather than instructional to a computer.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as a computer programme determines the specific rights conferred under Section 14(b), including the exclusive right to sell or give on commercial rental any copy, and triggers criminal liability under Section 63B for knowing use of an infringing copy of a computer programme; it also affects moral rights under Section 57 and the scope of permitted acts under Section 52.

definitions.definition: A 'computer system' is not formally defined in the Copyright Act, 1957, but as used in Section 65A, it refers to any device or collection of devices, including input and output support devices, that contains computer programmes and other data and is capable of performing substantial computation, including numerous arithmetic operations or logic operations, without human intervention during the computation or operation. It encompasses the hardware, software, and data components functioning together as an integrated unit for processing, storing, or transmitting information.
definitions.plain_english: A computer system is essentially any machine or set of machines — like a laptop, desktop, server, or even a smartphone — that runs software and processes data. It includes all the physical components (hardware) as well as the programs and data stored on it. In the context of copyright law, it refers to the system whose security measures may be tested or whose technological protections may be interacted with.
real_world_examples: A cybersecurity firm in Bengaluru is hired by a software company to test whether its DRM (Digital Rights Management) server — a computer system — can be bypassed by unauthorised users, and they do so with the company's written authorisation under Section 65A(2)(d).

A government-authorised investigative agency in Delhi conducts a lawful investigation into piracy by examining the computer systems of a suspected illegal movie distribution network to gather evidence of copyright infringement.

A researcher at IIT Mumbai conducting encryption research uses a lawfully obtained encrypted copy of a software program and analyses the computer system running it to study vulnerabilities, which is permitted under Section 65A(2)(b).

A streaming platform in Mumbai employs a security team to regularly test the company's content delivery computer systems for weaknesses in its technological protection measures, ensuring that encrypted Bollywood films cannot be unlawfully extracted.

A state police cyber cell in Hyderabad, during a lawful investigation into software piracy, forensically examines the computer systems of a printing and duplication shop to determine whether circumvention tools were used to copy protected software.
what_it_covers: A standalone desktop or laptop computer used to store, process, or distribute copyrighted works such as software, films, or music.
A server or cluster of servers operated by a streaming service that hosts encrypted copyrighted content with technological protection measures applied.
An embedded computing device such as a set-top box or gaming console that runs proprietary software with built-in DRM systems protecting copyrighted content.
A cloud computing infrastructure owned or operated by an Indian enterprise where copyrighted data is processed and protected by access-control technologies.
what_it_excludes: A purely mechanical device or analogue machine that does not process digital data or run computer programmes, such as a traditional photocopier without digital storage.
A computer network itself, which is treated as a distinct concept under Section 65A (referred to separately as 'computer network') and defined independently in the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Human administrators or operators of a computer system, who are persons rather than the system itself, even if their actions relate to managing security of the system.
Non-electronic storage media such as printed books, vinyl records, or photographic film that contain copyrighted content but do not constitute a computing system.

definitions.definition: A contract of service, as used in Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to an employment relationship under which an author creates a work in the course of their employment with an employer, giving rise to an employer-employee relationship distinguished by control, supervision, and the obligation to serve, as opposed to an independent contractual engagement. Where a work is created under such a contract, the employer becomes the first owner of copyright in the absence of any agreement to the contrary.
definitions.plain_english: A 'contract of service' is essentially a regular employment contract where someone is hired as an employee and creates work as part of their job duties. In copyright law, this matters because when an employee creates something as part of their job, the employer — not the employee — usually owns the copyright to that work. It is different from hiring a freelancer or contractor, where ownership rules can be different.
real_world_examples: A staff journalist employed by The Hindu newspaper writes news articles and features as part of their regular job — the newspaper owns the copyright in those articles under a contract of service.

A graphic designer on the permanent payroll of an advertising agency in Mumbai creates logo designs and marketing materials during office hours as part of assigned tasks — the agency is the first owner of copyright in those designs.

A software developer employed full-time by an IT company in Bengaluru writes source code for a client product as part of their employment duties — the employer company owns the copyright in the code, not the developer.

A cinematographer employed on a fixed salary by a Bollywood production house shoots footage for a film as part of their employment — the production house holds the copyright in the footage under a contract of service.

A teacher employed at a CBSE school in Delhi is asked by the school management to write textbook content and educational materials as part of their official duties — the school, as employer, becomes the first owner of copyright in those materials.
what_it_covers: A full-time salaried employee who creates literary, dramatic, artistic, or other copyrightable works as part of their assigned job responsibilities.
A staff writer or journalist employed under a regular employment contract by a newspaper, magazine, or periodical proprietor who produces content for publication.

Any employee working under a master-servant relationship where the employer has the right to control not just the outcome but the manner and method of work, resulting in copyright vesting in the employer.
A permanent or fixed-term employee in any sector (media, IT, publishing, film) whose employment terms require creation of copyrightable works as part of core duties.
what_it_excludes: Freelancers or independent contractors engaged for a specific project without an ongoing employer-employee relationship, as they operate under a contract for service, not a contract of service.
Authors who create works on their own initiative, outside of their employment duties and without direction from an employer, even if they happen to be employed elsewhere.
Persons engaged under apprenticeship agreements, which are treated separately and distinctly from contracts of service in the proviso to Section 17.
Works commissioned from an external creator (such as a portrait or photograph) at the instance of a person, which fall under a separate clause in Section 17 governing commissioned works.

Addresses or speeches delivered in public by an employee, where Section 17 expressly carves out an exception and vests copyright in the speaker or the person on whose behalf the speech is delivered, regardless of the employment relationship.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work is created under a contract of service is decisive in determining who holds the first ownership of copyright under Section 17 — if it applies, the employer owns the copyright by default, stripping the author-employee of ownership rights unless there is a contrary written agreement. This directly affects who may license, assign, enforce, or commercially exploit the copyrighted work, and determines standing in any infringement proceedings.

definitions.definition: The term 'conversion' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957, but is used in Section 58 in the context of civil remedies, where the owner of copyright or exclusive licensee is entitled to all such remedies by way of damages, injunction, accounts and otherwise as are or may be conferred by law for the infringement of a right; specifically, Section 58 provides that all infringing copies of any work and all plates used or intended to be used for the production of such infringing copies shall be deemed to be the property of the owner of the copyright, who may take proceedings for the recovery of possession thereof or in respect of the conversion thereof.
definitions.plain_english: Conversion, in the context of Indian copyright law, refers to the civil wrong of wrongfully taking or using another person's property — specifically infringing copies of a work or plates used to make them — as if it were your own, without the copyright owner's permission. Under Section 58, the copyright owner is treated as the legal owner of all infringing copies and production plates, so if someone else holds or uses them, the copyright owner can sue for 'conversion' just like suing for theft of their personal property. This gives the copyright owner an additional powerful civil remedy beyond just suing for copyright infringement.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based printing press produces thousands of pirated copies of a bestselling Hindi novel without the publisher's consent. The publisher, as copyright owner, treats those pirated books as their own property under Section 58 and sues the printer for conversion, claiming the value of all infringing copies in their possession.

A Mumbai music label discovers that a local CD manufacturer has pressed unauthorised copies of their sound recordings using duplicate stamper plates. The label files a conversion claim under Section 58, seeking recovery of both the infringing CDs and the stamper plates used to produce them.

A Bengaluru software company finds that a reseller is distributing pirated copies of their proprietary accounting software on DVDs. The company invokes Section 58 and initiates proceedings for conversion to recover the infringing DVDs and any duplicating equipment used, treating all such materials as their property.

A Kolkata film production house discovers that a local vendor is selling unauthorised DVD copies of their recently released Bengali film at a local market. The production house brings a conversion action under Section 58, seeking damages equivalent to the market value of all infringing copies seized from the vendor.

A Chennai-based textbook publisher learns that a photocopying shop near a university has been reproducing entire chapters of their protected textbooks using industrial photocopiers and selling them to students. The publisher pursues a conversion remedy under Section 58, claiming ownership over all infringing printed copies and seeking their recovery along with damages.

what_it_covers: Infringing copies of any copyrighted work (books, films, software, music recordings) that are wrongfully held or dealt with by a person other than the copyright owner.
Plates, stampers, moulds, duplicating equipment, or other tools used or intended to be used for the production of infringing copies of a work.

Any act of dealing with, selling, distributing, or retaining possession of infringing copies or production plates in a manner inconsistent with the copyright owner's rights, giving rise to a civil action for conversion.
Proceedings initiated by the copyright owner or exclusive licensee for recovery of possession of infringing materials or for compensation equivalent to the value of those materials.
what_it_excludes: Works or copies that are lawfully licensed or authorised by the copyright owner — such copies are not infringing and therefore cannot be the subject of a conversion action under Section 58.

Criminal proceedings for copyright infringement under Sections 63–65 of the Act, which are separate from the civil remedy of conversion and operate under different procedural and evidentiary standards.
Moral rights violations or claims relating to distortion, mutilation, or modification of a work under Section 57, which are distinct from the property-based remedy of conversion.
Conversion claims arising out of general property disputes unrelated to copyright, which are governed by ordinary tort law or the Transfer of Property Act and not by Section 58 of the Copyright Act.

definitions.definition: "Copyright" means the exclusive right, by virtue of and subject to the provisions of the Copyright Act, 1957, to do or authorise the doing of any of the acts specified in section 14 in respect of a work or any substantial part thereof, including the rights to reproduce, issue copies, perform, translate, adapt, or communicate the work to the public.
definitions.plain_english: Copyright is a legal right that gives the creator of an original work — such as a book, song, film, painting, or software — exclusive control over how that work is used, copied, distributed, performed, or adapted. No one else can do these things without the creator's permission, unless the law specifically allows it. This protection exists automatically once the work is created and does not require formal registration, though registration provides additional legal advantages.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based novelist writes and publishes a Hindi novel; she holds the copyright and can stop a publisher in Delhi from reprinting the novel without her consent or payment of royalties.
A Bengaluru software company develops a proprietary accounting application; copyright in the computer programme prevents competitors from copying and redistributing the source code without a licence.
A Chennai film production house produces a Tamil feature film; it holds copyright in the cinematograph film and can take legal action against websites that stream or sell pirated DVDs of the film.
A Bollywood music composer creates an original score for a film; he retains copyright in the musical work and is entitled to royalties whenever the song is broadcast on radio stations across India.

A Hyderabad-based graphic designer creates an original logo for a client; the copyright in the artistic work initially vests in the designer and can only be transferred to the client through a written assignment.
An academic textbook author at Delhi University holds copyright in the literary work, enabling her to authorise or refuse translation of the book into regional Indian languages by a publisher.
what_it_covers: The exclusive right to reproduce a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work in any material form including digital storage.
The exclusive right to issue copies of a cinematograph film or sound recording to the public.
The exclusive right to perform or communicate a work to the public, including broadcast, streaming, or public recitation.
The exclusive right to make any translation or adaptation of the original work.
The exclusive right to sell or give on commercial rental any copy of a computer programme or sound recording.
The exclusive right to include a work or part thereof in any cinematograph film or sound recording.
what_it_excludes: Ideas, procedures, methods of operation, or mathematical concepts in themselves — copyright protects expression, not underlying ideas.
Works whose copyright term has expired and which have entered the public domain under the Act.
Acts specifically permitted under the fair dealing, compulsory licence, or other exceptions enumerated in sections 52 and related provisions of the Act.
Designs capable of being registered under the Designs Act, 2000, that have been applied industrially to articles more than fifty times, which are excluded from copyright protection under section 15.
News of the day or miscellaneous facts having the character of mere items of press information, which do not attract copyright protection as original works.
Government works where copyright vests in the Government and private persons have no independent copyright, unless otherwise assigned.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work is protected by copyright determines whether unauthorised reproduction, distribution, performance, or communication of that work constitutes civil infringement under section 51 or a criminal offence under section 63 of the Act, attracting injunctions, damages, accounts of profits, seizure of infringing copies, and imprisonment. Conversely, once the definition applies, it triggers obligations for licensees, copyright societies, and broadcasting organisations regarding royalty payments, compulsory licences, and registration requirements.

definitions.definition: The Copyright Office is the office established under Section 9 of the Copyright Act, 1957, for the purposes of the Act, under the immediate control of the Registrar of Copyrights, who acts under the superintendence and direction of the Central Government, and which maintains the Register of Copyrights and indexes thereof.
definitions.plain_english: The Copyright Office is the official government office in India set up to administer copyright-related matters. It is headed by the Registrar of Copyrights and operates under the Central Government's supervision. It maintains official records of copyrights, processes registrations, handles relinquishments, and publishes relevant notices. Think of it as the central registry and administrative hub for all copyright matters in India.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music composer in Mumbai registers her original soundtrack with the Copyright Office in New Delhi, which then enters the work's details into the Register of Copyrights for public record.

A Delhi-based software company files a copyright registration application for its proprietary code at the Copyright Office, receiving an official certificate of registration bearing the Copyright Office seal.

An author in Chennai relinquishes her rights to a published novel by sending notice to the Registrar of Copyrights; the Copyright Office then publishes the notice in the Official Gazette and posts it on its official website for public access for at least three years.
A Kolkata publishing house consults the Copyright Office's indexes and Register of Copyrights to verify ownership details before entering into a licensing agreement for a literary work.

A Pune-based graphic designer disputes ownership of an artistic work; the Copyright Office's official records serve as prima facie evidence in the district court proceedings regarding authorship and registration.

A foreign film production company seeks to verify whether an Indian cinematograph film is already registered by querying the Register of Copyrights maintained at the Copyright Office before acquiring distribution rights.
what_it_covers: The physical and administrative office established under Section 9 of the Copyright Act, 1957, headed by the Registrar of Copyrights and operating under Central Government direction.
The maintenance and custody of the Register of Copyrights and prescribed indexes containing names, titles of works, and details of authors, publishers and copyright owners.
The official website of the Copyright Office on which relinquishment notices are posted and kept in the public domain for a minimum of three years as required under Section 21.
The processing of applications for copyright registration, receipt of relinquishment notices, and publication of such notices in the Official Gazette.
The official seal of the Copyright Office used on documents and certificates issued in the course of its statutory functions.
what_it_excludes: The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (now Commercial Courts / High Courts handling appeals), which is a separate statutory body and not part of the Copyright Office.
Copyright societies and collecting societies such as IPRS or PPL, which are private organisations registered under the Act and distinct from the Copyright Office.
State-level or district-level government offices, courts, or tribunals — the Copyright Office is a single central office and does not include any regional or state counterparts.
Private copyright registration services or agents who may assist in filing — they are not the Copyright Office itself and have no statutory authority.
The Patent Office, Trademark Registry, or other intellectual property offices established under separate statutes, which are distinct government offices with different jurisdictions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a body qualifies as the Copyright Office determines whether entries made in its register carry evidentiary weight as prima facie proof of ownership in infringement proceedings and disputes. Notices of relinquishment, registration certificates, and official publications derive their statutory validity only when processed through the Copyright Office, triggering or blocking rights and obligations under Sections 9, 21, 44, 46, and 48 of the Act.

definitions.definition: The 'copyright owner' in relation to any work means the owner of copyright in that work, being the person in whom the copyright vests — whether as the first owner by virtue of creation or authorship, or by assignment, testamentary disposition, or operation of law — and who holds the exclusive rights conferred by the Copyright Act, 1957 in respect of that work.
definitions.plain_english: The copyright owner is the person or entity who legally holds the rights over a creative work, such as a book, song, film, or software. This could be the original creator, or someone who acquired the rights through a legal agreement like a purchase, inheritance, or employment contract. Only the copyright owner (or someone they authorise) can legally reproduce, distribute, translate, or broadcast the work.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based author who writes and publishes a novel independently holds the copyright ownership over that literary work and must be contacted by any person seeking a compulsory licence under Section 32 to translate it into a regional language like Tamil.

A Bollywood production house such as Yash Raj Films, which has commissioned a film score from a composer under a contract of service, becomes the copyright owner of that musical work and must receive royalties if any broadcasting authority seeks a translation licence under Section 32B.

A Bengaluru software company that employs developers to build proprietary software owns the copyright in that computer programme and can grant or deny licences, or authorise publication of any adaptation or translation of the underlying literary work.

The legal heirs of a deceased Hindi poet who inherits copyright through a bequest under the poet's will become the copyright owners and are entitled to receive royalties determined by the Appellate Board if a compulsory translation licence under Section 32 is granted to a third party.

A university press in Hyderabad that publishes an academic textbook under an assignment agreement with the author becomes the copyright owner and is the entity that must be notified and offered an opportunity to be heard before the Appellate Board grants any compulsory translation licence under Section 32.

An independent documentary filmmaker in Delhi who has personally shot, directed, and edited a film owns the copyright in the cinematograph film and can authorise or refuse authorisation for any reproduction or translation of the work's incorporated text.
what_it_covers: The original author or creator of a work in whom copyright vests at first instance under Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957.
A person or entity that has acquired copyright through a valid written assignment from the original author, including a publisher or production company that obtained rights by contract.
Legal heirs, executors, or administrators who inherit copyright through testamentary disposition (bequest) or intestate succession upon the death of the original copyright holder.

An employer or a body corporate in cases where the work was created by an employee in the course of employment under a contract of service, making the employer the first and continuing copyright owner.
A collecting society or copyright society that holds assigned rights on behalf of members and acts as the copyright owner for the purposes of licensing and enforcement.
what_it_excludes: An exclusive licensee who holds a licence to exercise certain rights but has not received an assignment of the copyright itself — they are not the copyright owner.
A publisher who merely distributes or prints a work without having obtained a formal assignment of copyright — distribution rights do not constitute copyright ownership.
The general public or a compulsory licence holder who obtains a licence under Section 32 or 32B — a licence to translate or reproduce does not transfer ownership of the underlying copyright.

A performer whose performance is recorded — unless there is a separate assignment, the performer holds performer's rights but is not the copyright owner of the underlying literary, dramatic, or musical work.
A government body that merely funds a work without a contractual or statutory basis for copyright vesting — mere financial sponsorship does not make an entity the copyright owner.
definitions.why_it_matters: Identification of the 'copyright owner' is essential for triggering the mandatory notice, hearing, and royalty obligations under Sections 32, 32B, and 66 of the Copyright Act — only the copyright owner is entitled to receive royalties determined by the Appellate Board, must be given an opportunity to be heard before a compulsory licence is granted, and holds the standing to seek seizure of infringing copies or to authorise translations. Misidentification of the copyright owner can invalidate a compulsory licence application or expose a licensee to infringement liability.

definitions.definition: "copyright society" means a society registered under sub-section (3) of section 33.
definitions.plain_english: A copyright society is an officially registered organisation that collectively manages the rights of copyright owners — such as authors, musicians, or filmmakers — on their behalf. It issues licences to users who want to use copyrighted works, collects the fees or royalties for such use, and distributes the earnings back to the rights holders. Only a society that has gone through the formal registration process under the Copyright Act qualifies as a 'copyright society.'
real_world_examples: The Indian Performing Right Society (IPRS), registered under Section 33 of the Copyright Act, acts as a copyright society for musical composers and lyricists, licensing their works to radio stations, event organisers, and streaming platforms across India and collecting royalties on their behalf.

Phonographic Performance Limited (PPL India), registered as a copyright society, grants licences to hotels, restaurants, airlines, and FM radio stations to play commercially released sound recordings and distributes the collected fees to its member music labels and producers.

The Society for Copyright Regulation of Indian Producers for Film and Television (SCRIPT) is a copyright society that manages the rights of film producers and television content creators, allowing broadcasters to use their works upon payment of prescribed fees.

A Bollywood lyricist who is a member of a registered copyright society like IPRS does not need to individually negotiate with every FM radio station or OTT platform; the copyright society issues blanket licences on behalf of all its members and remits the collected royalties directly to the lyricist.

An independent visual artist wishing to collectively enforce their reproduction rights can join or form a copyright society registered under Section 33, which then monitors unauthorised use, issues licences to publishers and advertisers, and pursues infringers on the artist's behalf.
what_it_covers: A society of authors, composers, or other copyright owners that has been duly registered under Section 33(3) of the Copyright Act, such as IPRS for musical works.

An organisation registered under Section 33(3) that issues licences, collects fees, and distributes royalties for the public performance, broadcast, or communication of copyrighted works on behalf of its members.
A registered body that frames and publishes tariff schemes under Section 33A for licensing copyrighted works to users like broadcasters, streaming services, and public venues.

A society registered under Section 33(3) that is authorised to carry on the business of issuing or granting licences in respect of any class of works, such as literary, musical, sound recording, or dramatic works.
what_it_excludes: An unregistered collective or informal association of rights holders that has not completed the registration process under Section 33(3), even if it purports to manage copyrights collectively.
An individual copyright owner or author who manages and licences their own works personally, without forming or joining a registered collective society.
A private commercial licensing agency or talent management firm that negotiates individual copyright deals on behalf of creators but is not registered as a society under Section 33(3).

A foreign collecting society or performing rights organisation operating in another country (such as PRS for Music in the UK or ASCAP in the USA) that has not been registered under the Indian Copyright Act.
A trade association or industry body representing copyright owners for lobbying or policy purposes but not engaged in the collective issuance of licences or collection of royalties on their behalf.
definitions.why_it_matters: Only a registered copyright society has the legal authority under Section 33 to carry on the business of issuing licences in respect of copyrighted works on behalf of multiple owners; any person or body doing so without such registration commits an offence under the Act. The registered status triggers specific obligations and rights under Sections 33 to 36A, including the duty to publish tariff schemes, maintain accounts, submit to government oversight, and distribute royalties equitably to members, while also conferring standing to enforce rights collectively.
