definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 31C, 'cover version' means a sound recording made in accordance with that section, being a sound recording in respect of any literary, dramatic or musical work, where sound recordings of that work have been made by or with the licence or consent of the owner of the right in the work, produced under a statutory licence upon prior notice, advance royalty payment, and compliance with all prescribed conditions including medium, labelling, and non-alteration requirements.
definitions.plain_english: A cover version is a new audio recording of a song or musical work that has already been officially recorded before, made by someone other than the original copyright owner, but done legally under a government-granted licence. Think of it as a singer or music company re-recording a popular Bollywood song under a special legal permission without needing the original owner's direct consent. To qualify, the person making it must follow strict rules: pay royalties in advance, give prior notice, not change the lyrics or music without permission, and clearly label the recording as a cover version.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based independent music label re-records a classic Lata Mangeshkar song from the 1970s with a new singer and releases it on a streaming platform, paying advance royalties to the original music publisher at rates fixed by the Appellate Board and labelling the CD/digital release as a cover version under Section 31C.

A Punjabi music company produces a new bhangra-style sound recording of a popular Hindi film song originally composed by A.R. Rahman, gives prior notice to the copyright owner, pays royalties for a minimum of 50,000 copies, and does not depict or name the original singer on the cover art.

A devotional music label in Chennai re-records a Tamil Carnatic composition that was first commercially released in the 1990s, ensuring the new recording is in the same medium (digital audio file) as the last commercial release, and submits all required registers and books of account for inspection by the rights owner.

A Hyderabad-based music production house creates a new orchestral sound recording of a popular Telugu film song and applies for statutory licence under Section 31C, refraining from making any alterations to the original musical work and waiting until five calendar years have elapsed after the year of the first sound recording of that song.

An emerging Bollywood remix producer in Delhi re-records a 2010 Hindi pop song, pays royalties in advance for 50,000 copies as mandated, prints 'Cover Version made under Section 31C of the Copyright Act' on all packaging, and does not use the name or image of the original performer on any label or cover.
what_it_covers: A new sound recording of a literary, dramatic or musical work made by a person other than the copyright owner, provided prior sound recordings of that work already exist with the owner's consent or licence.

Re-recordings produced in the same medium as the last commercial recording of the original work, accompanied by advance royalty payment, prior notice, and compliant labelling clearly stating it is a cover version.
Sound recordings of a work where the minimum royalty has been paid for at least 50,000 copies per calendar year and no unauthorised alteration to the literary or musical work has been introduced.

A re-recording made after the expiration of five calendar years following the end of the year in which the first sound recording of the same work was made, ensuring the statutory waiting period is respected.
what_it_excludes: Sound recordings made without giving prior notice to the owner of rights or without paying royalties in advance, as these fail to meet the mandatory procedural conditions of Section 31C.

Re-recordings that alter the literary or musical work without the prior consent of the rights owner or without such alteration being technically necessary, since any unauthorised modification disqualifies the recording from being a valid cover version.

Sound recordings whose covers, labels, or packaging depict or name the performer of the earlier sound recording or any cinematograph film in which the original sound recording was incorporated, as this violates the anti-confusion and anti-misleading packaging requirement.
A new recording made within five calendar years of the end of the year in which the first sound recording of the work was made, since the statutory waiting period has not yet elapsed.
A re-recording made in a different medium from the last commercial recording when the original medium is still in current commercial use, as the medium-matching requirement has not been satisfied.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a recording qualifies as a 'cover version' under Section 31C determines whether the maker can exercise the statutory licence without obtaining direct consent from the copyright owner, thereby avoiding infringement liability; failure to satisfy the definition and its conditions exposes the maker to civil and criminal liability for copyright infringement, including injunctions, damages, and seizure of infringing copies, while compliance grants a legally protected right to commercially exploit the re-recording upon payment of Board-fixed royalties.

definitions.definition: "Design" as used in the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to the aesthetic or ornamental features of a work — including shape, configuration, pattern, ornamentation, or composition of lines or colours — applied to an article by any industrial process or means, being features which in the finished article appeal to and are judged solely by the eye. In the context of Section 15, it specifically refers to designs registrable or registered under the Designs Act, 2000.
definitions.plain_english: A 'design' here means the visual or decorative appearance of an object — how it looks, its shape, pattern, or colour arrangement — especially when that appearance is applied to manufactured goods. Under the Copyright Act, this term is important because if a design can be registered (or has been registered) under the Designs Act, copyright protection in it is limited or eliminated after it is applied industrially on a large scale. Essentially, the law prevents creators from using copyright as a backdoor to get indefinite protection for something that should only be protected as a registered industrial design.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based textile manufacturer creates a unique geometric pattern for printed sarees. The pattern, being applied industrially to more than 50 articles, loses copyright protection under Section 15 and must be protected, if at all, under the Designs Act, 2000.

A Pune furniture company develops a distinctive ornamental surface design for wooden chairs produced in bulk. Since this design is capable of registration under the Designs Act and is applied to over 50 articles, copyright in the artistic work ceases, making it a 'design' for purposes of Section 15.

A Delhi-based jewellery designer creates a hand-drawn sketch of a bracelet with a unique filigree pattern. As long as fewer than 50 articles are produced from it, the sketch retains copyright protection; once production crosses that threshold, Section 15 extinguishes copyright in the design.

A Bengaluru toy manufacturer applies a proprietary artistic pattern to plastic toy figurines manufactured in thousands. The pattern qualifies as a 'design' under the Designs Act framework and, having been applied industrially, the copyright in the original artistic drawing ceases under Section 15 of the Copyright Act.

A Chennai automotive parts company develops a decorative surface embossing pattern for car dashboard panels. Applied to mass-produced articles, this ornamental feature constitutes a 'design' triggering Section 15, meaning the company must rely on Designs Act registration rather than copyright for protection.
what_it_covers: Ornamental or decorative patterns applied to manufactured articles by an industrial process, such as printed textile patterns produced in bulk.
Shapes, configurations, or surface decorations of articles that appeal solely to the eye and are capable of registration under the Designs Act, 2000.
Artistic works originally protected by copyright that subsequently become 'designs' when applied industrially to more than 50 articles, thereby losing copyright protection under Section 15.
Architectural character or design features of buildings or structures as referenced in the definition of 'work of architecture' under Section 2 of the Act.
Colour compositions and line arrangements applied to industrial products, such as ceramic tile patterns or wallpaper designs produced at scale.
what_it_excludes: Purely artistic works such as paintings, sculptures, or drawings that are not applied to industrial articles and are not intended for mass production.
Designs that are not registrable under the Designs Act, 2000 — for example, designs dictated purely by functional or technical considerations with no aesthetic appeal.
Works of artistic craftsmanship that are hand-crafted and not reproduced by an industrial process, which continue to enjoy full copyright protection regardless of Section 15.
Literary, dramatic, musical, or cinematographic works, which are governed by separate copyright provisions and fall entirely outside the concept of 'design'.
Logos, trademarks, or brand insignia protected under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, which have their own distinct legal protection regime separate from both copyright and design law.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as a 'design' under this framework is critical because Section 15 of the Copyright Act extinguishes copyright protection in any artistic work that is also a registrable or registered design under the Designs Act once it has been applied to more than 50 articles by an industrial process — meaning the creator loses the right to sue for copyright infringement and must instead rely solely on Designs Act registration for protection. Misclassifying an industrial design as a pure artistic work (or vice versa) can result in either the loss of enforceable rights or an improper infringement claim being brought under the wrong statute.

definitions.definition: A 'developed country' under the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to a country that is not a developing country, i.e., a country which is not recognised as being in the process of economic development for the purposes of international copyright conventions and treaty obligations. In the context of Section 32, it signifies a country where a particular language is in general use and which does not qualify for the special concessions accorded to developing nations under translation licence provisions.
definitions.plain_english: A 'developed country' means a wealthy, economically advanced nation — such as the United States, United Kingdom, France, Germany, or Japan — that is not considered to be still developing its economy. In copyright law, this distinction matters because translation licences can be applied for more quickly (after just one year) when the translation language is not commonly spoken in any such developed country. Essentially, it separates rich nations from poorer ones to give developing nations easier access to educational and research materials.

definitions.plain_english: A developing country is a nation that has not yet reached a high level of economic and industrial development, as opposed to wealthy, industrialised nations. definitions.definition: "Director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm. In relation to a company, a director refers to any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company whose consent, connivance, or negligence is attributable to an offence committed by the company under the Copyright Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'director' under the Copyright Act is a person who holds a position of authority and responsibility within a company or firm. For companies, this includes directors, managers, secretaries, and other officers. For firms (like partnerships), a director means a partner. If a company breaks copyright law and it can be shown that such a person was involved or negligent, they can be personally held responsible and punished.
real_world_examples: A partner in a Delhi-based law firm that publishes pirated legal study material without authorization can be prosecuted as a 'director' under Section 69 of the Copyright Act, even if the firm itself is the primary accused entity.

The managing director of a Mumbai music production company that releases sound recordings by copying another artist's work without a licence can be personally held liable for copyright infringement under this provision.
A company secretary of a Bengaluru software firm that knowingly allows duplication and distribution of unlicensed computer programmes can be deemed a 'director' and prosecuted alongside the company.

A senior partner of a Kolkata advertising partnership firm that reproduces copyrighted artistic works in commercial campaigns without permission can be treated as a 'director' and face criminal liability under Section 69.

The production manager of a Chennai cinematograph film company who connives in releasing a film containing unauthorized musical compositions can be personally prosecuted as an officer of the company under this definition.

A partner in a Hyderabad book publishing firm who consents to printing and distributing unauthorized translations of copyrighted foreign literary works can be held liable as a 'director' under the Act.
what_it_covers: A partner in a partnership firm when the firm commits a copyright offence, who is treated as a 'director' for purposes of criminal liability.
A director, manager, secretary or other officer of a body corporate whose consent, connivance, or negligence contributed to the company's copyright offence.
Any senior officer of a company or firm who, though not directly committing the infringing act, held sufficient authority and whose negligence enabled the offence to occur.
A managing partner of a limited liability partnership (LLP) that engages in copyright infringement, as an LLP qualifies as a firm under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary employees or workers of a company who are not in a position of managerial authority or responsibility and did not consent to or connive in the offence.
A director or partner who proves that the copyright offence was committed entirely without their knowledge and that they exercised all due diligence to prevent it.
Shareholders of a company who have no active role in the management or conduct of business and did not participate in the infringing act.
Independent contractors or external consultants engaged by the company who do not form part of the company's internal management structure.
A sleeping or dormant partner in a firm who has no involvement in day-to-day business operations and no knowledge of or participation in the offending conduct.
definitions.why_it_matters: This definition determines who, beyond the company or firm itself, can be personally prosecuted and punished for copyright offences under Section 69; it extends criminal liability to individual partners and officers, making it possible for courts to impose imprisonment and fines on responsible persons even when the offending entity is a body corporate or firm. Whether a person qualifies as a 'director' under this definition directly triggers or blocks their individual criminal prosecution for offences such as infringement, unauthorized reproduction, or distribution of copyrighted works.

definitions.definition: Persons with disability as contemplated under Section 31B of the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to individuals who, by reason of any physical, sensory, or cognitive impairment, are unable to access or use a copyrighted work in its standard published format, and for whose benefit a compulsory licence may be sought to publish the work in an accessible format. The term is used in the context of enabling access to copyrighted works for those whose disability prevents enjoyment of such works in the manner ordinarily available to the general public.
definitions.plain_english: Disabled persons are people who have some kind of physical, sensory, or mental impairment that prevents them from reading or using a book, film, or other creative work in the way it is normally published. For example, a person who is blind cannot read a standard printed book. The Copyright Act allows special licences to be granted so that works can be converted into formats — like Braille or audio — that these individuals can actually use.
real_world_examples: A visually impaired student in Mumbai cannot read a standard printed textbook; an NGO applies under Section 31B for a compulsory licence to convert the book into Braille or a screen-reader-compatible digital format for the student's benefit.

A deaf individual in Chennai is unable to access an educational documentary film that lacks subtitles or sign-language interpretation; an organisation working for the hearing-impaired seeks a compulsory licence to produce a captioned version of the film.

A person with severe dyslexia in Delhi is unable to comprehend a standard printed novel; a disability support organisation applies for a compulsory licence to publish an audiobook version of the work for distribution among persons with similar reading disabilities.

A non-profit organisation in Pune working with persons having locomotor disabilities and who cannot handle physical books applies for a compulsory licence to create a digital accessible format under Section 31B so that affected individuals can use assistive technology to access the work.

An institution in Kolkata serving persons with visual and print disabilities applies to the Appellate Board for a compulsory licence to reproduce and distribute an accessible-format edition of a popular Hindi literary work whose publisher has not made any accessible version available.
what_it_covers: Visually impaired or blind persons who cannot access standard printed text and require Braille, large print, or audio formats.
Persons with hearing impairment who cannot access audiovisual works without subtitles, captions, or sign-language interpretation.
Persons with cognitive or learning disabilities such as severe dyslexia who are unable to process standard written formats of a work.
Persons with physical disabilities preventing them from handling conventional physical copies of books or other published materials.
Individuals whose combination of sensory and physical impairments makes it impossible to access copyrighted content in its originally published form.
what_it_excludes: Persons who merely prefer an alternative format for convenience but have no recognised disability preventing access to the standard format.
Organisations or intermediaries who seek to commercially exploit accessible-format works for profit rather than genuinely for the benefit of disabled persons.
Persons with temporary or minor ailments (such as a short-term eye infection) that do not constitute a substantive disability impairing access to copyrighted works.
General members of the public seeking access to works in alternative formats without any disability-related need.
Situations already covered by clause (zb) of sub-section (1) of Section 52, which falls outside the Section 31B compulsory licence regime entirely.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a beneficiary qualifies as a disabled person determines whether a compulsory licence under Section 31B can be validly sought and granted, thereby overriding the copyright owner's exclusive rights to control reproduction and publication of the work. If the definition does not apply, the applicant cannot invoke Section 31B and must instead obtain a voluntary licence or rely on a separate fair dealing exception, failing which reproduction of the work would constitute infringement of copyright.

definitions.definition: Distortion, in the context of a performer's moral rights under Section 38B and an author's special rights under Section 57, refers to any alteration, misrepresentation, or deformation of a performance or work that changes its essential character or meaning in a manner that is prejudicial to the performer's or author's reputation or honour. The term is used conjunctively with 'mutilation' and 'modification' to cover a spectrum of unauthorised alterations that damage the integrity of a performance or work.
definitions.plain_english: Distortion means any change or alteration made to an artistic performance or creative work that twists, warps, or misrepresents it in a way that harms the reputation or standing of the performer or author. Think of it as someone changing your work so significantly that it no longer reflects what you intended, and that change damages how people see you professionally or personally. It is not just any edit — it has to be the kind of change that would genuinely hurt your reputation.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood playback singer's recorded song is digitally altered to include offensive lyrics or distorted vocal effects, making it appear the singer supports a controversial message, thereby damaging their public image.

A classical Bharatanatyam dancer's live performance video is manipulated using deepfake technology to show them performing vulgar gestures, and the doctored video is circulated online without their consent.

A celebrated Indian novelist's literary work is translated and republished with the plot altered to portray the protagonist's community in a derogatory manner, contrary to the original intent of the author.

A street theatre performance by a well-known folk artist from Rajasthan is re-edited and broadcast on a regional TV channel with satirical commentary overlaid, making the performance appear mocking or politically offensive in a way the performer never intended.

An independent Marathi film director's cinematic work is re-cut and released on a streaming platform with entire scenes rearranged, fundamentally changing the narrative and creating a false impression of the director's artistic vision.
what_it_covers: Digital manipulation of a performer's recorded performance that alters its meaning in a way that harms the performer's professional reputation.
Alteration of an author's literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work that misrepresents the creator's intent and is prejudicial to their honour.
Re-editing or re-dubbing of a film performance to introduce elements offensive to the performer's community or contrary to their known public values.
Superimposition of misleading visuals or audio on a performer's recorded performance that creates a false and damaging impression of the performer.
what_it_excludes: Mere removal of a portion of a performance for the purpose of editing or to fit the recording within a limited duration, as expressly clarified under Section 38B.
Technical modifications to a performance or work that are required purely for technical reasons, such as format conversion or compression for broadcasting purposes.
Adaptation of a computer programme that falls within the scope of Section 52(1)(aa), in respect of which the author has no right to restrain or claim damages under Section 57.
Failure to display a work or displaying it in a manner not satisfactory to the author, which is explicitly excluded from constituting an infringement under Section 57.
Edits made to a performance with the informed consent and approval of the performer, as voluntary authorisation negates the claim of prejudicial distortion.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'distortion' determines if a performer or author can invoke their moral rights under Sections 38B or 57 respectively to restrain the act or claim damages, even after having fully assigned their copyright to another party. A finding of distortion that is prejudicial to reputation triggers the right to seek injunctive relief and monetary compensation independently of any economic rights in the work.

Examples: A Bollywood playback singer's recorded song is digitally altered to include offensive lyrics or distorted vocal effects, making it appear the singer supports a controversial message, thereby damaging their public image. | A classical Bharatanatyam dancer's live performance video is manipulated using deepfake technology to show them performing vulgar gestures, and the doctored video is circulated online without their consent. | A celebrated Indian novelist's literary work is translated and republished with the plot altered to portray the protagonist's community in a derogatory manner, contrary to the original intent of the author. | A street theatre performance by a well-known folk artist from Rajasthan is re-edited and broadcast on a regional TV channel with satirical commentary overlaid, making the performance appear mocking or politically offensive in a way the performer never intended. | An independent Marathi film director's cinematic work is re-cut and released on a streaming platform with entire scenes rearranged, fundamentally changing the narrative and creating a false impression of the director's artistic vision.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 62, a 'district court having jurisdiction' means a district court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction, at the time of the institution of the suit or other civil proceeding, the person instituting the suit or other proceeding, or where there are more than one such persons, any of them, actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 or any other law for the time being in force.
definitions.plain_english: A 'district court' in copyright law refers to the civil court at the district level that has the power to hear copyright infringement cases. What makes this special is that the copyright owner can file the case in the district court where they themselves live, work, or run their business — not just where the infringer is located. This gives the person whose rights have been violated the convenience of suing from their home location.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based author whose novel is reproduced without permission by a publisher in Delhi can file an infringement suit in the District Court at Mumbai (where the author resides), rather than being forced to travel to Delhi to sue the infringer.

A Bengaluru-based software company whose computer programme is pirated by a firm in Hyderabad can institute a copyright infringement suit in the District Court of Bengaluru where the company carries on its business.

A freelance graphic designer from Pune who personally works for gain in Pune can file a suit in the District Court at Pune against an advertising agency in Chennai that has used her artistic work without authorisation.

A music composer based in Chennai whose sound recording is illegally distributed online by a party in Kolkata can choose to file the civil proceeding in the District Court of Chennai, where she personally works for gain, invoking the special jurisdictional rule under Section 62.

A Bollywood production house headquartered in Mumbai whose cinematograph film is pirated in multiple cities can file a single suit in the District Court of Mumbai, leveraging its place of business as the jurisdictional anchor under the Copyright Act.
what_it_covers: A district court in the city or district where the plaintiff (copyright owner or exclusive licensee) actually and voluntarily resides at the time of filing the suit.
A district court in the location where the plaintiff carries on business, such as where a publishing house, software company, or film production company has its principal place of business.

A district court where any one of multiple co-plaintiffs (such as co-authors or joint copyright owners) resides, works, or carries on business — enabling filing at any one of several possible locations.
A district court where the plaintiff personally works for gain, covering freelancers, individual artists, composers, or performers who earn their livelihood from a particular location.
what_it_excludes: High Courts exercising original civil jurisdiction (such as the Bombay, Delhi, Calcutta, or Madras High Courts), which are governed by separate jurisdictional rules and do not fall within the definition of 'district court' under this provision.

A district court located solely where the defendant infringer resides, carries on business, or where the infringing act occurred, if the plaintiff has no connection to that district — the provision does not require the plaintiff to sue only at the defendant's location.

Consumer forums, criminal courts, or tribunals, which are not 'district courts' in the civil procedural sense and do not exercise jurisdiction over copyright infringement civil suits under Section 62.

District courts in locations where the plaintiff's residence or business presence is temporary, constructive, or involuntary — the Act requires the plaintiff to 'actually and voluntarily' reside or work in that jurisdiction.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'district court having jurisdiction' determines which court can validly entertain a copyright infringement suit; filing in a court without jurisdiction renders the suit liable to dismissal or transfer. It expands the plaintiff's choice of forum beyond the ordinary CPC rules, meaning a copyright owner who fails to invoke Section 62 correctly may lose the procedural advantage of suing in their home district, while a defendant may challenge territorial jurisdiction if the plaintiff's connection to the chosen district is not genuine.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of the Copyright Act, a body corporate shall be deemed to be domiciled in India if it is incorporated under any law in force in India. In the case of an individual, domicile refers to the country in which a person has their permanent home or legal residence, and where the making of an unpublished work is extended over a considerable period, the author is deemed domiciled in the country wherein he was domiciled during any substantial part of that period.
definitions.plain_english: Domicile means the country or place that a person or company officially 'belongs to' as their permanent legal home. For companies, this is simply the country where they were registered or incorporated. For individual authors, it is the country where they permanently live or reside. This concept matters in copyright law because it determines whether an author or company is entitled to copyright protection under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A publishing company registered under the Companies Act, 2013 in Mumbai is automatically considered domiciled in India, making its works eligible for copyright protection under the Copyright Act without needing to prove any further Indian connection.

An Indian author who lives and works in Germany for several years while writing a novel over a prolonged period is assessed for domicile based on whichever country she was domiciled in during a substantial part of that writing period, which could affect whether Indian copyright subsists in the unpublished manuscript.

The Central Government issues an International Copyright Order under Section 40 extending protection to works by authors domiciled in a particular foreign country (e.g., the UK), treating such domicile as equivalent to Indian domicile for the purposes of granting copyright protection in India.

A software company incorporated in Bengaluru under Indian law is deemed domiciled in India, so the computer programmes it develops are protected under the Copyright Act regardless of where its directors or shareholders actually reside.

A Bollywood music composer who was born in India but moved to Canada permanently is considered domiciled in Canada; if he composes an unpublished musical work, the domicile rule under Section 7 will determine which country's domicile applies during the substantial period of creation to assess Indian copyright eligibility.
An NGO registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act in Delhi is treated as domiciled in India, ensuring that artistic works it produces are covered by Indian copyright law.
what_it_covers: A company or body corporate incorporated under any Indian law (e.g., Companies Act, 2013), which is automatically deemed domiciled in India.
An individual author who permanently resides in India and is domiciled here at the time of making an unpublished work, qualifying the work for Indian copyright protection.
An author whose work is created over a long period and who was domiciled in India during a substantial part of that period, even if later residing abroad.
Foreign authors domiciled in a country to which a Central Government order under Section 40 applies, whose domicile is treated as equivalent to Indian domicile for copyright purposes.
A society, trust, or statutory body incorporated or established under Indian law, treated as domiciled in India for copyright ownership purposes.
what_it_excludes: A foreign company incorporated outside India that merely operates a branch office or has business activities in India — it is not deemed domiciled in India under Section 8.
An individual who is temporarily residing in India on a visa or short-term basis but whose permanent domicile is in another country — temporary residence does not constitute domicile.
A body corporate incorporated in a foreign country, even if it is wholly owned by Indian shareholders or has its principal place of business in India.

An author who was only briefly or incidentally present in India during a small, non-substantial part of the period of creating an unpublished work — such brief presence does not establish Indian domicile under Section 7.
A foreign partnership firm or unincorporated association that is not incorporated under any Indian law, which cannot claim Indian domicile under the Section 8 deeming provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an author or body corporate is domiciled in India directly determines whether copyright subsists in their unpublished works under Section 13, and whether protection can be claimed or extended under Section 40 through international copyright orders; if domicile in India is not established, the unpublished work may fall outside the scope of Indian copyright protection entirely, leaving the author or owner without legal remedies against infringement.

definitions.definition: An author of a work shall be deemed to be domiciled in a country if, during any substantial part of the period over which the making of an unpublished work is extended, the author was domiciled in that country. For the purposes of this Act, a body corporate shall be deemed to be domiciled in India if it is incorporated under any law in force in India.
definitions.plain_english: Being 'domiciled' in a country means that a person has made that country their permanent home or place of settled residence. For an individual author, domicile is assessed during the period when the work was being created. For companies and other corporate bodies, they are treated as domiciled in India if they were registered or incorporated under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A Punjabi novelist living and working permanently in Chandigarh writes a novel over five years. Even if he briefly visits Canada during that period, his domicile remains India, so his unpublished manuscript qualifies for copyright protection under the Copyright Act, 1957.

A software company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 in Bengaluru is automatically deemed to be domiciled in India, entitling it to copyright protection for its computer programmes under Indian law.

A Tamil filmmaker who is a citizen of Sri Lanka but has been living and working in Chennai for the last ten years while making a documentary is considered domiciled in India, making the unpublished work eligible for copyright subsistence in India.

An artist of Indian origin who has permanently settled in the United Kingdom and has made the UK her home creates a series of paintings over three years. She is domiciled in the UK, not in India, so her unpublished works would not automatically attract Indian copyright protection on the basis of domicile.

A foreign NGO registered and incorporated in India under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act for educational purposes is deemed domiciled in India for copyright purposes, enabling it to claim copyright in its unpublished training materials.

A Bengali author who migrated to Germany permanently mid-way through writing a novel would be assessed for domicile: if the substantial part of the writing period was spent in India before migration, Indian domicile applies for that work.
what_it_covers: An individual author who has established his permanent home and settled residence in India during a substantial part of the period over which an unpublished work was created.
A body corporate, such as a private limited company or a public limited company, that is incorporated under any law in force in India, including the Companies Act, 2013.

An author of mixed or dual nationality who was domiciled in India for a substantial part of the period during which a long-duration unpublished work (such as a multi-year research manuscript) was being made.
A foreign national who has made India their permanent home and centre of life during the relevant creative period, even if they retain citizenship of another country.
A cooperative society or other body corporate registered under Indian law that produces copyrightable works such as films or sound recordings.
what_it_excludes: An individual author who is merely visiting or temporarily residing in India on a short-term visa during the creation of a work, without having established a permanent home in India.
A foreign company incorporated outside India, even if it operates a branch office or has significant business presence in India, as it is not incorporated under any Indian law.
An author of Indian origin who has permanently emigrated abroad and established domicile in a foreign country, even if he occasionally visits India during the creative period.
A partnership firm or unregistered association that is not a body corporate and therefore cannot be 'domiciled' in India in the corporate sense under Section 8.
An author who was domiciled in a foreign country during the substantial part of the period of creating an unpublished work, regardless of Indian citizenship.
definitions.why_it_matters: The domicile of an author is a key qualifying criterion under Section 13 for copyright to subsist in an unpublished work in India — if neither citizenship nor domicile in India is established for the substantial part of the creation period, copyright does not arise under the Act. Similarly, under Section 42, authors not domiciled in India may be denied copyright protection if their home country fails to provide reciprocal protection to Indian authors.

definitions.definition: "dramatic work" includes any piece for recitation, choreographic work or entertainment in dumb show, the scenic arrangement or acting, form of which is fixed in writing or otherwise but does not include a cinematograph film.
definitions.plain_english: A dramatic work is any creative work meant to be performed, such as a play, a dance choreography, a mime act, or a piece written for recitation, as long as the form of the performance has been recorded or written down in some way. The key requirement is that the work must be fixed — meaning it exists in some tangible or recorded form — and it must be intended for performance. Movies and films are specifically not included in this category.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood choreographer creates a signature dance routine for a stage musical and notates it in a choreography script; this constitutes a dramatic work protected under copyright.
A Hindi theatre group in Mumbai writes and rehearses a stage play script based on an original story; the script and its scenic arrangement qualify as a dramatic work.
A classical Bharatanatyam performer composes and records (in notated form) a new dance composition for a public performance at a sabha in Chennai; the choreographic work is a dramatic work.
A mime troupe in Kolkata creates an original dumb show performance and records the sequence of acts in written form; this entertainment in dumb show is a dramatic work.

A poet writes and performs a structured piece for recitation at a literary festival in Delhi, with the text fixed in writing; the recitation piece qualifies as a dramatic work under the Copyright Act.
A street theatre group (Nukkad Natak) in Pune scripted an original social awareness performance and wrote down the acting form; that script and arrangement constitutes a dramatic work.
what_it_covers: A written stage play script including its scenic arrangement and acting directions fixed in writing.
A choreographic work such as a Bharatanatyam or contemporary dance composition that is notated or otherwise fixed in some form.
An entertainment in dumb show (mime performance) whose sequence and form has been recorded in writing or otherwise.
A piece written and fixed for public recitation, such as a spoken word performance or dramatic monologue.
A theatrical performance script with fixed acting forms used in Nukkad Natak or community theatre productions.
what_it_excludes: A cinematograph film, which is expressly excluded from the definition of dramatic work and is separately protected under the Act.
A purely musical work consisting only of music and graphical notation without any dramatic or acting element, which falls under the definition of 'musical work'.
An improvised live performance that has not been fixed in writing or in any other form, as fixation is a required element of the definition.
A painting, sculpture, or other artistic work that may depict a dramatic scene but is itself not a work intended for performance.
A sound recording of a dramatic performance, which is separately categorised and protected as a 'sound recording' under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as a 'dramatic work' determines the subsistence of copyright under Section 13, the identity of the first owner under Section 17, the specific rights granted (including performance and adaptation rights) under Section 14, and the applicable term of protection under Sections 22 and 24. It also governs which compulsory licensing provisions, fair dealing exceptions under Section 52, and infringement actions under Sections 51 and 55 are triggered or available.

definitions.definition: "duplicating equipment" means any mechanical contrivance or device used or intended to be used for making copies of any work.
definitions.plain_english: Duplicating equipment refers to any machine or device that is used, or is meant to be used, to make copies of a creative work such as a book, music, film, or artwork. This includes photocopiers, printers, recording machines, and similar devices. The term covers both equipment currently in use for copying and equipment that is intended for that purpose even if not yet used.
real_world_examples: A photocopier at a Delhi printing shop used to reproduce pages from a copyrighted textbook without the publisher's permission constitutes duplicating equipment under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'educational institution' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957. However, as used in Section 52, it refers to any institution established and recognised for the purposes of imparting formal education, including schools, colleges, universities, and other institutions of learning that are recognised by the government or a statutory authority, and whose primary activity is systematic instruction or academic teaching.
definitions.plain_english: An educational institution is any school, college, university, or similar place of learning that is officially recognised and whose main purpose is to teach students. This includes government schools, private colleges, universities, and polytechnics. Such institutions are given special permissions under copyright law because their activities are focused on learning and not on making a profit from copyrighted works.
real_world_examples: A government school in Rajasthan photocopies chapters from a prescribed NCERT textbook for students who cannot afford the full book — the school qualifies as an educational institution under Section 52, making such reproduction permissible.

IIT Bombay, a centrally funded technical university, reproduces journal articles and distributes them to students during a course — as a recognised educational institution, it can rely on the fair dealing exceptions under Section 52.

A CBSE-affiliated private school in Chennai performs a copyrighted play during its annual cultural function for students and teachers — this falls within the ambit of Section 52 exemptions applicable to educational institutions.

A state university in West Bengal records a professor's lecture and circulates it among enrolled students via an internal portal for examination preparation — being a recognised educational institution, it can do so without infringing copyright.

A polytechnic institute in Maharashtra, recognised by the state government under the AICTE framework, creates a compilation of short extracts from engineering textbooks for use in practical classes — this is covered by the educational institution exception under Section 52.

Kendriya Vidyalaya in Delhi broadcasts a documentary on Indian history over its internal closed-circuit TV system solely for classroom instruction — permitted because the institution qualifies as an educational institution under the Act.

Private unaided schools and colleges that hold recognition from a competent government authority and whose principal activity is the imparting of education.
what_it_excludes: Private coaching centres and tuition classes such as those preparing students for JEE or NEET, which are not formally recognised as educational institutions by any statutory authority.

definitions.definition: An effective technological measure means any technology, device, or component that, in the normal course of its operation, controls access to a work or protects any of the rights conferred by the Copyright Act, 1957, and that restricts acts not permitted by the right-holder. Such a measure is considered 'effective' when it achieves its intended protective function in restricting unauthorised access or use of the protected work.
definitions.plain_english: An effective technological measure is a digital lock or protection system that a copyright owner puts in place to prevent people from accessing or copying their work without permission. Examples include password protection, encryption, digital rights management (DRM) software, and region-coding on DVDs. The law protects these locks by making it a crime to break or bypass them with the intent to infringe copyright.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood production house releases a film on a streaming platform like Netflix India with DRM encryption that prevents downloading or screen-recording; breaking this encryption to pirate the film constitutes circumventing an effective technological measure.

An Indian music label distributes songs on a CD protected with copy-control software that prevents the disc from being ripped to MP3 files; a person who uses specialist software to bypass this copy protection to distribute the songs illegally circumvents such a measure.

An Indian educational publisher sells e-textbooks through a platform that uses access-control passwords and device-locking technology limiting use to one registered device; a student who cracks the DRM to share the e-book freely across multiple users circumvents an effective technological measure.

A software company based in Bengaluru ships its enterprise software with a hardware dongle and licence-key system that restricts installation to authorised machines; a competitor who reverse-engineers or bypasses this dongle protection to create unlicensed copies circumvents an effective technological measure.

A major Indian OTT platform like Hotstar uses region-locking and token-based authentication to restrict certain content to Indian subscribers only; using a VPN combined with tools that spoof authentication tokens to bypass this access control could amount to circumvention of an effective technological measure.

A graphic design firm in Mumbai sells digital artwork files embedded with encrypted watermark-based access controls that disable printing beyond a set number of copies; bypassing the encryption to enable unlimited printing would constitute circumvention.
what_it_covers: DRM software embedded in e-books, music files, or video content sold by Indian publishers and content platforms that restricts copying, redistribution, or format conversion.
Encryption systems applied to cinematograph films or sound recordings distributed on physical media (e.g., Blu-ray, DVDs) or digitally, which prevent unauthorised reproduction.
Access-control mechanisms such as licence keys, hardware dongles, and authentication tokens used by Indian software companies to limit use of computer programmes to authorised users.
Region-coding and geo-restriction technologies deployed by Indian and international OTT platforms to limit access to copyright-protected works to licensed territories.
Watermarking and fingerprinting technologies that embed invisible access restrictions or usage limits in digital artistic or literary works distributed in India.
what_it_excludes: Technological measures applied for purposes other than protecting rights conferred by the Copyright Act, such as purely commercial subscription paywalls that do not relate to copyright protection per se.
Circumvention carried out for lawful encryption research using a legitimately obtained encrypted copy, as expressly permitted under Section 65A(2)(b).
Acts of circumvention conducted for the purpose of testing the security of a computer system or network with the authorisation of its owner or operator, as permitted under Section 65A(2)(d).
Circumvention of technological measures intended for identification or surveillance of users rather than for protecting copyright, which is explicitly excluded from liability under Section 65A(2)(e).
Measures taken in the interest of national security under Section 65A(2)(f), which are entirely outside the scope of this provision's prohibitions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a protective mechanism qualifies as an 'effective technological measure' determines whether its circumvention triggers criminal liability under Section 65A, including imprisonment up to two years and a fine. If the measure does not qualify, circumventing it carries no criminal consequence under this section, even if other copyright infringement provisions may still apply.

definitions.definition: 'Engravings' include etchings, lithographs, wood-cuts, prints and other similar works, not being photographs.
definitions.plain_english: An engraving is an artistic work created by cutting, carving, or pressing a design into a hard surface like metal, wood, or stone, and then using it to make printed copies. This includes etchings, lithographs, woodcuts, and similar print-making works. Photographs are specifically not included in this category, even though they may look similar in final form.
real_world_examples: A traditional Indian artist in Jaipur creates a copper-plate etching depicting a miniature Mughal court scene and prints multiple copies for sale — each print is protected as an engraving under the Copyright Act.

A printmaker in Santiniketan produces woodcut prints inspired by Rabindranath Tagore's artwork using hand-carved wooden blocks; these woodcuts qualify as engravings and attract full copyright protection.
A lithography studio in Mumbai creates limited-edition lithograph prints of a Bollywood film poster for collectors — these lithographs are engravings within the meaning of the Act.

A craftsman in Varanasi produces silk-screen prints of traditional Banarasi motifs by carving designs onto a block and pressing them onto paper for commercial sale — these prints are protected as engravings.

An art institution in Chennai preserves 19th-century colonial-era wood-cut prints of Indian maps; when a publisher reproduces them without permission, infringement is assessed under the engraving provisions of the Act.

A contemporary artist in Delhi creates a series of mezzotint prints (a form of intaglio engraving) of Indian wildlife and exhibits them at a gallery — these are covered as engravings under copyright law.
what_it_covers: Etchings — works made by using acid to cut into a metal plate and then printing from it.
Lithographs — prints made from a flat stone or metal plate on which the image is drawn with a greasy substance.
Wood-cuts — prints made from a design carved into the surface of a wooden block.
Other similar print-works such as mezzotints, aquatints, screen prints, linocuts, and intaglio prints that are produced through analogous mechanical or manual processes.
Limited-edition hand-pulled prints produced from engraved or carved plates or blocks by traditional or contemporary printmakers in India.
what_it_excludes: Photographs — explicitly excluded by the statutory definition; photographic prints are governed separately under the 'artistic work' definition as 'photographs'.
Paintings and drawings — even if they depict similar imagery, freehand paintings or drawings are not engravings as they are not produced through a plate, block, or surface-cutting process.
Digital prints produced directly from a computer file without any physical engraved plate or carved block as an intermediate medium.
Cinematograph films or video recordings — these are governed under a distinct category of 'cinematograph film' in the Act.
Sculptures — three-dimensional works carved from stone, metal, or wood are protected as sculptures or works of artistic craftsmanship, not as engravings.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as an 'engraving' determines the authorship and first ownership of copyright under Section 17, as well as the duration of copyright protection under Section 25; it is specifically relevant to Section 24, which governs copyright in engravings and determines who holds the copyright when an engraving is made pursuant to a commission or contract. Misclassification can affect the assignment of rights, calculation of the protection period, and identification of the infringer in reproduction-related offences under Section 51.

definitions.definition: "Exclusive licence" means a licence which confers on the licensee or on the licensee and persons authorised by him, to the exclusion of all other persons (including the owner of the copyright) any right comprised in the copyright in a work, and "exclusive licensee" shall be construed accordingly.
definitions.plain_english: An exclusive licence is a special permission granted by the copyright owner to another person (the licensee), giving that person the sole right to use the work in a specific way — even the copyright owner themselves cannot exercise that right during the licence period. It is stronger than an ordinary licence because it locks out everyone else, including the original owner. The licensee can also authorise others to use the work within the scope granted.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music label (e.g., T-Series) grants an exclusive licence to a streaming platform (e.g., JioSaavn) to stream a film's soundtrack in India, meaning no other platform — not even T-Series itself — can stream those songs in India during the licence term.

A Chennai-based software company grants an exclusive licence to a Bengaluru IT firm to reproduce and distribute its accounting software in South India, preventing the original company from selling the software directly to South Indian customers.

A Delhi publisher grants an exclusive licence to a Kolkata publisher to translate and publish a Hindi novel in Bengali, so that neither the original Hindi publisher nor any third party can publish a Bengali translation during the licence period.

A Pune-based photographer grants an exclusive licence to an advertising agency to use a series of photographs for a national commercial campaign, barring the photographer from licensing the same images to any competing brand for the duration of the campaign.

A Mumbai film production house grants an exclusive licence to a foreign distributor to exhibit a Hindi film in the United States, meaning the production house itself cannot separately license the film to any other US distributor or exhibit it there independently.
what_it_covers: A licence that grants the licensee any one or more rights comprised in copyright (e.g., reproduction, distribution, communication to the public) to the exclusion of all others, including the copyright owner.
A licence that permits the exclusive licensee to further authorise specified persons to exercise the licensed right within the scope of the exclusivity.
Territorially or temporally limited exclusive licences, such as an exclusive licence to distribute a work only in India or only for a period of five years.
An exclusive licence covering a specific mode of exploitation, such as exclusive digital streaming rights or exclusive print publication rights, while other modes remain with the owner.
what_it_excludes: A non-exclusive or ordinary licence, where the copyright owner retains the right to grant the same permission to multiple other parties simultaneously.
A bare permission or implied consent to use a work, which does not confer any formal right comprised in copyright and does not exclude the owner or third parties.
An assignment of copyright, which transfers ownership of the copyright itself rather than granting a licence to exercise rights under it.

A licence that merely restricts the owner's ability to compete commercially but does not formally confer a right 'comprised in the copyright', such as a non-compete clause in a publishing contract without a corresponding copyright licence.
definitions.why_it_matters: An exclusive licensee has statutory standing under the Copyright Act to institute infringement proceedings in their own name (akin to the copyright owner), making the classification critical for determining who can sue for infringement and seek remedies. Whether a licence qualifies as 'exclusive' also determines the scope of moral and economic rights that can be enforced, and affects the validity of subsequent licences or assignments granted by the copyright owner over the same rights.

definitions.plain_english: An exclusive licensee is a person who has been granted a special permission by the copyright owner to use a copyrighted work in a way that no one else — not even the copyright owner — is allowed to use it during the licence period. This is different from an ordinary licence where the owner can give the same permission to multiple people. The exclusive licensee essentially steps into a privileged position and has stronger legal rights to protect and enforce those rights.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music label, T-Series, is granted an exclusive licence by a composer to distribute and stream a film's soundtrack digitally in India, meaning no other platform or the composer himself can distribute it digitally during the licence term.

A Delhi-based publishing house receives an exclusive licence from an author of a Hindi novel to translate and publish the work in English, preventing the author and all other publishers from releasing their own English translation.

A Mumbai-based OTT platform like ZEE5 acquires an exclusive licence from a regional film producer to stream a Malayalam film, barring the producer and competing platforms such as SonyLIV from streaming the same film in that territory.

A software company in Bengaluru is granted an exclusive licence by a foreign firm to reproduce and sell a proprietary computer programme in India, giving it the sole right to market and distribute the software locally, even to the exclusion of the original developer.

A theatre production company in Chennai obtains an exclusive licence from a playwright to perform a dramatic work publicly across South India for two years, meaning no other theatre group or the playwright's own troupe can stage the work in that region during that period.
what_it_covers: A licensee who has been granted sole rights to reproduce, distribute, or perform a copyrighted work to the exclusion of all others including the copyright owner.
Persons specifically authorised by the exclusive licensee to exercise the licensed rights, as the definition extends exclusivity to those authorised by the licensee.
An exclusive licensee who holds rights over a specific territorial region, medium, language, or time period, provided the grant meets the exclusivity requirement.
A company or individual who receives an exclusive licence for a subset of rights comprised in copyright, such as the exclusive right to broadcast or the exclusive right to translate.
what_it_excludes: A non-exclusive licensee who holds a mere permission to use the work alongside others, including the copyright owner, as there is no exclusivity in such arrangements.
The copyright owner themselves, who, under an exclusive licence, is expressly excluded from exercising the rights granted to the exclusive licensee.
A bare assignee of copyright, who holds ownership rather than a licence and is governed by assignment provisions rather than the exclusive licence framework.
A sub-licensee or third party authorised by an ordinary (non-exclusive) licensee, as such authorisation does not carry the exclusionary character required by the definition.
A person with a compulsory licence granted under statutory provisions, which operates by force of law rather than by contractual grant conferring exclusivity.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as an exclusive licensee is critical because under Section 54, an exclusive licensee is entitled to the same remedies for infringement as the copyright owner, including injunctions, damages, and accounts of profits; under Section 61, the copyright owner must be joined as a party in any infringement suit brought by the exclusive licensee, ensuring procedural safeguards. Failure to satisfy this definition means a licensee cannot independently sue for infringement and loses these elevated statutory protections.

definitions.definition: Fair dealing refers to the use of a copyrighted work (not being a computer programme) for purposes of private or personal use including research, criticism or review of that work or any other work, or the reporting of current events and current affairs including the reporting of a lecture delivered in public, as enumerated under Section 52(1)(a); and in the context of broadcast reproduction right and performer's right, the use of excerpts of a performance or broadcast consistent with such fair dealing for reporting current events or for bona fide review, teaching or research under Section 39.
definitions.plain_english: Fair dealing is a legal exception that allows a person to use someone else's copyrighted material without permission or payment, but only for specific limited purposes such as personal study, research, writing a review or critique, or reporting news. It does not apply to computer programmes. Think of it as a 'permitted use' carve-out that balances the rights of copyright owners with the public's interest in education, information and creative commentary.
real_world_examples: A journalist at The Hindu quotes several paragraphs from a recently published novel while writing a book review — this qualifies as fair dealing for the purpose of criticism or review under Section 52(1)(a).

A student at Delhi University photocopies a chapter from a textbook for personal study and research for her semester exams — this constitutes fair dealing for private or personal use including research.

A news anchor on NDTV plays a brief clip from a copyrighted Bollywood film while reporting on a controversy surrounding the film's release — this is permitted fair dealing for reporting current events and current affairs.

A documentary filmmaker uses a short excerpt from a recorded classical music performance broadcast on All India Radio while reviewing the concert in a bona fide arts critique programme — this is fair dealing consistent with Section 39 in the context of performer's right.

A professor at IIT Bombay reproduces short passages from a published academic paper in her lecture notes distributed to students for purposes of criticism and scholarly commentary — this falls within fair dealing for review and research.

A blogger in Mumbai quotes extensively from a politician's public speech (delivered as a lecture in public) while writing a commentary piece — this is permitted fair dealing under the reporting of a lecture delivered in public.
what_it_covers: Reproduction or quotation of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work for private or personal use including research by an individual.
Use of excerpts from a copyrighted work in a published criticism or review of that work or any other work, such as a book review or film critique.
Reporting of current events and current affairs in newspapers, television or online media, including reporting of a lecture delivered in public.

Use of excerpts from a performance or broadcast — consistent with fair dealing — for reporting current events, bona fide review, teaching or research, in the context of broadcast reproduction right and performer's right under Section 39.
Quoting from a published work in academic or scholarly commentary intended for genuine research purposes.
what_it_excludes: Any fair dealing with a computer programme — the Section 52(1)(a) exception expressly excludes computer programmes, which are governed by separate provisions.
Commercial exploitation of copyrighted material disguised as research or review, where the predominant purpose is profit rather than genuine critique or personal study.
Reproduction of an entire work or a substantial portion thereof in a manner that substitutes for purchasing the original, even if labelled as research or personal use.
Use of copyrighted material for purposes not listed — such as entertainment, advertising or general public communication — which cannot claim the fair dealing defence.
Unauthorised adaptation or modification of a work beyond mere quotation or reproduction for the specified fair dealing purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a use qualifies as fair dealing is decisive in determining whether an act constitutes infringement of copyright under Section 51 or infringement of broadcast reproduction right and performer's right under Section 39 — if fair dealing applies, no infringement arises and no civil or criminal liability under Sections 55 or 63 is triggered. Conversely, if the use falls outside the fair dealing exception, the copyright owner may seek injunction, damages or criminal prosecution for the unauthorised use.

definitions.definition: A false statement or representation made knowingly, with a view to deceiving any authority or officer in the execution of the provisions of the Copyright Act, or with a view to procuring or influencing the doing or omission of anything in relation to the Act or any matter thereunder, as contemplated under Section 68.
definitions.plain_english: A 'false statement' under copyright law means any untrue claim or representation that a person knowingly makes to a copyright official or authority in order to trick them or manipulate their decisions. The key requirement is that the person making the statement must know it is false at the time of making it. It is essentially deliberate lying to copyright authorities for personal gain or to influence official actions.
real_world_examples: A music producer submits false ownership documents to the Copyright Office in Mumbai, falsely claiming to be the sole author of a musical composition, in order to register copyright and block royalty payments to the actual composer.

A publisher in Delhi files a false affidavit before the Registrar of Copyrights stating that a literary work was first published in India, when it was actually first published abroad, to obtain a compulsory licence at a lower rate.

A software company representative in Bengaluru makes a false representation to a copyright officer during an inspection, claiming that a particular computer programme was originally developed by their employees, knowing it was copied from another developer.

A film production house in Mumbai falsely declares to the Copyright Board that it has not been able to contact the original copyright owner of a cinematograph film, in order to procure a compulsory licence, when in fact the owner had already been contacted and had refused consent.
An individual submits a false statement to the Appellate Board during a copyright dispute, misrepresenting the date of assignment of copyright to influence the Board's ruling in their favour.

A collecting society official in Chennai provides false information to the Registrar of Copyrights about the number of rights holders represented, in order to influence registration or tariff scheme approvals.
what_it_covers: Any knowingly untrue oral or written statement made to the Registrar of Copyrights or any authorised copyright officer during registration, inspection, or licensing proceedings.

False representations made in documents submitted to the Copyright Board or Appellate Board with the intent to influence a decision, such as fabricated ownership claims or false first-publication dates.
Deliberate misstatements made during official inquiries under the Act, including false claims about authorship, assignment, or publication history, made with knowledge of their falsity.
False declarations submitted by a copyright society or collecting society to the Copyright Office to influence tariff schemes or registration of rights.
Knowingly incorrect statements made to procure a compulsory licence by misrepresenting inability to contact the copyright owner or misrepresenting the nature of the work.
what_it_excludes: Honest mistakes or inadvertent errors in statements made to copyright authorities, where the person genuinely believed the information to be true at the time of making it.
Statements made in private commercial negotiations or contracts between private parties not involving any copyright authority or officer acting under the Act.
Opinions, legal arguments, or interpretations of law presented before the Copyright Board or Appellate Board in good faith, even if ultimately found to be incorrect.
Incomplete disclosures or omissions that do not constitute an affirmative false representation intended to deceive or influence an authority.
Statements made in judicial proceedings before civil courts, which are governed by separate provisions of perjury law under the Indian Penal Code rather than under this section.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a statement qualifies as a 'false statement' under Section 68, the person making it is liable to criminal prosecution, with punishment extending to imprisonment of up to one year, a fine, or both; this provision directly triggers penal consequences and can invalidate any copyright registration, licence, or official action procured through such deception.

definitions.definition: Fees, in the context of copyright societies, means the amounts collected by a copyright society from licensees pursuant to licences issued under section 30 in respect of rights administered by the society, which are subject to approval of collection and distribution procedures by the authors and other owners of right, and which shall, as far as may be, be distributed among such authors and owners in proportion to the actual use of their works after deductions for the society's own expenses.
definitions.plain_english: Fees are the money that a copyright society collects from people or organisations who use copyrighted works, on behalf of the creators and rights holders. This money is gathered under licences and then distributed back to the authors and owners after the society deducts its running costs. The authors and owners have the right to approve how these fees are collected and shared out.
real_world_examples: The Indian Performing Right Society (IPRS) collects fees from radio stations like All India Radio or private FM channels for broadcasting copyrighted musical compositions, and then distributes these fees among its registered composers and lyricists in proportion to how frequently their songs were played.

Phonographic Performance Limited (PPL) collects fees from hotels, restaurants, and shopping malls in Mumbai and Delhi that play recorded music as background entertainment, and distributes the collected amounts to the producers of sound recordings whose works were used.

A copyright society administering literary works collects fees from an e-learning platform that uses excerpts from books written by registered authors, and the society distributes the fees proportionally based on usage data provided by the platform.

A copyright society collects fees from a Bollywood film production house that licences a catalogue of pre-existing musical works for inclusion in a film soundtrack, and subsequently distributes those fees to the respective composers and lyricists after deducting administrative expenses.

IPRS obtains approval from its author-members for the utilisation of a portion of the collected fees for legal proceedings against persistent infringers, as any use of fees beyond distribution requires member approval under section 35.
what_it_covers: Amounts collected by a copyright society from broadcasters, streaming platforms, or public performance venues under licences issued in respect of musical, literary, or other copyrighted works.
Sums gathered by a copyright society from foreign societies or organisations for rights administered in India on behalf of foreign rights holders, subject to non-discrimination requirements.

Monies collected under licences for reprographic reproduction, digital distribution, or public performance, which are subject to member-approved distribution procedures and distributed proportionally to actual use.
Fees retained by the copyright society itself as deductions for its own administrative and operational expenses before distributing the remainder to authors and owners of right.
what_it_excludes: Damages or compensation awarded by a court in an infringement suit, which are judicial remedies and not fees collected under a licensing arrangement by a copyright society.
Statutory fees payable to the Copyright Office or Registrar of Copyrights for registration, renewal, or filing of applications, which are government charges under the Act's administrative framework.

Payments made directly between a copyright owner and a licensee under a privately negotiated exclusive licence without the involvement of a copyright society, as these do not pass through the collective administration mechanism.
Fines or penalties imposed under the Act for criminal infringement, which are punitive in nature and not amounts collected for the use of copyrighted works.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of fees determines which amounts fall under the mandatory collective-control regime of section 35, obligating the copyright society to obtain member approval for collection and distribution procedures and to distribute amounts proportionally to actual use; failure to comply with these obligations in relation to collected fees can expose the copyright society to regulatory action by the Registrar of Copyrights under section 36, including scrutiny of whether fees are being utilised or distributed in accordance with the Act.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 69, 'firm' is included within the meaning of 'company', which means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of persons; and 'director', in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm.
definitions.plain_english: A 'firm' in copyright law refers to a partnership business — a group of people who have come together to run a business under a common name. For the purpose of copyright offences, a firm is treated just like a company, meaning it can be held responsible for copyright violations. When a firm commits a copyright offence, the partners who were in charge of the business at the time can also be personally held guilty.
real_world_examples: A law firm in Delhi operating as a partnership (e.g., 'Sharma & Associates') photocopies and distributes copyrighted legal textbooks without licence — the firm and its managing partners can both be prosecuted under the Copyright Act.

A Bollywood music production partnership firm in Mumbai unlawfully reproduces and sells pirated sound recordings — the firm as an entity and each partner responsible for the business operations can be charged with copyright infringement.

A small textile design firm in Surat, operating as a registered partnership, copies protected artistic designs from a fashion house and uses them in commercial fabric printing — the firm and the partner overseeing production are both liable.

A software development partnership firm in Bengaluru distributes cracked versions of proprietary software to clients — both the firm and the partner managing client delivery can be deemed guilty of the offence under the Copyright Act.

A publishing partnership firm in Chennai reproduces and sells unauthorised copies of a popular Tamil novel — the firm and the partner responsible for editorial and distribution operations face criminal prosecution under Section 69.
what_it_covers: A registered partnership firm operating under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, that commits a copyright offence.
Partners of a firm who were in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the firm's business at the time the copyright offence was committed.
A partner of a firm whose consent, connivance, or negligence led to the commission of a copyright offence, making them personally liable.
Any unregistered partnership or informal association of persons carrying on business together that commits an act of copyright infringement.
what_it_excludes: Sole proprietorship businesses, which are not an association of persons and do not constitute a firm or company under this section.
A limited liability company (private or public company) incorporated under the Companies Act, which is covered separately as a 'body corporate' rather than as a 'firm'.
Employees of the firm who are not partners and have no managerial responsibility or control over the business, unless their specific negligence or connivance is independently proven.
Non-business associations such as unincorporated clubs or societies that are not engaged in trade or business activities similar to a firm.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'firm' under Section 69 determines whether it — and its partners — can be criminally prosecuted for copyright offences committed in the course of business; if this definition applies, partners are deemed guilty and liable to punishment unless they prove absence of knowledge or exercise of due diligence, triggering penal consequences under the Copyright Act.
