definitions.definition: The author of a work shall be the first owner of the copyright therein; provided that in specified circumstances—such as works created during employment under a contract of service or apprenticeship, works commissioned for valuable consideration, Government works, works by public undertakings, or works of international organisations—the employer, commissioning person, Government, public undertaking, or international organisation, as applicable, shall in the absence of any agreement to the contrary be the first owner of the copyright therein.
definitions.plain_english: The 'first owner' is the person or entity who initially holds copyright in a work the moment it is created. Usually this is the creator (author, artist, composer), but in certain situations—like when the work is made as part of a job, or commissioned and paid for, or made by a government employee for the government—the employer, the person who paid for it, or the government becomes the first owner instead. This is the starting point of all copyright ownership, and it can only be changed by a written agreement.
real_world_examples: A journalist employed by The Hindu writes a news article as part of her regular duties under a contract of service. The Hindu, as the newspaper proprietor, becomes the first owner of copyright in that article for purposes of publication in the newspaper, not the journalist.

A Bollywood production house commissions a portrait painter in Mumbai to create a painting for a film poster and pays him a fee. The production house, having commissioned the work for valuable consideration, becomes the first owner of copyright in that painting, not the painter.

A software developer employed by an IT company in Bengaluru writes a computer programme during the course of his employment. The IT company, as employer under a contract of service, is the first owner of the copyright in that programme, absent any contrary agreement.

The Archaeological Survey of India, a body established under Central law and therefore a public undertaking, directs the creation of a detailed illustrated heritage document. The Archaeological Survey of India is the first owner of the copyright in that work under Section 17.

An independent freelance photographer in Delhi takes photographs on her own initiative and publishes them in her portfolio. She, as the author, is the first owner of the copyright in those photographs since no employment or commission relationship exists.

The Government of Maharashtra commissions a documentary film about its irrigation projects and funds its production. The State Government is the first owner of the copyright in that cinematograph film as a Government work under Section 17.
what_it_covers: The author of an independent work who creates it outside any employment or commission arrangement, automatically becoming the first owner upon creation.

An employer (individual or company) whose employee creates a literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, or other work in the course of employment under a contract of service or apprenticeship, where no contrary agreement exists.
A person who commissions a photograph, painting, portrait, engraving, or cinematograph film for valuable consideration, making them the first owner in the absence of a contrary agreement.
The Central or State Government in respect of Government works created by or under its direction or control.
A public undertaking (government company, body corporate established by statute, or government-owned/controlled entity) in respect of works made or first published under its direction or control.
An international organisation in respect of works to which Section 41 applies, such as works of the United Nations or its agencies.
what_it_excludes: A person who merely purchases or acquires a physical copy of a work—ownership of the physical object does not make one the first owner of copyright.
An assignee or licensee who acquires copyright through a subsequent transaction—they are not the first owner but a derived owner, and therefore cannot claim the resale share right under Section 53A.
An editor, publisher, or distributor who contributes to the publication of a work but does not author or commission it under the qualifying conditions of Section 17.

A person who delivers an address or speech on behalf of their employer—in such cases, the principal on whose behalf the speech is delivered is the first owner, not the employing entity that arranged the venue.
Collaborators or contributors whose involvement does not meet the threshold of 'author' or qualifying commissioner or employer under Section 17's provisos.
definitions.why_it_matters: Identifying the first owner is foundational to all copyright disputes, licensing, and enforcement, because only the first owner (or those deriving rights from them) can assert infringement, grant licences, or claim royalties under the Act; additionally, under Sections 28 and 28A, whether the first owner is the Government or a public undertaking determines the duration of copyright, and under Section 53A, only an author who was the first owner (or their legal heirs) qualifies for the resale share right in original copies of paintings, sculptures, drawings, and manuscripts.

definitions.definition: The term 'first publication' refers to the initial act of making a work available to the public for the first time, from which date statutory periods for compulsory licensing, translation rights, and other copyright obligations are calculated. A work is considered first published on the date when copies of it are first issued to the public with the consent of the owner of the copyright, and in cases of simultaneous publication in multiple countries, the date of publication in the country that affords the shorter or shortest period of copyright protection governs.
definitions.plain_english: First publication means the very first time a book, play, song, film, or other creative work is officially released or made available to the public. This date is important because many legal deadlines — such as when someone else can apply for permission to translate or reproduce a work — are counted from this date. Think of it as the 'launch date' of a work, after which the copyright clock starts ticking for various purposes.
real_world_examples: A Hindi novel by a Delhi-based author is printed and sold in bookstores across India for the first time in January 2010. That date of release becomes the 'first publication' date, and after seven years (January 2017), any person may apply to the Appellate Board for a compulsory licence to translate it into Tamil or Telugu.

A foreign English-language academic textbook on biotechnology is published in the United Kingdom in March 2019. An Indian educational publisher wishing to translate it into Hindi for teaching purposes must wait three years from March 2019 (i.e., until March 2022) before applying for a compulsory translation licence under Section 32(1A) of the Copyright Act.

A Kannada dramatic work is performed and simultaneously its script is published in Bengaluru in June 2015. A publisher in Odisha wants to bring out an Odia translation. The 'first publication' date of June 2015 triggers the seven-year waiting period under Section 32(1), making a compulsory licence application eligible only from June 2022.

An Indian scientific journal publishes a research paper in both print and digital formats on its website simultaneously in September 2020. The date of that simultaneous release constitutes the 'first publication', and any broadcasting authority seeking a licence to broadcast a translation for instructional purposes under Section 32(5) must count its waiting period from that date.

A children's picture book authored by a Mumbai-based illustrator is first offered for sale at a book fair in Pune in October 2016. Even though the author had privately circulated copies among friends earlier, the first public release at the book fair constitutes 'first publication' for copyright timing purposes, including eligibility for compulsory licence applications.
semantic_tags: date of first issue to public
what_it_covers: The date on which copies of a literary or dramatic work are first made available and issued to the public with the copyright owner's consent, whether in print or analogous forms.
Simultaneous publication in India and a foreign country on the same day, where the earlier or same date is treated as the first publication date for determining applicable copyright provisions.

The first release of a translated, adapted, or revised edition of a work if that version is being treated as a new work for the purpose of calculating compulsory licence waiting periods under Sections 32 and 32A.

Digital or online first publication, where a work is made accessible to the public for the first time through electronic means with the owner's authorisation, triggering the same statutory time periods.
what_it_excludes: Private or restricted circulation of manuscripts or copies among a limited group of individuals without any intent to make the work available to the general public, as this does not constitute publication.
Unauthorised or pirated release of a work by a third party without the copyright owner's consent, since first publication requires the owner's authorisation for the initial issue to the public.

A subsequent edition, reprint, or new translation of a previously published work, as these do not reset the 'first publication' date of the original work for the purpose of calculating licence waiting periods.

Internal distribution of a work within a government department, company, or organisation that has not been made available to the public at large, which falls short of the threshold of public issuance.
definitions.why_it_matters: The date of 'first publication' is the mandatory reference point from which all statutory waiting periods under Sections 32 and 41 are calculated — determining when a person may lawfully apply for a compulsory translation or reproduction licence; if this date is disputed or incorrectly identified, an applicant's licence application may be premature and liable to rejection, or a copyright owner may wrongly lose the exclusive period of protection they are entitled to.

definitions.definition: A work is 'first published' when it is published for the first time anywhere in the world; and in the case of a work published in two or more countries simultaneously, it shall be deemed to have been first published in the country where it was first made available to the public. For the purposes of this Act, the country of first publication determines nationality and protectability of the work under Section 5.
definitions.plain_english: A work is 'first published' when it is made available to the public for the very first time, anywhere in the world. The country where this first release happens is treated as the country of first publication. If a work is released in multiple countries at nearly the same time, the country where it was made available earliest is considered the place of first publication. This matters because Indian copyright law protects certain foreign works based on where they were first published.
real_world_examples: A Hindi novel written by an Indian author and released by a Mumbai-based publisher for the first time in India — the novel is 'first published' in India, making it an 'Indian work' under Section 2(l) of the Copyright Act.

A software application developed by a Bengaluru startup and launched globally via an Indian website on 1st January before any foreign release — the software is considered first published in India, attracting full Indian copyright protection under Section 5.

A British author's book released simultaneously in the United Kingdom and India on the same date — since India is a signatory to the Berne Convention, if the Indian edition is released even one day earlier, India qualifies as the country of first publication, granting the work protection under Indian copyright law.

A Bollywood film produced in Mumbai and premiered in Indian cinemas before any international screening — the cinematograph film is first published in India, establishing it as an Indian work eligible for all copyright protections under the Act.

A classical Carnatic music composition recorded and commercially released by a Chennai-based music label for the first time — the sound recording is first published in India on the date of commercial release, securing the producer's rights under the Act.

A foreign academic journal article published in the United States before being reproduced in India — the article is first published in the USA, and its protection in India depends on whether the USA is a reciprocating country under Section 5.
what_it_covers: A literary, dramatic, or musical work released to the public for the first time through any mode — print, digital, or broadcast — in India or abroad.
A work released in multiple countries where the earliest date of public availability determines the country of first publication.
An unpublished Indian work that is subsequently published for the first time in India, thereby qualifying as an 'Indian work' under Section 2(l)(ii).
A cinematograph film or sound recording made available to the public for the first time through commercial distribution or public screening.
A computer programme released publicly for the first time via an Indian platform or publisher, establishing India as the country of first publication.
what_it_excludes: Internal or private circulation of a work within a company or organisation without public release — such distribution does not constitute 'first publication'.
A work that has already been published elsewhere in the world prior to its Indian release — India cannot be the country of first publication in that case.
Unpublished works that are only performed or communicated to a private group without being made available to the general public.
Re-publication or reprinting of a previously published work — only the original first release qualifies as 'first published'.
A work published posthumously or under a different edition if the original edition was already first published in another country at an earlier date.
definitions.why_it_matters: The place of first publication directly determines whether a work qualifies as an 'Indian work' under Section 2(l) and whether it is entitled to copyright protection in India under Section 5; works not first published in India or a reciprocating country may be denied protection entirely, while first publication in India secures the full term of copyright and all associated rights under the Act.

definitions.plain_english: A 'foreign country' is simply any country outside India. Under Indian copyright law, the government can decide to extend copyright protections to works originating from specific foreign countries, especially those that have similar protections in place for Indian works. This allows Indian copyright law to recognise and protect works from other nations and vice versa.
real_world_examples: The Central Government issues the International Copyright Order extending copyright protections to works first published in the United States, treating a Hollywood film the same as an Indian film for copyright purposes.

A music composer from France, a Berne Convention signatory country, has their musical composition protected in India under the International Copyright Order, preventing unauthorised reproduction by Indian publishers.

A UK-based broadcasting organisation whose headquarters is in the United Kingdom (a foreign country) has its broadcast reproduction rights recognised in India because the Central Government has extended Chapter VIII protections to that country by gazette notification.

An Indian copyright society like IPRS enters into an agreement with SESAC of the United States (a foreign country) to administer performing rights of Indian composers in the US and reciprocally administer US composers' rights in India.

A software company in Germany (a foreign country) seeks to enforce its computer programme copyright against an Indian firm; the Central Government's order in respect of Germany enables this enforcement under Indian copyright law.

A performer from Japan gives a live performance at an international festival; because Japan is designated a foreign country under an applicable order, the performer's rights under Chapter VIII of the Copyright Act apply to that performance in India.

Countries where a foreign broadcasting organisation or foreign performer is headquartered or from which a broadcast is transmitted, and to which the Central Government has directed the application of Chapter VIII protections under Section 40A.
what_it_excludes: India itself, which is the domestic jurisdiction and cannot be a 'foreign country' for the purposes of these provisions.

Territories or countries to which the Central Government has not issued any order under Section 40 or 40A and which are neither party to any treaty nor convention to which India is also a party, meaning their works receive no automatic protection under the Act.
International organisations or stateless entities that are not recognised as a 'country' under international law, as the definition inherently requires a recognised sovereign nation-state.

definitions.definition: A 'foreign society' means any society or organisation established outside India that administers rights in works corresponding to rights under the Copyright Act, 1957, with which a copyright society registered in India is competent to enter into an agreement under Section 34(2) for the mutual administration of such rights across jurisdictions.
definitions.plain_english: A foreign society is an organisation based in another country that does the same job as an Indian copyright society — it collects fees and manages rights for creators in that country. Indian copyright societies can make formal agreements with these foreign organisations so that rights are protected and royalties are collected internationally on behalf of each other's members. Think of it as a partner organisation abroad that looks after Indian creators' rights in foreign countries, and vice versa.
real_world_examples: IPRS (Indian Performing Right Society) entering into a reciprocal agreement with PRS for Music (UK) so that when Indian musical compositions are performed in the UK, PRS for Music collects royalties on behalf of IPRS and remits them to Indian composers and lyricists.

PPL India entering into an agreement with SOCAN (Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada) to administer the broadcast reproduction rights of Indian sound recordings on Canadian radio and streaming platforms.

Phonographic Performance Limited (PPL India) collaborating with ASCAP (USA) so that American film producers using Indian sound recordings in their US releases are properly licensed and royalties are channelled back to Indian music producers.

A literary rights society in India entering into a mutual agreement with Authors' Licensing and Collecting Society (ALCS) in the UK, enabling British publishers to obtain licences for reproducing Indian literary works and ensuring Indian authors receive fees collected abroad.

IPRS executing an agreement with JASRAC (Japan) to ensure that Japanese broadcasters and karaoke operators who use Bollywood music pay the appropriate licence fees, which are then distributed to the relevant Indian music rights holders.
what_it_covers: Overseas collecting societies such as PRS for Music (UK), ASCAP (USA), or JASRAC (Japan) that administer performing rights, mechanical rights, or broadcast rights corresponding to those managed by Indian copyright societies.

Foreign organisations that enter into formal reciprocal agreements with Indian copyright societies to collect licence fees and distribute royalties for Indian works used in their respective countries.
Any foreign body administering rights corresponding to rights under the Copyright Act, 1957, in a foreign country, including rights in literary, musical, dramatic, artistic, or sound recording works.

Foreign societies that administer rights in their home country and agree to permit Indian copyright societies to administer those rights in India on behalf of foreign rights holders, subject to the non-discrimination proviso.
what_it_excludes: Individual foreign authors or rights holders who have not delegated administration of their rights to any recognised society or organisation abroad.
Indian copyright societies themselves, even if they operate internationally or have foreign members, as these are registered and governed under Indian law.
Foreign government agencies or diplomatic bodies that do not specifically administer copyright rights corresponding to those under the Indian Copyright Act.
Informal networks, agents, or individual licensing representatives abroad who are not constituted as a society or organisation for the collective administration of copyright.
Foreign companies or studios that merely exploit or use copyright works commercially but do not function as collective rights administration bodies.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of an entity as a 'foreign society' under Section 34(2) determines whether an Indian copyright society can lawfully enter into a reciprocal administration agreement with it, thereby enabling the collection and remittance of royalties across borders. Critically, any such foreign society is bound by the non-discrimination proviso, meaning it cannot apply different licensing terms or distribution conditions between Indian works and other works, and failure to comply can affect the validity and enforceability of the entire reciprocal arrangement.

definitions.definition: A 'future work' is a work that is not yet in existence at the time of assignment or licence but is intended or anticipated to be created subsequently; the copyright in such a work may be assigned or licensed by the prospective owner, provided that any such assignment or licence shall take effect only when the work comes into existence.
definitions.plain_english: A 'future work' is a creative work that has not yet been made or written at the time a deal (assignment or licence) is signed about it. For example, if an author agrees to give a publisher the copyright in a book they haven't written yet, that book is a 'future work.' The agreement about that work only becomes legally operative once the work is actually created.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music composer signs a contract with a film production house in Mumbai assigning copyright in all background scores they will compose for an upcoming film that is still in pre-production — those scores are 'future works' and the assignment activates only when each score is composed.

A novelist in Bengaluru enters into a publishing agreement with Penguin India granting them copyright in a sequel novel that has not yet been written; the sequel is a 'future work' and the licence takes effect only upon the novel's completion.

A software developer in Hyderabad agrees to assign copyright in a mobile application to a startup; since the application code has not yet been written, it qualifies as a 'future work' and the assignment will only become enforceable once the code is actually created.

A Delhi-based journalist enters into an agreement with a news agency granting them the copyright in all articles they will write over the next year; each unwritten article at the time of signing is a 'future work,' and the copyright in each transfers to the agency only when that article is written.

A film director in Chennai agrees to license the rights to a documentary about a forthcoming sports event; since the documentary has not yet been filmed or edited, it constitutes a 'future work,' and the licence becomes operative only once the documentary is produced.
what_it_covers: A novel, script, or literary piece that an author has contracted to write but has not yet created at the time of the agreement.
Musical compositions or sound recordings that a composer or musician has agreed to create and assign or license to a label or production house in the future.
Software programmes, computer applications, or databases that a developer has agreed to build and assign copyright in before actual development has commenced.
Artistic works such as paintings, illustrations, or photographs commissioned under contract but not yet executed at the time the copyright agreement is signed.
Cinematograph films or documentaries that are in development or pre-production stages where no footage or final work exists at the date of assignment.
what_it_excludes: Works that are already in existence at the time the assignment or licence is executed — those are governed as 'existing works' under Section 18 and Section 30.
Works where no intention or contractual framework exists at all for their future creation, as a 'future work' presupposes a prospective owner who contemplates its creation.
Works that can never come into existence due to impossibility or abandonment — if the work is never created, the assignment or licence in a 'future work' never takes effect and confers no rights.

Moral rights and the author's right to receive royalties under the proviso to Section 18, which cannot be waived even in agreements concerning future works involving literary or musical works in cinematograph films or sound recordings.
Anonymous or pseudonymous works already published before the agreement is signed, which fall under existing work categories rather than future work.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as a 'future work' determines when an assignment or licence becomes legally operative — if the work never comes into existence, the assignee acquires no rights and cannot enforce the agreement. It also determines who bears the rights if the assignee or licensee dies before the work is created, as the Act expressly extends entitlement to their legal representatives under Sections 18 and 30.

definitions.definition: The Act does not formally define 'good faith', but as used in Section 76 and Section 31B, it means an act done honestly, without fraud, deceit, collusion, or any ulterior motive, with genuine and sincere intent to comply with or act pursuant to the provisions of the Copyright Act. An act is done in good faith when the person acting has an honest belief in the legality and propriety of the action, without negligence so gross as to constitute bad faith.
definitions.plain_english: Good faith means acting honestly and sincerely, without any hidden or dishonest purpose. If you do something under the Copyright Act genuinely believing it is lawful and proper — not trying to cheat anyone or bend the rules — you are acting in good faith. It is essentially the opposite of acting with deception, fraud, or deliberate wrongdoing.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based NGO applies to the Appellate Board for a compulsory licence to publish books in Braille for visually impaired students, genuinely working for their benefit and not concealing any commercial motive — the Board may treat this as an application made in good faith under Section 31B.

A Registrar of Copyrights official, acting on instructions from the Appellate Board and following the prescribed procedure, registers a compulsory licence that later turns out to be based on incomplete records — the official is protected from a civil suit under Section 76 because the act was done in good faith.

A Mumbai publisher, acting on a Copyright Board direction believed to be valid, prints and distributes accessible format copies of a textbook for persons with disability; even if a procedural defect is later discovered, the publisher's honest compliance shields them from liability under Section 76.

A government officer in the Copyright Office, without any corrupt intent, makes an administrative entry in the Register of Copyrights that is later found to be erroneous — since the act was done honestly in pursuance of the Act, no legal proceedings can lie against them under Section 76.

A Chennai-based disability rights organisation applies for a compulsory licence under Section 31B and openly discloses all its funding sources and activities; the Appellate Board, satisfied with the transparent disclosure, finds the application to have been made in good faith and proceeds to grant the licence.
what_it_covers: An act performed honestly and without deception by any person in pursuance of a provision of the Copyright Act, even if the act later turns out to be procedurally imperfect.

An application made to the Appellate Board for a compulsory licence for the benefit of disabled persons where the applicant genuinely and transparently discloses all material facts without concealment.

Actions of government officers, the Registrar of Copyrights, or members of the Appellate Board carried out sincerely in the discharge of their duties under the Act, without personal gain or corrupt intent.
A licensee or publisher acting under the honest belief that a compulsory licence has been validly issued and distributing accessible format copies accordingly.
what_it_excludes: Actions taken with knowledge of their illegality or with deliberate intent to defraud the copyright owner or any other party.
Applications for compulsory licences filed under Section 31B by persons who conceal their true commercial motive or misrepresent the nature of their organisation to the Appellate Board.
Acts done with gross negligence, recklessness, or wilful blindness to obvious illegality, which courts may treat as tantamount to bad faith.
Conduct involving fraud, collusion, or misrepresentation in dealing with the Copyright Office or the Appellate Board, even if cloaked in procedural compliance.
definitions.why_it_matters: Section 76 provides a complete immunity from civil suits and other legal proceedings for any act done in good faith in pursuance of the Copyright Act, meaning that determining whether a person acted in good faith is the decisive factor in whether they can be held legally liable. Under Section 31B, the Appellate Board's satisfaction that an application was made in good faith is a prerequisite to proceeding with the grant of a compulsory licence, directly affecting the rights of both the applicant and the copyright owner.

definitions.definition: "Government work" means a work which is made or published by or under the direction or control of the Government or any department of the Government, any Legislature in India, or any court, tribunal or other judicial authority in India.
definitions.plain_english: A government work is any creative or written work that is produced or officially released by a government body in India, including central or state governments, Parliament or state legislatures, or courts and tribunals. This includes things like official reports, laws, judicial judgments, and government publications. The key factor is that the work must be made or published under government direction or control.
real_world_examples: A report prepared and published by the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, such as the Union Budget documents or Economic Survey, qualifies as a government work.
A judgment delivered by the Supreme Court of India or a High Court in a civil or criminal matter is a government work as it is produced under the direction of a judicial authority.
The Official Gazette notification issued by the President of India or a State Governor promulgating a new law or ordinance constitutes a government work.
A legislative Bill debated and passed in the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha, along with its official printed version published by the Lok Sabha Secretariat, is a government work.
A training manual or educational pamphlet prepared and distributed by the National Commission for Women under the direction of the Ministry of Women and Child Development is a government work.
A cartographic survey map produced and published by the Survey of India, a department under the Government of India, qualifies as a government work.
what_it_covers: Official reports, white papers, and policy documents prepared and published by any department of the Central or State Government of India.
Statutes, bills, ordinances, and official records published by Parliament of India, State Legislatures, or the Union Territory legislatures.
Judgments, orders, decrees, and official cause lists issued by courts, tribunals, and quasi-judicial authorities such as the National Green Tribunal or the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal.
Maps, surveys, and technical publications prepared under the direction of government departments such as the Survey of India or the Geological Survey of India.
Educational and informational materials produced under the direction or control of government bodies such as NCERT textbooks developed under Ministry of Education oversight.
what_it_excludes: Works created by private individuals or organisations even if commissioned or funded by the government, unless made under direct government direction or control.
Works authored by a government employee in a personal capacity outside the scope of their official duties, which would not qualify as made under government direction or control.

Works produced by autonomous statutory bodies or public sector undertakings that operate independently and are not departments of the government, such as works by the BCCI or independent regulatory bodies acting on their own authority.
Indian works as defined under Section 2 of the Act that merely relate to government subject matter but are authored and published by private publishers or authors.
Works of international organisations operating in India, which are governed by separate provisions, not the government work definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a work as a government work determines the first ownership of copyright under Section 17 of the Copyright Act, vesting it in the government rather than the individual author, and governs the term of copyright protection under Section 28, which differs from that applicable to works authored by individuals. It also affects the scope of permitted use, reproduction rights, and whether government permission is required before copying or republishing such works.

definitions.plain_english: A 'Government work' is any creative or written work that has been made or published by, or under the direct control or direction of, the Indian government (central or state), any parliament or state legislature in India, or any court or tribunal in India. This means that if a government body commissioned, directed, or controlled the creation or release of a work, it qualifies as a government work. Such works are treated differently under copyright law compared to works created by private individuals or companies.
real_world_examples: The Survey of India publishes topographical maps of Indian states under the direction of the Ministry of Science and Technology — these maps are government works.
A judgment delivered by the Supreme Court of India or a High Court and published in the official law reports qualifies as a government work since it is made by a judicial authority in India.
The Gazette of India, which publishes official notifications, legislative amendments, and government orders under the authority of the Government of India, constitutes a government work.

Educational textbooks authored and published by the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) under the direction of the Ministry of Education are government works.

definitions.definition: The term 'honour' as used in Section 57 of the Copyright Act, 1957, refers to the personal dignity, integrity, and moral standing of an author in relation to their creative work, such that any distortion, mutilation, modification, or other act done to the work that is prejudicial to the author's honour would entitle the author to restrain such act or claim damages. It forms part of the author's moral rights, existing independently of and surviving any assignment of copyright.
definitions.plain_english: An author's 'honour' means their personal dignity and the respect they are owed as the creator of a work. Even if an author has sold or transferred the copyright in their work, they still have the right to stop others from changing or misusing the work in a way that damages their personal dignity or standing. It is about protecting how the world sees the author as a creative person, not just their financial interests.
real_world_examples: A celebrated Indian poet assigns the copyright in their anthology to a publisher, but the publisher later republishes the poems with sexually explicit imagery added to the text without consent. The poet can invoke Section 57 to claim that their honour has been prejudiced and seek damages or an injunction.

A Bollywood film composer's original background score is remixed and used in a vulgar adult comedy film in a manner that associates the composer's creative identity with offensive content. The composer can restrain this use as being prejudicial to their honour under Section 57.

A Dalit activist author's social reform essay is distorted by a casteist organisation to remove its progressive message and insert contrary views, and then circulated under the original author's name. The author can seek damages for prejudice to their honour even if they had earlier assigned the copyright.

A renowned Indian classical painter's painting is digitally altered to portray the subject in a degrading or politically offensive manner and shared widely on social media. The painter can restrain such modification as being prejudicial to their honour under their moral rights.

An Indian architect's award-winning building design is substantially altered during construction by the developer in ways that the architect publicly disowns as structurally and aesthetically distasteful. The architect may claim their honour has been prejudiced by such modification.
what_it_covers: An author's personal dignity and standing as a creator that may be harmed by distortion, mutilation, or modification of their work.
Situations where a work is altered in a way that associates the author with ideas, content, or contexts that demean or disgrace the author in the eyes of the public.
The moral dimension of an author's rights that survives even after full or partial assignment of copyright, protecting the author's identity and creative reputation.
Acts done in relation to a work — not limited to direct alteration — that result in a prejudicial impact on how the author is perceived by society.
Claims by legal representatives of a deceased author whose honour was posthumously prejudiced by acts done to the author's work.
what_it_excludes: Failure to display a work or failure to display it to the author's satisfaction, which is explicitly stated not to constitute infringement of rights under Section 57.
Adaptation of a computer programme that falls within the permitted use under Section 52(1)(aa), which is expressly excluded from the author's right to restrain under the proviso to Section 57(1).
Mere financial or commercial loss suffered by an author due to modification of the work, without a prejudicial impact on the author's personal honour or dignity.
Lawful criticism, review, or commentary about a work or the author that does not involve distortion or mutilation of the work itself.
Changes to a work made pursuant to a valid contractual agreement with the author's informed consent, where the author has explicitly authorised such modifications.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is found to be prejudicial to an author's 'honour' under Section 57 determines whether the author (or their legal representatives) can obtain an injunction to restrain the act or claim damages even after having assigned copyright — triggering a remedy that is independent of ordinary copyright infringement. If this threshold is not met, no moral rights remedy under Section 57 is available, and the author would have no recourse solely on the ground of distortion or modification.

definitions.definition: "Indian work" means a literary, dramatic or musical work,— the author of which is a citizen of India; or which is first published in India; or the author of which, in the case of an unpublished work, is, at the time of the making of the work, a citizen of India.
definitions.plain_english: An 'Indian work' is a book, play, or piece of music that qualifies as Indian by meeting at least one of three conditions: it was written by an Indian citizen, it was first published in India, or — if it has never been published — its author was an Indian citizen when the work was created. Only literary, dramatic, and musical works can qualify as Indian works; paintings, films, and sound recordings do not fall under this category.
real_world_examples: A Hindi novel written and published in Mumbai by an Indian author qualifies as an Indian work because its author is a citizen of India and it was first published in India.

A classical Carnatic music composition created by a Chennai-based musician who has never published or recorded it still qualifies as an Indian work because the author was an Indian citizen at the time the work was made.

A play script written by a foreign playwright but first staged and published in India qualifies as an Indian work under the 'first published in India' criterion, even though the author is not an Indian citizen.

A Bengali poem authored by an Indian citizen living abroad and first published in a Kolkata literary journal qualifies as an Indian work on both grounds — citizenship of the author and first publication in India.

An unpublished folk song composed by a tribal artist in Odisha qualifies as an Indian work because the composer is an Indian citizen at the time of creating the work, even though it has never been formally published or recorded.
semantic_tags: author's citizenship at time of creation
what_it_covers: A literary work (e.g., a novel or poem) whose author holds Indian citizenship, regardless of where it is published.
A dramatic work (e.g., a play script or choreographic work) that was first published in India, even if authored by a foreign national.
An unpublished musical work composed by an Indian citizen at the time of its creation, even if it has never been recorded or released.
A work that satisfies any one of the three alternative conditions — Indian authorship, first publication in India, or Indian citizenship at time of making an unpublished work.
A literary work first published simultaneously in India and another country, where India qualifies as the country of first publication under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Artistic works such as paintings, sculptures, photographs, and drawings — these are not within the definition of 'Indian work' regardless of the author's nationality or place of publication.
Cinematograph films and sound recordings — these categories of works are expressly outside the scope of 'Indian work', which is confined to literary, dramatic, and musical works.
A literary or musical work authored by a foreign national and first published outside India, even if it has a large Indian readership or is widely distributed in India.
A work authored by a person who was not an Indian citizen at the time of its creation, if the work remains unpublished and was not first published in India.
Computer programmes or databases created by Indian citizens but not qualifying independently as literary works under the Act's specific definitions, if not meeting the three stated criteria.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a work as an 'Indian work' is a prerequisite for the grant of compulsory licences under Section 32 of the Copyright Act, which allows the government to authorise reproduction or translation of works for public benefit — this classification thus directly determines whether the compulsory licensing regime applies. It also affects which works receive protection under the Act's provisions that are specifically reserved for Indian works, including certain default terms of copyright protection and eligibility for statutory licences.

definitions.definition: An 'industrial process' means a mechanical or manufacturing process by which articles are produced or reproduced in multiple copies through machinery, automation, or systematic mass-production techniques, as opposed to hand-crafted or individual production by hand. Under Section 15, reproduction of an article to which a design has been applied by such a process more than fifty times extinguishes copyright protection in that design.
definitions.plain_english: An industrial process is any mechanised or factory-based method used to make multiple copies of a product, such as using machines in a manufacturing plant. When a design is applied to physical products using such a process and more than fifty such products are made, the design loses its copyright protection under the Copyright Act. This rule exists because once a design is mass-produced industrially, it should instead be protected under the Designs Act, not copyright law.
real_world_examples: A Pune-based textile manufacturer uses a CNC printing machine to print an original artistic pattern on cotton fabric. Once more than 50 metres or articles bearing that design are produced through this automated printing process, copyright in the original artistic design ceases and the manufacturer must rely on registration under the Designs Act instead.

A Mumbai ceramic company uses injection moulding machines to reproduce a decorative pattern on ceramic tiles. After the 51st tile bearing the unregistered design is produced industrially, copyright protection in that decorative design lapses under Section 15 of the Copyright Act.

A Chennai-based consumer goods company uses an industrial stamping press to emboss an original artistic motif on stainless steel tiffin boxes. Once more than fifty such boxes are manufactured through this mechanical process, the artistic work used as the design loses copyright protection.

A Delhi garment exporter runs an automated embroidery machine to reproduce a designer's original embroidery pattern on kurtas for bulk export. After the fiftieth kurta is produced by this industrial embroidery process, the copyright in the underlying artistic pattern ceases under Section 15, compelling the designer to register it under the Designs Act to retain protection.

A Bengaluru furniture maker uses a computer-controlled wood-routing machine to carve an original decorative pattern onto wooden panels for mass-market furniture. The mechanised, repeatable nature of this production qualifies as an industrial process, and copyright in the unregistered design extinguishes after fifty panels are produced.
what_it_covers: Mechanised factory processes such as injection moulding, die-casting, or stamping used to reproduce articles bearing an artistic design
Automated printing or embossing machines in textile or packaging industries that apply an original design to multiple articles systematically
Computer-controlled manufacturing equipment such as CNC routers, laser cutters, or automated embroidery machines that replicate a design on articles at scale
Assembly-line production methods in which the same design is applied to each unit of a product through a repeatable mechanical operation
what_it_excludes: Hand-crafted or individually hand-painted reproduction of a design by an artisan, even if the same design is used repeatedly, as this lacks the mechanised character of an industrial process

Digital reproduction of a design in electronic or online formats, such as displaying an artistic work on a website or reproducing it in a digital catalogue, which does not involve physical article production

Limited studio or workshop production where an artist personally applies a design to articles one at a time without machinery, such as a potter hand-throwing and individually decorating fewer than fifty ceramic pieces

Photographic or print-media reproduction of the artistic work itself (e.g., reproducing the artwork in a book or poster), which is governed by ordinary copyright rules and not by the Section 15 industrial process threshold
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a reproduction qualifies as an 'industrial process' is the critical factual determination under Section 15: if it does, copyright in an unregistered design ceases automatically once more than fifty articles are produced, stripping the owner of copyright remedies and forcing reliance on the Designs Act. Conversely, if production does not constitute an industrial process, copyright subsists indefinitely regardless of the number of articles made, preserving the owner's full range of copyright infringement claims and remedies.

definitions.definition: Copyright in a work shall be deemed to be infringed when any person, without a licence granted by the owner of the copyright or the Registrar of Copyrights or in contravention of the conditions of a licence so granted, does anything the exclusive right to do which is conferred upon the owner of the copyright, or permits for profit any place to be used for communication of the work to the public where such communication constitutes an infringement; or when any person makes for sale or hire, sells, distributes, publicly exhibits, or imports into India any infringing copies of the work.
definitions.plain_english: Infringement of copyright occurs when someone uses, copies, distributes, sells, or performs a protected creative work without the permission of the copyright owner or without a valid licence. It also covers situations where a person profits by allowing a venue to be used for unauthorised public showing or performance of a work. Essentially, any act that only the copyright owner is legally entitled to do, performed by someone else without authorisation, counts as infringement.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based printing shop photocopies an entire textbook authored by an Indian publisher and sells the copies to college students without obtaining any licence from the publisher.
A Delhi cinema hall screens a Bollywood film that is still under theatrical release using a pirated digital print downloaded from the internet, without authorisation from the film production house.
A Bengaluru software company reproduces a proprietary computer programme developed by an Indian IT firm and distributes it to its employees without purchasing the required number of licences.
A Chennai music streaming startup uploads and streams sound recordings of popular Tamil film songs on its platform without obtaining licences from the music label owning the copyright.
A Kolkata event organiser permits a commercial wedding venue to publicly perform copyrighted musical works through a live band without obtaining a licence from the relevant copyright society.
An e-commerce seller on a major Indian platform imports pirated physical copies of a best-selling Indian novel printed abroad and offers them for sale at a discounted price.

definitions.definition: A copy of a work shall be an infringing copy if it is made or used in contravention of the copyright in that work, including any copy made or imported for sale, hire, trade display, distribution, or public exhibition without the licence of the copyright owner; and the reproduction of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work in the form of a cinematograph film shall be deemed to be an infringing copy.
definitions.plain_english: An infringing copy is any physical or digital reproduction of a copyrighted work that was made or is being used without the permission of the person who owns the copyright. This includes pirated books, unauthorised CDs or DVDs, illegally downloaded files that have been burned onto discs, and any film that reproduces a protected literary or artistic work without a licence. Simply put, if a copy was not authorised by the copyright owner, it is an infringing copy.
real_world_examples: A street vendor in Palika Bazaar, New Delhi, sells photocopied editions of a bestselling novel published by Penguin India without any licence from the publisher — these photocopied books are infringing copies.

A Bollywood production house in Mumbai produces a film that reproduces lyrics from a protected musical composition owned by a music label without obtaining a licence — the resulting film prints are deemed infringing copies under the Act.

An importer in Chennai brings in a shipment of pirated Blu-ray discs containing unauthorised copies of Tamil films — the Customs Commissioner, acting on a notice under Section 53, treats these discs as prohibited infringing copies.

A software distributor in Bengaluru sells USB drives pre-loaded with copies of a proprietary accounting software without authorisation from the software company — each USB drive constitutes an infringing copy of the computer programme.

A textbook printing press in Hyderabad reproduces and sells copies of a foreign academic textbook whose Indian rights are held by an Indian publisher, without obtaining permission — all printed copies are infringing copies liable to be seized under Section 64.

An online content aggregator in Pune downloads and re-distributes MP3 files of songs from a major Indian music label's catalogue without a licence from the collecting society — each distributed file copy is an infringing copy.

Any cinematograph film that reproduces a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work without a licence — the film itself is statutorily deemed an infringing copy.
Imported goods consisting of copies of copyrighted works brought into India without the consent of the rights owner, which the Customs Commissioner may treat as prohibited goods under Section 53.
Plates or other devices used or intended to be used for the production of infringing copies, which are also deemed property of the copyright owner under Section 58.
what_it_excludes: A single copy of any work imported into India for the private and domestic use of the importer, which is expressly exempted from the import-related infringement provision under the proviso to Section 51.

Copies made under a valid licence granted by the copyright owner or by the Registrar of Copyrights, including compulsory licences issued under the Act — such copies are authorised and therefore not infringing copies.

Copies made for purposes that qualify as fair dealing under the Act, such as private study, research, criticism, or review, as these uses do not constitute infringement and the copies produced are not infringing copies.

Original copies of a work lawfully purchased or obtained from the copyright owner or an authorised licensee — lawfully made copies cannot be characterised as infringing copies merely by resale or transfer.
Works in which copyright has expired and entered the public domain — reproductions of such works cannot be infringing copies as there is no subsisting copyright to infringe.

definitions.definition: "infringing copy" means— in relation to a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, a reproduction thereof otherwise than in the form of a cinematographic film; in relation to a cinematographic film, a copy of the film made on any medium by any means; in relation to a sound recording, any other recording embodying the same sound recording, made by any means; in relation to a programme or performance in which such a broadcast reproduction right or a performer's right subsists under the provisions of this Act, the sound recording or a cinematographic film of such programme or performance, if such reproduction, copy or sound recording is made or imported in contravention of the provisions of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: An infringing copy is an unauthorised duplicate or reproduction of a copyrighted work — such as a book, song, film, or live performance — made or imported without the permission of the copyright owner and in violation of the Copyright Act. For example, a pirated DVD of a Bollywood film, a bootleg printout of a novel, or an unlicensed MP3 copy of a song would all be infringing copies. The key factor is that the reproduction was made or brought into India in contravention of the law.
real_world_examples: A street vendor in Palika Bazaar, New Delhi selling photocopied textbooks of NCERT or university course material without the publisher's authorisation — those photocopies are infringing copies of the original literary works.

A local cable operator in Mumbai recording a live IPL broadcast and distributing pirated DVDs of the matches — these DVDs are infringing copies of both the cinematograph film and the broadcast in which a broadcast reproduction right subsists.

An online seller on an Indian e-commerce platform importing cheap pirated CDs of Bollywood music albums manufactured abroad and selling them domestically — each CD is an infringing copy of the sound recordings contained therein.

A printing press in Surat reproducing unauthorised copies of a celebrated Indian author's novel and distributing them at a fraction of the original price without the author's or publisher's consent — every such printed copy qualifies as an infringing copy.

A YouTube channel operator downloading and re-uploading a full Kannada film without the producer's licence — the downloaded digital file and any copies made from it for redistribution are infringing copies of the cinematograph film.

A music school in Bengaluru printing out and distributing copyrighted sheet music of a famous composer's work to students without obtaining a licence from the copyright owner — those printouts are infringing copies of the musical work.
what_it_covers: A photocopy or printout of a copyrighted literary or dramatic work made without the author's or publisher's licence.
A pirated digital or physical copy of a Bollywood or regional language cinematograph film reproduced on any medium — DVD, pen drive, hard disk, or streamed file.
An unauthorised duplicate sound recording of a copyrighted song or album, whether pressed on a CD, stored as an MP3, or transferred via Bluetooth.
A sound recording or film of a live concert or stage performance made without authorisation where a performer's right subsists.
Copies of copyrighted works manufactured abroad and imported into India without the consent of the Indian copyright owner, in contravention of the Act.
what_it_excludes: A reproduction of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work in the form of a cinematographic film — such a reproduction is separately governed as a copy of the cinematograph film, not as a reproduction of the underlying work under clause (i) of the definition.
A lawfully acquired copy of a work purchased with the copyright owner's consent — such a copy is not made in contravention of the Act and therefore falls outside the definition.

A fair dealing use — for example, reproducing a short extract for private study, research, criticism, or review under Section 52 — does not constitute an infringing copy since it is not made in contravention of the Act.
An authorised licensed copy produced under a compulsory licence granted by the Copyright Board under the Act, as such copies are made within the law.
An accessible format copy made by a person with disability or a recognised organisation under Section 52(1)(zb) for the benefit of persons with disability, which is explicitly permitted by the Act.

Conversely, if a copy does not meet this definition, none of these penal or remedial provisions can be invoked against the person who made, possesses, or distributes it.

definitions.definition: An 'international organisation' means any organisation to which section 41 applies, being an organisation declared by the Central Government by order published in the Official Gazette to be an organisation of which one or more sovereign powers or the Government or Governments thereof are members, and to which it is expedient that section 41 shall apply.
definitions.plain_english: An international organisation, for copyright purposes, is a body made up of one or more countries or their governments that the Indian Central Government has officially recognised by a gazette notification. Such organisations can own copyright in India even if they would not normally qualify for it under ordinary rules. Examples include bodies like the United Nations or the World Health Organization, once notified by the Central Government.
real_world_examples: The United Nations publishes an educational report in India; if declared an international organisation under section 41 by the Central Government via an Official Gazette order, the UN holds copyright in that report in India for 60 years from the year following first publication.

The World Health Organization (WHO) produces a health policy document first published under its direction in India; upon Central Government declaration, WHO enjoys statutory copyright protection under section 41, even though it is not a natural person or Indian body corporate.

UNESCO creates and publishes a cultural heritage compendium under its control without reserving copyright to the contributing authors; having been declared an international organisation under section 41, UNESCO holds copyright throughout India and can enforce it in Indian courts.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) publishes a labour standards manual first issued under its direction; if notified by the Central Government, ILO is entitled to copyright for 60 years under section 29, and can sue for infringement in India even though it is not incorporated under Indian law.

A jointly authored scientific work is made under the direction of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and first published by it; once declared under section 41, the WTO holds copyright in India and can deal with, assign, or license that copyright just as a body corporate would.
what_it_covers: Organisations like the United Nations, WHO, UNESCO, or ILO that are composed of sovereign powers or their governments and have been declared by the Central Government via Official Gazette order to fall within section 41.

An organisation that lacks the legal capacity of a body corporate under its own constitution but is nevertheless deemed to have such capacity for the purpose of holding, dealing with, and enforcing copyright in India.
A body whose work is made or first published under its direction or control and in respect of which there would otherwise be no copyright in India at the time of making or first publication.
An organisation where copyright in a work would vest in it under section 17, or where the work is published pursuant to an agreement with the author that does not reserve copyright to the author.
what_it_excludes: Private multinational corporations or commercial entities, even if operating across multiple countries, since they are not composed of sovereign powers or their governments.
Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) or international non-profits that are not declared by the Central Government under section 41, regardless of their international character or membership.
Foreign companies or foreign government agencies acting in their individual national capacity, as they are not intergovernmental organisations of which sovereign powers are members.
Indian domestic bodies, statutory corporations, or public undertakings created under Indian law, which are governed by separate copyright provisions without requiring a section 41 declaration.
Organisations of which only sub-national entities (such as state governments or municipal bodies) are members, unless the Central Government specifically declares them under section 41.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as an 'international organisation' under section 41 determines whether copyright subsists in its works in India at all — without this designation, such works may fall into the public domain. definitions.definition: A 'work of joint authorship' means a work produced by the collaboration of two or more authors in which the contribution of one author is not distinct from the contribution of the other author or authors. The term 'joint authorship' refers to the authorship of such a work.
definitions.plain_english: Joint authorship means two or more people created a work together, where it is impossible to separate out exactly which part each person wrote or contributed. All the contributors are considered co-authors and share ownership of the copyright. This is different from a situation where one person writes Chapter 1 and another writes Chapter 2 — in that case, each person's contribution can be clearly identified.
real_world_examples: Two Bollywood lyricists, Javed Akhtar and a co-writer, collaborating so closely on song lyrics for a Hindi film that individual contributions cannot be distinguished, making the lyrics a work of joint authorship.

Two software engineers at a Bengaluru startup jointly developing a computer programme code together in a paired-programming session where neither's individual lines of code can be separated from the other's.

Two classical musicians in Chennai co-composing a Carnatic fusion musical work where one develops the melodic structure and the other builds upon it simultaneously, so their contributions are inseparable.
Two novelists based in Mumbai co-writing a Hindi literary novel by writing alternating passages that are so integrated and edited by both that it is impossible to identify who wrote which sentence.
Two academic researchers at a Delhi university jointly authoring a textbook on Indian constitutional law where both contributed to every chapter in an intertwined and indistinguishable manner.
what_it_covers: A literary work co-written by two or more authors whose individual contributions are merged and cannot be separately identified.
A musical composition jointly created by two composers whose melodic and harmonic contributions are so intertwined that attribution to a single composer is impossible.
A screenplay written by a team of writers working collaboratively where the dialogue and plot structure are the result of their combined, inseparable effort.
An artistic work created by two illustrators working simultaneously on the same canvas or digital file such that their individual strokes cannot be distinguished.
what_it_excludes: A work where each author's contribution is distinct and separable, such as an anthology where different authors write clearly identifiable separate chapters or sections.

A cinematograph film or sound recording, which is treated as a separate category under the Act with its own authorship rules (producer as author), not as a work of joint authorship in the general sense.

A work where one person merely provides ideas, suggestions, or feedback without actually executing or expressing any part of the creative work, as ideas are not protected and that person would not qualify as a joint author.

Works created under a contract of service by employees for an employer, where the employer is the first owner of copyright, removing the need to determine joint authorship among employee contributors.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a work as one of joint authorship directly determines the duration of copyright under Sections 22, 23, and 24 — where the term is calculated from the death of the author who dies last among the joint authors, rather than from the death of a single author. It also determines who qualifies as an 'author' under Section 54 for the purpose of moral rights, and governs how co-owners may exercise, assign, or license their rights, requiring consent of all joint authors for certain acts.

definitions.definition: "lecture" includes address, speech and sermon.
definitions.plain_english: A lecture, under the Copyright Act, is any spoken communication delivered to an audience and broadly includes not just formal academic lectures but also addresses, speeches, and sermons. This means a variety of oral presentations — from a politician's public address to a religious discourse — qualify as 'lectures' for copyright purposes. The term is interpreted inclusively, covering any form of sustained oral delivery to an audience.
real_world_examples: A professor at the University of Delhi delivering a course lecture on constitutional law, which is recorded by a student and later uploaded online without permission — this constitutes a potential infringement of the copyright in the lecture.

A renowned swami delivering a religious sermon at a temple in Rishikesh, where the temple records and sells DVDs of the sermon without the swami's consent — the sermon qualifies as a 'lecture' attracting copyright protection.

A senior advocate delivering a keynote address at a bar association conference in Mumbai, whose speech is transcribed and published in a law journal without authorisation — the address falls within the definition of 'lecture'.

A political leader delivering a public speech during an election rally in Chennai, where a media house broadcasts the speech and later sells compiled recordings commercially without consent — the speech qualifies as a 'lecture' under the Act.

A TED-style speaker delivering an original motivational talk at a corporate event in Bengaluru, whose presentation is recorded by the organiser and monetised on YouTube without the speaker's approval — the talk is protected as a 'lecture'.
what_it_covers: A formal academic lecture delivered by a university professor to students in a classroom or auditorium.
A political speech or public address delivered by a leader at a gathering or official function.
A religious sermon delivered by a priest, imam, or spiritual leader during a religious ceremony or gathering.
A keynote address delivered at a professional conference, seminar, or symposium.
An educational talk or discourse delivered via broadcast or through mechanical means, as contemplated by the definition of 'delivery' in the same section.
what_it_excludes: A dramatic performance or theatrical recitation that constitutes a 'dramatic work' under the Act, which has its own distinct category.
A musical performance or recital, which falls under the definition of 'musical work' rather than a lecture.
A purely written text or manuscript of a speech that has not been delivered orally, which would be treated as a 'literary work' rather than a lecture.
A cinematograph film or audio-visual recording in itself, which is governed under the definition of 'cinematograph film' in Section 2.
Spontaneous or informal conversation not intended as a structured oral presentation to an audience.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a spoken work as a 'lecture' determines whether it attracts copyright protection as a literary work and establishes who qualifies as its 'author' for the purposes of ownership and enforcement under the Act. It also directly engages the definition of 'delivery' in Section 2, which extends protection to lectures delivered by broadcast or mechanical means, meaning unauthorised recording, reproduction, or broadcast of a lecture can constitute copyright infringement.

definitions.definition: In the context of the Copyright Act, 1957, 'legal representatives' means the persons who in law represent the estate of a deceased person, including those who take the rights and liabilities of the deceased by operation of law such as heirs, executors, and administrators. As used in Section 18, the legal representatives of a deceased assignee step into the shoes of the assignee in respect of an assignment of copyright in a future work where the assignee dies before the work comes into existence; as used in Section 30, the legal representatives of a deceased licensee are entitled to the benefit of a licence relating to copyright in a future work in the absence of any contrary provision in the licence.
definitions.plain_english: Legal representatives are the people who are legally entitled to act on behalf of, or inherit the rights and obligations of, a person who has died. In copyright law, if someone was given a copyright assignment or licence but died before the work they were expecting actually came into being, their legal representatives — such as their heirs, executors, or administrators — would step in and enjoy those rights. Essentially, it ensures that a dead person's copyright interests are not lost but are passed on to the people who represent their estate.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based music composer assigns the copyright in a future film score to a production house and dies before the film is completed. The composer's legal heirs (spouse and children), acting as legal representatives, are entitled to enforce or receive the benefit of that assignment once the film score comes into existence.

A Delhi publisher grants a licence to a novelist for a yet-to-be-written novel and the novelist dies before completing the book. The novelist's executor, appointed under a will, steps in as the legal representative and is entitled to the benefit of the licence under Section 30 of the Copyright Act.

A Kolkata-based software developer enters into an assignment agreement transferring copyright in a future computer programme to a tech company but passes away during development. The developer's legal heirs, as legal representatives, acquire the assignee's rights under Section 18 once the programme is finalised.

An author of an unpublished literary work in Chennai dies intestate. Under Section 31A, when the Central Government directs publication in national interest, it issues the direction to the author's heirs and legal representatives, who must then publish the work or face compulsory licensing proceedings.

A Pune theatre director is granted a licence by a playwright for a future dramatic work and dies before the play is written. In the absence of any contrary clause in the licence, the director's legal representatives (children and surviving spouse as per succession law) are entitled under Section 30 to exploit the licence once the dramatic work comes into existence.
what_it_covers: Heirs of a deceased assignee who inherit the benefit of a copyright assignment in a future work that had not yet come into existence at the time of death.
Executors or administrators of the estate of a deceased licensee who are entitled to the benefit of a copyright licence in a future work under Section 30.

Legal heirs or representatives of a deceased author to whom royalties may be directed by the Registrar of Copyrights under Section 31A when the owner of copyright in an unpublished work cannot be found.
Persons appointed under a will (testamentary executors) or under letters of administration (court-appointed administrators) who represent the estate of the deceased assignee or licensee.
Legal heirs of a deceased author required by the Central Government under Section 31A to publish an unpublished work in national interest.
what_it_excludes: Legal heirs of the author in their capacity as recipients of inalienable royalty rights under the proviso to Section 18 — that is a distinct protective right for authors' heirs, not merely 'legal representatives' as defined in the assignment context.
Third parties or strangers to the estate who have no legal entitlement under succession law, even if they claim a moral or informal interest in the deceased's copyright.
A copyright society or collecting society, which is a separate institutional entity and not a legal representative of a deceased individual's estate.
A subsequent assignee or sub-licensee who derives rights through a commercial transaction rather than by operation of law upon the death of the assignee or licensee.
The assignor or original copyright owner, who retains rights not assigned and is not treated as a legal representative of the deceased assignee.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition determines whether copyright assignments and licences in future works survive the death of the assignee or licensee and vest in their estate, preventing valuable intellectual property rights from lapsing on death; if a claimant does not qualify as a legal representative, they cannot enforce or benefit from such assignments or licences and may be liable for infringement if they attempt to exploit the work.
