definitions.definition: The Act does not provide a standalone general definition of 'licence' in Section 2, but it is used throughout to mean a permission or authorisation granted by the owner of copyright in a work to another person to exercise any right comprised in the copyright, subject to such conditions and limitations as may be specified. An 'exclusive licence' is separately defined as a licence which confers on the licensee, or on the licensee and persons authorised by him, to the exclusion of all other persons (including the owner of the copyright), any right comprised in the copyright in a work.
definitions.plain_english: A licence under copyright law is essentially a permission slip given by the person who owns a copyright to someone else, allowing them to do something with the copyrighted work — such as copying, publishing, performing, or broadcasting it — that they would otherwise not be legally allowed to do. It does not transfer ownership of the copyright itself; the original owner retains the copyright. The licence can be limited to specific purposes, time periods, territories, or types of use, and may or may not be exclusive.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music label (copyright owner) grants a streaming platform like Spotify India a licence to make its catalogue of songs available to Indian subscribers for streaming, without transferring ownership of the sound recordings.

A Hindi novelist grants a film production house in Mumbai a licence to adapt her novel into a feature film, specifying that the licence is limited to India, is non-exclusive, and is valid for five years.

A software company based in Bengaluru licences its computer programme to a corporate client under an end-user licence agreement (EULA), permitting the client to install and use the software on a specified number of machines.

A copyright society such as IPRS (Indian Performing Right Society) issues blanket licences to hotel chains across India, permitting them to publicly perform musical works in the IPRS repertoire at their properties in exchange for a royalty fee.

A textbook publisher grants a licence to an educational institution in Kerala to reproduce selected chapters of a textbook for distribution to students enrolled in a specific course, subject to a per-copy royalty.

A photographer grants a newspaper in Delhi a one-time, non-exclusive licence to publish a specific photograph in its print and digital editions, with no right to sub-license or use the image for any other purpose.
what_it_covers: A written agreement by which a music composer permits a film producer to use a musical composition in a film in exchange for royalties, constituting a licence under Section 30.
A blanket licence issued by a registered copyright society under Section 33 to broadcasters permitting them to broadcast works in the society's repertoire subject to a tariff scheme.

A compulsory licence granted under Section 32B or Section 31 by the Copyright Board/Appellate Board allowing a person to publish or broadcast a work in the public interest where the owner withholds consent.
An exclusive licence under Section 2(j) read with Section 30A, granting the licensee sole rights to publish a literary work in a defined territory, to the exclusion of even the copyright owner.
A performer's licence granted under Section 37 by a performer allowing a broadcaster to broadcast a live performance.
A non-exclusive licence granted by a copyright owner to multiple publishers to print and distribute the same artistic work in different regional markets across India.
what_it_excludes: An assignment of copyright, which transfers ownership or a part thereof permanently to the assignee and is governed by Section 18, as opposed to a licence which does not transfer ownership.
Permissions that arise purely by operation of law or statutory exceptions such as fair dealing under Section 52, which do not require a licence from the copyright owner.
Moral rights (special rights) of an author under Section 57, which cannot be the subject of a licence since they are personal and inalienable to the author regardless of any licence granted.
Acts of mere possession or private use of a lawfully acquired copy, which do not require a licence as they fall outside the exclusive rights of the copyright owner.
A sub-licence granted by a licensee without express authorisation from the copyright owner, which has no legal validity under Indian copyright law.

Oral or implied permissions that do not meet the written requirements prescribed under Section 30, which mandates that licences under copyright be in writing and signed by the owner or his duly authorised agent.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a valid licence exists is legally decisive in determining copyright infringement under Section 51 — using a copyrighted work without a licence (or beyond its terms) constitutes infringement, attracting civil remedies and criminal penalties, whereas acting within the scope of a valid licence provides a complete defence. The existence, scope, and exclusivity of a licence also determine whether a licensee has standing to institute infringement proceedings and governs the rights of third parties, including sub-licensees and assignees.

definitions.definition: 'literary work' includes computer programmes, tables and compilations including computer databases.
definitions.plain_english: A literary work is any written or text-based creative work that is expressed in words, numbers, or symbols. It does not need to have any literary or artistic merit — even a simple list, a database, or a software program qualifies. The key requirement is that it be expressed in some form, not merely an idea in someone's mind.
real_world_examples: A Tamil novelist in Chennai writes and publishes a novel — the novel is a literary work protected under the Copyright Act, giving the author exclusive rights to reproduce and translate it.

A Bengaluru-based software company develops a mobile banking application — the source code and object code of that application are treated as a 'computer programme' falling under literary work, entitling the company to copyright protection.

A Mumbai publishing house compiles a railway timetable or a stock market data compilation — this table or compilation qualifies as a literary work, protecting the effort involved in selection and arrangement of data.

A Delhi-based ed-tech startup creates a proprietary database of UPSC exam questions and model answers — this computer database is explicitly covered as a literary work under Section 2(o), preventing competitors from copying it wholesale.
A journalist in Kolkata writes a news article for a daily newspaper — the article is a literary work, and the author or employer holds copyright in it, controlling reproduction in other publications.

An IIT professor in Pune authors a textbook on thermodynamics — the textbook is a literary work, granting the author or publisher exclusive rights to print, translate, and make adaptations for the term of copyright.
what_it_covers: Novels, poems, short stories, plays in script form, essays, and articles written in any language including regional Indian languages
Computer programmes including source code, object code, and scripts, regardless of the programming language used
Tables, compilations, and computer databases where there is some originality in selection or arrangement, such as a compiled legal digest or a curated product catalogue
Academic textbooks, research papers, lecture notes, and educational materials authored or compiled by individuals or institutions
Letters, emails, and personal diaries that are expressed in written or recorded form
Song lyrics and screenplay scripts (the literary component, distinct from any musical work or dramatic work element)
what_it_excludes: Musical works — a composition consisting of music and graphical notation is separately defined and protected as a 'musical work' under Section 2(p), not as a literary work
Dramatic works — choreographic works, scripts fixed for performance, and pieces for recitation are covered under 'dramatic work' and not under literary work
Mere ideas, concepts, principles, or information not expressed in any fixed form, as copyright does not protect ideas but only their expression
Artistic works such as paintings, sculptures, drawings, maps, and photographs, which fall under the separate definition of 'artistic work' under Section 2(c)
Cinematograph films and sound recordings, which have their own distinct categories and definitions under the Act
Raw, unoriginal data with no creative selection or arrangement, such as an alphabetical telephone directory held to lack sufficient originality
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as a 'literary work' determines if copyright subsists in it under Section 14, which in turn defines the bundle of exclusive economic rights the owner holds — including reproduction, translation, adaptation, and communication to the public. Misclassification can affect the term of protection (Section 22), eligibility for compulsory licensing (Sections 31C, 31D), assignment and licensing rights (Sections 18, 20), and liability for infringement under Sections 51 and 55.

definitions.definition: The expression 'manuscript' means the original document embodying the work, whether written by hand or not. In the context of Section 53A, it refers to the original manuscript of a literary, dramatic, or musical work that is subject to resale share rights.
definitions.plain_english: A manuscript is the original physical document in which a creative work — like a novel, play, or song — was first recorded or set down, regardless of whether it was handwritten or typed. It is not a copy or a printout made later; it is the actual original document itself. Think of it as the 'master original' from which everything else is derived.
real_world_examples: A renowned Hindi novelist from Lucknow passes away leaving behind the typed original pages of an unpublished novel; those typed sheets constitute the 'manuscript' and copyright passes to the legatee under Section 20.

A classical music composer from Chennai has hand-notated the original score of an unpublished raaga composition on paper; this hand-written score is the manuscript for purposes of Section 53A resale rights.

A Bollywood screenwriter's original printed script — the very first printout from the word processor bearing handwritten corrections — is auctioned at a Mumbai heritage sale for ₹15 lakhs, triggering the Section 53A resale share right in favour of the writer's legal heirs.

A deceased Marathi playwright's will bequeaths 'the manuscript of my unpublished play Antarnad' to a theatre foundation; under Section 20, the foundation acquires both the physical document and the copyright in the play because no contrary intention was expressed in the will.

An original typewritten manuscript of R.K. Narayan's unpublished short story, bearing his handwritten edits, is sold at a Bengaluru auction for ₹12 lakhs; the author's legal heirs are entitled to a share in the resale price under Section 53A.

A Delhi-based journalist's original typed investigative report — the first physical document embodying the work — is donated to a national archive; this constitutes the manuscript even though it was produced on a typewriter rather than written by hand.
what_it_covers: The original handwritten pages of a literary or dramatic work, such as a hand-penned novel or poem set down by the author.
The original typed or digitally printed first-generation document embodying a work, even if not written by hand, as explicitly stated in Section 20.
The original hand-notated musical score constituting the first physical record of a musical work.
An original typescript bearing handwritten corrections and annotations by the author, as the document that originally embodied the work.
The original document (whether produced by typewriter, word processor printout, or any other means) that is the primary, originating record of a literary, dramatic, or musical work.
what_it_excludes: Photocopies, scanned printouts, or reproductions of the original document, which are copies and not the original manuscript.
Published editions, printed books, or commercially reproduced versions of the work, as these are not the original document embodying the work.
Digital files stored on a computer or electronic medium, as these lack the character of an 'original document' in the physical sense contemplated by the Act.
Secondary drafts, revised copies, or duplicate printouts made after the first original, even if made by the author personally.
Artistic works such as paintings, sculptures, or drawings, which are governed separately under Section 53A and are not referred to as 'manuscripts'.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'manuscript' determines whether a testamentary bequest of that document automatically carries copyright in the underlying work under Section 20, and whether the author or legal heirs are entitled to a resale share right under Section 53A when that original document is resold for more than ten thousand rupees. Misclassifying a copy as a manuscript could wrongly vest or deny copyright ownership and deprive rightful heirs of statutory resale royalties.

definitions.definition: In the context of Section 38B of the Copyright Act, 1957, 'modification' means any change, alteration, or variation made to a performer's performance, including changes to the manner in which the performance is presented, reproduced, or communicated to the public, which is prejudicial to the performer's honour or reputation. It encompasses any distortion, mutilation, or other treatment of the performance that deviates from its original form as rendered by the performer.
definitions.plain_english: A 'modification' means any change made to a performer's original performance — such as altering, editing, distorting, or rearranging it — especially when that change harms how the performer is perceived by the public. For example, if a musician's live performance is edited in a way that makes it sound offensive or out of context, that would be a modification. It is essentially any tampering with the performance that differs from what the performer originally intended.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood playback singer's recorded live performance at a concert is digitally edited by a production house to include offensive lyrics or sounds, damaging the singer's public image — this constitutes a modification under Section 38B.

A classical Bharatanatyam dancer's performance footage is altered by a streaming platform by cropping out portions and adding unrelated background music, changing the artistic intent and harming her reputation in the dance community.

A stand-up comedian's performance video uploaded on YouTube is maliciously re-edited by a third party to make it appear the comedian made communally insensitive remarks, constituting a harmful modification of the original performance.

A tabla player's studio recording session is modified by a record label by overlaying it with electronic beats without consent, fundamentally altering the classical character of the performance and prejudicing the musician's standing among classical music patrons.

A theatre actor's stage performance recording is sped up, pitch-shifted, and used in a satirical advertisement without consent, distorting the original performance in a manner prejudicial to the actor's professional honour.
what_it_covers: Digital editing or remixing of a performer's recorded performance in a way that misrepresents or defames the performer.
Deliberate distortion, mutilation, or cropping of audio-visual recordings of a performance that damages the performer's reputation.
Adding, removing, or substituting elements of a performance recording — such as dubbing different words or sounds — without the performer's consent, altering its original character.
Alteration of the context in which a performance is presented, such as juxtaposing it with offensive content, so as to harm the performer's honour.
Any treatment of a performance — whether in print, digital, or broadcast form — that prejudicially changes how the performer is perceived by their audience or professional peers.
what_it_excludes: Technical adjustments such as standard audio mastering, volume normalisation, or format conversion that do not alter the artistic or expressive content of the performance.
Adaptations or arrangements made with the express written consent of the performer, which do not prejudice the performer's honour or reputation.
Fair dealing uses of a performance for purposes of criticism, review, or reporting of current events, provided they do not amount to prejudicial distortion.
Editorial cuts made for broadcast time constraints that do not misrepresent the performer or harm their professional reputation.
Modifications made to a work (as opposed to the performance itself) by the author or copyright owner, which fall under the author's moral rights rather than the performer's rights under Section 38B.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes a 'modification' under Section 38B determines whether a performer's moral rights — specifically the right to integrity of performance — have been infringed, entitling the performer to seek legal remedies including injunction and damages even after assignment of their performer's rights. It triggers liability for any person who alters a performance in a prejudicial manner, irrespective of whether they hold an economic licence over the performance.

definitions.definition: 'Musical work' means a work consisting of music and includes any graphical notation of such work but does not include any words or any action intended to be sung, spoken or performed with the music.
definitions.plain_english: A musical work is any original composition made up purely of music — the melody, harmony, and rhythm created by a composer. It includes the written sheet music or score (graphical notation) of that composition. Importantly, it does not cover the lyrics sung along with it or any choreography or actions performed to the music — those are treated separately under different categories.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood composer like A.R. Rahman creates the background score for a Hindi film — the orchestral arrangement and melodic composition constitute a 'musical work' under the Copyright Act, separate from the song lyrics written by the lyricist.

A classical Hindustani musician composes a new raag-based composition in Bhoopali and notates it on staff paper — both the composition itself and its written notation are protected as a 'musical work'.

An independent musician in Chennai produces an instrumental fusion track blending Carnatic and jazz elements and uploads it to a streaming platform — this instrumental track qualifies as a 'musical work' even though no words are sung.

A music teacher in Pune creates original piano exercises and publishes them as a sheet music book — the musical compositions, being represented as graphical notation, are protected as 'musical works' under the Act.

A jingle composed for a television advertisement by a Mumbai-based composer, consisting solely of a musical tune without any accompanying words, constitutes a 'musical work' entitled to copyright protection.

A folk music composer in Rajasthan transcribes and arranges a traditional folk tune into a new original composition — the arrangement, if sufficiently original, qualifies as a 'musical work', attracting copyright protection for the arranger.
what_it_covers: Original musical compositions consisting of melody, harmony, or rhythm created by a composer, even if never written down.
Any graphical notation or written score of a musical work, such as staff notation, sargam notation, or any other system of musical transcription.
Instrumental compositions that contain no sung words or lyrics, such as orchestral scores, background music, or instrumental fusion tracks.
Arrangements or transcriptions of existing musical works, to the extent they embody original creative input by the arranger.
Computer-generated musical compositions, where the person who causes the work to be created is recognised as the author.
what_it_excludes: Lyrics, words, or textual content intended to be sung or spoken along with the music — these are protected separately as 'literary works'.
Actions, choreography, or movements intended to be performed with the music — such elements may fall under 'dramatic work' but are expressly excluded from 'musical work'.
Sound recordings of musical works — a phonogram or audio recording is a distinct category of copyright subject matter governed by separate provisions.
Cinematograph films that incorporate music — the film as a whole is separately protected and not classified as a 'musical work'.
Mere rhythmic beats or sounds that do not constitute an original work of authorship, such as generic drum patterns with no original creative expression.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a creation qualifies as a 'musical work' directly determines who holds authorship (the composer), the duration of copyright protection (lifetime plus sixty years), and what acts constitute infringement — including unauthorised reproduction, public performance, broadcasting, or making cover versions under Section 31C. It also triggers specific compulsory licensing obligations under Section 31D for internet broadcasting organisations and governs the assignment of rights and royalties payable to composers through copyright societies.

definitions.definition: Mutilation, as used in the Copyright Act, refers to any unauthorised act of cutting, altering, distorting, or otherwise damaging the integrity of a work or a performance in a manner that is prejudicial to the honour or reputation of the author or the reputation of the performer. It is not formally defined in a standalone provision but is consistently employed in Sections 57 and 38B as a specific category of harmful modification distinct from mere editing or technical adjustment.
definitions.plain_english: Mutilation means seriously damaging or disfiguring a creative work or a performer's performance in a way that harms how the creator or performer is seen by others. Think of it as someone taking a painting, a song, or a dance performance and cutting or altering it so badly that it misrepresents or disrespects the original creator's vision and reputation. It is different from simple editing done for legitimate technical or time reasons.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music producer takes a classical vocalist's recorded performance and removes crucial melodic phrases and splices in off-key dubbing, releasing it commercially in a way that makes the vocalist sound unskilled — this constitutes mutilation of the performer's performance under Section 38B.

A regional publisher reproduces a celebrated Hindi poet's poem but deliberately omits several stanzas that carry the poem's central moral argument, publishing the truncated version under the poet's name in a way that makes the poem appear shallow and contrary to the poet's known views — this amounts to mutilation of a literary work under Section 57.

A digital streaming platform uses automated cropping tools that cut off the edges of a noted Indian painter's digital artwork displayed on their interface, distorting the composition and colour balance in a manner that makes the work look amateurish — this constitutes mutilation of an artistic work prejudicial to the painter's honour.

A theatre company performs a renowned playwright's original Marathi drama but rewrites entire scenes to insert crude humour, then credits the original playwright — the alteration so fundamentally changes the dramatic work that it constitutes mutilation prejudicial to the playwright's reputation under Section 57.

A television channel airs a classical Bharatanatyam dancer's recorded stage performance but edits out the devotional sequences and replaces them with unrelated pop-music overlays, misrepresenting the dancer's artistic intent — this constitutes mutilation of the performer's performance under Section 38B.
what_it_covers: Deliberate removal or alteration of substantial portions of a work or performance that misrepresents the creator's or performer's artistic vision in a reputationally harmful way.
Splicing, dubbing, or digitally manipulating a performer's recorded performance so that it no longer accurately reflects the performer's skill or intent, to their reputational detriment.
Physical or digital defacement of an artistic work, such as a painting or sculpture, that destroys its compositional integrity and prejudicially reflects on the author's honour.
Combining a work or performance with objectionable or contradictory content in a manner that tarnishes the reputation of the author or performer even if individual elements remain intact.
what_it_excludes: Mere removal of a portion of a performance for the purpose of editing or to fit a recording within a limited broadcast duration, as explicitly clarified under Section 38B proviso.

Any modification required purely for technical reasons such as format conversion, compression, or platform compatibility adjustments that do not prejudicially affect the author's or performer's reputation.
Adaptations of a computer programme permitted under clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of Section 52, which the author cannot restrain even under the moral rights provision of Section 57.

Failure to display a work or displaying it in a manner unsatisfactory to the author, which is expressly excluded from the scope of Section 57 rights and therefore cannot constitute mutilation by mere non-display.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as mutilation determines whether an author or performer can invoke moral rights under Sections 57 or 38B respectively to restrain the act or claim damages, independently of any copyright assignment — meaning even a creator who has sold all economic rights retains the power to sue for mutilation. definitions.definition: A 'non-commercial public library' is a library that is open to the public and is not established or conducted for the purpose of making profit or commercial gain, as used in Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957 in the context of acts that do not constitute infringement of copyright, including the electronic storage of works for preservation and the making of not more than three copies of a book unavailable for sale in India.
definitions.plain_english: A non-commercial public library is a library that is accessible to the general public and does not operate for profit. It is run to serve the public interest — such as a government library, municipal library, or charitable library — rather than to earn money. Such libraries receive special permissions under copyright law to preserve and copy works in limited circumstances without being liable for copyright infringement.
real_world_examples: The National Library of India in Kolkata, a government-funded public institution, stores a digital copy of an old Hindi novel for preservation purposes because it already holds a physical print copy — this is permitted under Section 52(n).

A district public library in Pune run by the local municipal corporation makes two photocopies of a rare academic textbook on Indian classical music that is out of print and unavailable for sale in India, for use within the library — permitted under Section 52(o).

The Delhi Public Library, a non-profit institution open to all citizens, digitises a deteriorating manuscript for archival preservation since it holds the original physical copy, without seeking the publisher's permission — valid under the copyright exception.

A charitable trust-run public library in Chennai, open free of charge to the community, makes three copies of a rare out-of-print legal commentary not available for sale in India, for lending within its reading rooms — covered under Section 52(o).

A state government-operated public library in Bhopal electronically stores a regional language literary work to prevent loss due to deterioration of its only physical copy, qualifying as a non-commercial public library under Section 52(n).

The Asiatic Society Library in Mumbai, a non-profit public research library, preserves a rare colonial-era map by storing it electronically, having already possessed a physical copy — this falls within the permitted acts under Section 52.
what_it_covers: A government-funded public library open to all citizens without a commercial membership fee, such as a national, state, or municipal library.
A library run by a charitable trust or non-profit organisation that provides free or subsidised access to the public and does not distribute profits.
A public university or institution library that is open to the general public and does not operate for commercial gain.
A library operated by a local body (e.g., panchayat or municipality) for the benefit of the community with no profit motive.
An institution that already holds a non-digital copy of a work and seeks to preserve it by creating an electronic version under Section 52(n).
what_it_excludes: A commercial lending library that charges subscription or rental fees for borrowing books as a profit-making business.
A private members-only library or club library that restricts access to paying members and operates for commercial gain.
A hotel, resort, or commercial establishment that maintains a library or reading room for its paying guests as part of a profit-driven hospitality service.
An online digital library platform that sells or licenses access to digital content for profit, even if it labels itself a library.
A library run by a private company exclusively for its employees and not accessible to the general public, even if non-profit in intent.

definitions.definition: An 'officer' under the Copyright Act refers to any person duly authorised by a competent authority — including the Central Government, the Commissioner of Customs, or any other empowered body — to exercise statutory functions under the Act, such as inspecting records, enforcing prohibitions, or executing provisions of the Act. The term encompasses government officials acting in an official capacity in the execution of the provisions of this Act, as contemplated in Section 68.
definitions.plain_english: An 'officer' is any government official or authorised person who has been given the power to carry out duties under the Copyright Act. This could be someone checking compliance at a copyright society, a customs official stopping pirated goods at the border, or a police officer seizing illegal copies of a book or film. The term is used broadly to cover anyone in an official role who enforces or administers the law under the Act.
real_world_examples: A sub-inspector of police in Mumbai who raids a shop selling pirated DVDs and seizes the infringing copies under Section 64 is acting as an 'officer' in the execution of the Act's provisions.

A Central Government-authorised official who visits the Indian Performing Right Society (IPRS) in Delhi to inspect its financial records and verify that royalties are being properly distributed to member composers and lyricists under Section 36.

A Commissioner of Customs at Chennai Port who, upon receiving notice from a Bollywood production house, detains a shipment of pirated Blu-ray discs being imported from China, acting as an 'officer' authorised under Section 53.

A Registrar of Copyrights or their delegated official who receives and processes applications for copyright registration at the Copyright Office in New Delhi, exercising statutory authority under the Act.

A person who submits forged documentation to a Copyright Office official in Kolkata, falsely claiming ownership of a literary work to obtain registration, is deceiving an 'officer' within the meaning of Section 68 and is liable for criminal punishment.

A customs officer at Indira Gandhi International Airport in Delhi who detains imported textbooks suspected of being unauthorised reproductions of Indian educational publications, following a notice from the publisher under Section 53.
what_it_covers: A police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector authorised to seize infringing copies under Section 64 of the Act.
A Central Government-authorised official empowered to call for reports and records from copyright societies under Section 36.
The Commissioner of Customs or any officer authorised by the Central Board of Excise and Customs to treat infringing copies as prohibited goods under Section 53.
The Registrar of Copyrights and officials of the Copyright Office who exercise functions conferred by the Act.
Any customs officer who detains goods and notifies parties of detention under Section 53 of the Act.
what_it_excludes: Private individuals or agents of copyright owners, such as lawyers or authorised representatives, who do not hold a public or government-delegated statutory role under the Act.
Officers of private companies or copyright societies themselves, who are not acting under government authorisation to execute provisions of the Act.
Judicial officers such as Magistrates or judges, who exercise judicial rather than executive or administrative functions under the Act and are addressed separately.
Informal or self-appointed enforcement actors, such as anti-piracy personnel employed by film studios, who lack statutory authorisation under the Copyright Act.
Foreign government officials or officers of international organisations who have not been specifically authorised under Indian law to execute provisions of this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'officer' is critical for triggering criminal liability under Section 68: any person who makes a false statement or representation to deceive an 'officer' in the execution of the Act's provisions is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, a fine, or both. Whether the recipient of a false statement qualifies as an 'officer' directly determines whether the offence under Section 68 is made out.

definitions.definition: An 'organisation' in the context of the Copyright Act refers to an international organisation as contemplated under Section 41, being a body established by a treaty, convention, or agreement between two or more States or governments, to which the provisions relating to copyright in works of international organisations apply. The term encompasses any such body that is recognised as an international organisation for the purposes of copyright subsistence and protection under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An 'organisation' here refers to an international body formed by agreement between multiple countries or governments, such as the United Nations or the World Health Organization. Works created or published by such bodies receive special copyright protection under Indian copyright law. This is distinct from a private company or domestic government body.
real_world_examples: The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes a technical health report in India — as an international organisation, the copyright in that report is protected under Section 41 of the Copyright Act, lasting 60 years from first publication.

UNESCO produces an educational curriculum guide distributed in India — UNESCO, being an international organisation formed by treaty among member states, qualifies under Section 41, and its works receive copyright protection accordingly.

The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) releases a climate report first published in India — the copyright in this work subsists for 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following the year of publication, as governed by Section 29 read with Section 41.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) publishes a labour standards manual for use in Indian factories — this publication, created by an intergovernmental organisation, is protected as a work of an international organisation under the Act.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) issues a trade policy report first published in New Delhi — this falls under the special copyright regime applicable to international organisations, distinct from works authored by Indian citizens or companies.
what_it_covers: Intergovernmental organisations established by international treaties or conventions between two or more sovereign states, such as the United Nations, UNESCO, or WHO.
Bodies formed by multilateral agreements between governments that publish works for international or domestic use, where copyright is vested in the organisation itself.

Any international body recognised by the Central Government under Section 41 as an organisation to which special copyright provisions apply, including those with a presence or publication activity in India.
what_it_excludes: Private multinational corporations or companies incorporated under domestic law of any country, even if operating internationally.
Domestic Indian government bodies, public undertakings, or statutory authorities operating solely within India, which fall under 'Government work' provisions instead.
Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) or civil society bodies, even if operating across multiple countries, as they are not established by intergovernmental treaty.
Foreign societies or organisations administering copyright rights on behalf of authors, as referred to in Section 34, which are distinct from international organisations under Section 41.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a body qualifies as an 'organisation' under Section 41 determines whether its works receive the special 60-year copyright term under Section 29, as opposed to the standard author's lifetime plus 60 years term. This classification directly affects whether copyright subsists, for how long, and who can enforce or licence the work in India.

definitions.definition: An original literary work is a work falling within the class of literary works in which copyright subsists under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957, provided that it originates from the author and is the product of the author's own skill, judgment, and creative effort, and not merely a copy of another work. The term 'original' does not require novelty or inventiveness but demands that the work has not been slavishly copied and bears the imprint of the author's independent intellectual effort.
definitions.plain_english: An original literary work is any written or expressed work — such as a novel, poem, article, computer code, or database — that was created by the author using their own skill and effort, rather than simply copied from someone else. The word 'original' here does not mean the idea has to be new or unique; it just means the author produced it themselves. Such works automatically receive copyright protection in India.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based author writes a Hindi novel set in rural Maharashtra — this is an original literary work protected under copyright from the moment it is written down.
A software developer in Bengaluru independently writes source code for a mobile banking application — the code qualifies as an original literary work under the Copyright Act, 1957.
A professor at Delhi University compiles and annotates a collection of legal judgments with original commentary — the compilation and commentary together constitute an original literary work.

A journalist in Chennai writes an investigative article about water pollution for a national newspaper — the article is an original literary work and copyright vests in the journalist or their employer depending on the employment contract.
A Kolkata-based screenwriter drafts the dialogue and script for a web series — the script, as an original literary work, enjoys copyright protection separate from the cinematograph film made from it.

A data scientist in Hyderabad creates an original database with a unique selection and arrangement of publicly available financial data — the database qualifies as an original literary work to the extent the selection and arrangement reflect independent intellectual effort.
what_it_covers: Novels, poems, short stories, and essays written by an Indian author using their own creative effort.
Computer programmes and source code independently developed by a programmer, as computer programmes are expressly included in the definition of literary work under the Act.
Original compilations, databases, or anthologies where the selection or arrangement reflects the author's independent intellectual effort.
Academic theses, research papers, and textbooks authored by scholars or educators with original expression of ideas.
Translations and adaptations that themselves involve sufficient original creative effort by the translator or adapter.
what_it_excludes: Works that are mere copies or reproductions of existing works without any independent creative contribution from the purported author.
Ideas, concepts, principles, methods, or facts in themselves — copyright protects original expression, not the underlying idea.
Works that do not meet the citizenship, domicile, or publication nexus conditions specified under Section 13(2), regardless of their originality.
Works created by someone other than a human author (e.g., purely machine-generated text with no human creative input), as authorship requires a human originator under the Act.
Purely functional or mechanical arrangements of words or data where no skill, judgment, or creativity was exercised in their selection or arrangement.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as an 'original literary work' is the threshold condition for copyright to subsist under Section 13(1)(a); if it does not meet this standard, no copyright protection arises and the work falls into the public domain, meaning no infringement action can be brought for its unauthorised use. Conversely, once a work is recognised as an original literary work, it triggers the full suite of exclusive rights, moral rights, and remedies available to the copyright owner under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'owner' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957, but as used in sections 30 and 56, it refers to the owner of copyright in a work, being the person or entity in whom the copyright vests — whether as the first owner under section 17, an assignee under section 18, or a successor-in-interest — and who holds the exclusive rights conferred by the Act in respect of that work.
definitions.plain_english: The 'owner' is the person or organisation who legally holds the copyright in a creative work. This could be the original creator, a company that commissioned the work, or someone who has legally received the copyright through a formal transfer or inheritance. The owner is the one who has the right to permit or prevent others from using the work.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based publishing house that commissioned and paid for a textbook to be written by a freelance author under a contract of service becomes the owner of copyright in that textbook and can grant licences to reproduce it under Section 30.

A Bollywood music label that obtained a valid written assignment of copyright from a film composer is the owner of the musical work and can initiate infringement proceedings under Section 56 against an unauthorised streaming platform.
A software company in Bengaluru whose employee developed a computer programme in the course of employment holds ownership of the copyright and may license or restrict its use as per the Act.

An heir who inherits copyright through a bequest in the will of a deceased Punjabi novelist becomes the new owner of copyright and can grant or withhold licences for translation or adaptation of the novels.

A Hyderabad-based film production house that produced a cinematograph film is the owner of copyright in the film and can take action under Section 56 against cable operators who broadcast the film without permission.
A photographer in Chennai who personally takes wedding photographs and has not assigned the copyright to anyone remains the owner and can licence or refuse commercial use of those photographs.
what_it_covers: The original creator of a work in whom copyright first vests as first owner under Section 17 of the Act.

The owner has the exclusive right to reproduce, publish, adapt, and otherwise exploit the work.
real_world_examples: A software developer employed by an IT company in Bengaluru writes code during the course of employment under a contract of service — the IT company, as employer, is the first owner of copyright in that software, not the individual developer.

A Bollywood music composer creates an original score independently and assigns the recording rights to a Mumbai-based music label — the composer remains owner of the underlying musical work for non-assigned rights, while the label becomes owner for the assigned rights, such as broadcast reproduction.

A freelance photographer in Delhi is commissioned by a magazine to photograph a celebrity for valuable consideration — the magazine (commissioning person) becomes the first owner of copyright in those photographs under Section 17(b), absent any contrary agreement.

A novelist from Jaipur publishes a book independently without any employment or commission arrangement — she is the first and continuing owner of copyright in that literary work, entitled to grant compulsory licences under Section 31A or object to infringement under Section 51.

A documentary filmmaker assigns partial rights (theatrical distribution) to a streaming platform while retaining broadcast rights — both the filmmaker and the platform are co-owners for their respective portions and can independently act against infringement within their share.

The Government of India commissions a report through its ministry employees in the course of their official duties — the Government becomes the first owner of copyright in that Government work under Section 17(d), and can grant or refuse licences under Section 32A.

definitions.definition: "Owner of right" refers to the person who holds the relevant copyright or related right (including broadcast reproduction right or performer's right) in a work, and in whose favour such right subsists under the Act at the relevant time, including any assignee or successor-in-title to such right.
definitions.plain_english: The 'owner of right' is simply the person or entity who legally holds a particular copyright or related right in a creative work at any given point in time. This could be the original creator, a company that bought the rights, or anyone who has legally received those rights through an assignment or inheritance. It is the person who can exercise, licence, or enforce that specific right.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music composer assigns the recording rights of his songs to a major music label such as T-Series; T-Series becomes the owner of right for those sound recordings and can register with a copyright society or grant licences under Section 34 and 35.

A Delhi-based publishing house acquires the translation rights to a bestselling Hindi novel; it becomes the owner of right to authorise or prohibit translations, and can approach the Copyright Board if a compulsory licence is sought under Section 32.

All India Radio holds broadcast reproduction rights over its live cricket commentary recordings; as owner of right it can take action under Section 53 to prevent importation of infringing copies of those broadcasts at Indian ports.

A Pune-based software company creates a computer programme and assigns copyright to an investor; the investor, as the new owner of right, is entitled to be a member of a copyright society under Section 34 and to authorise the society to collect royalties on its behalf.

A cinematograph film producer based in Mumbai dies and bequeaths all copyright in his films to his daughter; she becomes the owner of right and can instruct a copyright society or pursue border enforcement remedies under Section 53 against pirated DVD imports.
A classical dancer registers her performer's right; as owner of right she can object under Section 35 to a copyright society acting beyond the scope of rights she has authorised it to administer.
what_it_covers: The original author or creator of a work in whom copyright first vests under Section 17 of the Act.
An assignee who has received copyright or a specific right comprised in copyright through a written assignment under Section 19.
A legal heir or legatee who inherits copyright upon the death of the original owner.
A producer of a cinematograph film or sound recording who is deemed the author and first owner of copyright in those works.
A broadcasting organisation that holds broadcast reproduction rights and is therefore the owner of that specific right.
A performer who holds performer's right under Chapter VIII and is accordingly the owner of that right for purposes of Sections 34 and 35.
what_it_excludes: A mere licensee (including an exclusive licensee) who has been granted permission to exercise a right but has not been assigned ownership of the right itself.
A copyright society registered under Section 33, which administers rights on behalf of owners but does not itself become the owner of those rights.
An employee or contractor who creates a work in the course of employment where the employer is the first owner, unless the rights have been expressly reassigned to that individual.
A distributor or retailer of legitimately purchased copies of a work, who holds no right in the underlying copyright.
A user who obtains a compulsory licence under Sections 31–32B, as such a licence confers authorised use, not ownership of the right.

definitions.definition: "Owner of rights" is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Copyright Act, 1957, but as used in Sections 31C and 31D, it refers to the person or entity in whom the rights in a work vest, including the copyright owner or any person who has been assigned or otherwise holds the relevant rights in the underlying literary, musical, or other work in question, and who is entitled to receive royalties or grant licences in respect of those rights.
definitions.plain_english: The 'owner of rights' is the person or organisation who legally holds the rights over a creative work — such as a song, poem, or book. This could be the original creator, a company that has bought or been assigned those rights, or a legal heir who inherited them. In the context of the Copyright Act, this person is entitled to receive payment (royalties) when their work is used under a statutory licence, such as for cover versions or broadcast purposes.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based music composer who has retained the musical rights to his compositions is the 'owner of rights' when a radio station seeks a statutory licence under Section 31D to broadcast his songs.

A Delhi publishing house that has acquired full copyright in a novel through a deed of assignment from the original author becomes the 'owner of rights' entitled to royalties when a cover version of an audio adaptation is made under Section 31C.

A Bollywood production company that owns the music rights in a film soundtrack is the 'owner of rights' and must be approached and compensated when an internet streaming platform broadcasts those songs under Section 31D.

The legal heirs of a deceased Carnatic music composer based in Chennai, who have inherited the copyright in his unpublished compositions, are the 'owners of rights' for the purposes of receiving royalties under a statutory licence.

A copyright society such as IPRS (Indian Performing Right Society), acting on behalf of its member composers and lyricists, effectively represents the 'owner of rights' when negotiating and collecting royalties under Section 31D statutory broadcasting licences.
what_it_covers: The original author or composer who has not assigned or licensed away their rights and retains full ownership of the copyright.
A company or individual who has received a valid assignment of copyright in a literary, musical, or artistic work and thus holds the rights in that work.
Legal heirs or successors who have inherited the copyright in a work upon the death of the original author, and are entitled to receive royalties under a statutory licence.
A copyright society registered under Section 33 that administers rights on behalf of its members and collects royalties as the representative of the owner of rights.
A producer or publisher who is the first owner of copyright by operation of law, such as in a work made under a contract of service or a commissioned work.
what_it_excludes: A mere licensee who has been granted a non-exclusive licence to use the work but does not own or hold the underlying rights.
A distributor or retailer of copies of a work who has no proprietary interest in the copyright itself.
A performer whose performance rights are recognised separately under the Act, unless they are also the copyright owner of the underlying literary or musical work.
A person who has an equitable or contractual claim to ownership that has not been formalised through a written assignment as required under the Act.
An assignee of merely neighbouring or related rights (such as broadcast reproduction rights) who does not hold rights in the underlying literary or musical work referenced in Sections 31C and 31D.

definitions.definition: "performance", in relation to a performer's right, means any visual or acoustic presentation made live by one or more performers; and includes a performance in a cinematograph film or sound recording.
definitions.plain_english: A 'performance' is a live presentation — whether seen, heard, or both — given by one or more performers, such as a singer on stage, a dancer, or an actor. It also covers performances that have been captured in a film or sound recording. Essentially, it refers to the act of presenting a creative work live before an audience, whether in person or recorded.
real_world_examples: A classical Carnatic vocalist performing live at the Margazhi Music Festival in Chennai, where their singing constitutes a 'performance' attracting performer's rights.
A Bollywood playback singer recording a song in a Mumbai studio — that recorded rendition qualifies as a 'performance' within a sound recording for the purposes of the Act.
A Bharatanatyam dancer performing live at the Konark Dance Festival in Odisha — her visual and acoustic presentation is a protected 'performance' under Section 38.
A stand-up comedian performing live at a venue in Bengaluru, where their live delivery of jokes and expressions before an audience constitutes a 'performance'.
An actor's performance in a Bollywood film captured on a cinematograph film — this recorded performance is covered within the definition of 'performance' for the purposes of performer's rights.
A tabla player performing live at a concert in Delhi — both the acoustic and visual elements of their live rendition are protected as a 'performance' under the Copyright Act.
what_it_covers: Live singing, dancing, acting, or musical rendition presented before an audience in any venue.
A performer's contribution captured within a cinematograph film, such as an actor's role in a Hindi feature film.
A musician's recorded rendition in a sound recording, such as a playback singer's voice in an audio track.
Live recitations, dramatic enactments, or choreographic works presented visually and acoustically.
Performances broadcast live or diffused to the public via radio, television, or digital means.
what_it_excludes: The underlying literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work itself — the performance is distinct from the work being performed.
A mere broadcast or re-broadcast of a pre-recorded work where no live performer is involved in that instance.
Computer-generated audio-visual outputs produced without any human performer's live input.
The physical medium or copy (e.g., a vinyl record or DVD) as an object — the definition covers the presentation, not the carrier.
Mechanical or automated playback of a pre-recorded track without any live human performative element.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as a 'performance' determines whether performer's rights under Sections 38, 38A, and 38B vest in the performer, entitling them to royalties, moral rights, and protection against unauthorised reproduction or broadcast. It also governs eligibility for compulsory licensing under Section 31D, fair dealing exceptions under Section 52, and liability for infringement under Sections 53 and 65B.

definitions.definition: A work is 'performed in public' when it is performed before an audience in a public setting with the licence of the owner of the copyright; a performance made without such licence shall not be deemed to be a performance in public except for the purposes of determining infringement of copyright.
definitions.plain_english: A performance 'in public' means presenting a work (like a play, song, or lecture) to an audience outside of a purely private or domestic setting, but only when the copyright owner has given permission for it. If someone performs a work without the copyright owner's permission, it is not counted as a legitimate public performance under the law — except when the question is whether copyright was infringed. This distinction affects how long copyright lasts and whether a work can be considered 'published' or publicly available.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai theatre company stages a performance of a copyrighted Hindi play with the playwright's written permission — this counts as a valid 'performance in public' and can be used to determine whether the work has entered the public domain.

A Bengaluru music school conducts a public concert featuring a copyrighted classical composition without obtaining a licence from the copyright owner — this performance is NOT deemed a 'performance in public' for purposes like calculating posthumous copyright terms, but it IS treated as one for determining copyright infringement.

A deceased Tamil poet's unpublished literary work is publicly recited at a Chennai literary festival with the permission of the poet's legal heirs (as copyright owners) — this licensed performance in public can trigger the start of the copyright term under Section 24 for posthumous works.

A Bollywood film production house performs songs from an upcoming movie at a paid press event open to the public, having obtained a performing rights licence — this qualifies as a performance in public and establishes the work as having been made accessible, relevant for compulsory licence proceedings under Section 31.

A Delhi-based NGO organises a free open-air screening and live dramatic reading of a copyrighted short story without the author's consent — while not a valid 'performance in public' for copyright term calculation, it constitutes infringement, showing the dual operation of Section 4.
what_it_covers: A licensed stage performance of a dramatic or musical work before a paying or free public audience in India.
A public recitation or reading of a literary work conducted with the express permission of the copyright owner, such as at a literary festival or public event.

A public concert or musical performance authorised by the copyright owner or a registered copyright society, which can serve as the triggering event for posthumous copyright term calculation under Section 24.
A licensed public performance of a work that has been withheld, relevant to compulsory licence proceedings under Section 31 where the owner's refusal to allow performance is challenged.
what_it_excludes: A performance of a copyrighted work without the licence of the copyright owner — such an unauthorised performance is not 'deemed' to be a performance in public except for the purpose of establishing copyright infringement.
Private or domestic performances, such as a family gathering where a copyrighted song is sung within a home, which do not constitute performances 'in public' regardless of consent.

A performance before a purely internal or closed institutional audience (e.g., an in-house corporate rehearsal not open to any external public), which would not satisfy the 'public' element of the definition.

Unauthorised street performances or flash mobs performing copyrighted choreography or music without a licence, which cannot be relied upon to establish publication or public performance for copyright term or posthumous work purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work has been 'performed in public' (with the owner's licence) determines whether it qualifies as 'published' for the purposes of Section 24, thereby triggering the 60-year posthumous copyright term for unpublished literary, dramatic, or musical works. It also determines eligibility for compulsory licence proceedings under Section 31, where only works that have been published or performed in public can be the subject of a complaint — making this definition a gateway to both copyright duration calculations and compulsory licensing remedies.

definitions.definition: "performer" includes an actor, singer, musician, dancer, acrobat, juggler, conjurer, snake charmer, a person delivering a lecture or any other person who makes a performance.
definitions.plain_english: A performer is any person who presents or enacts something live before an audience, such as an actor in a play, a singer at a concert, a dancer, a musician, or even someone delivering a speech or lecture. The term is broadly defined and covers a wide range of live artistic and expressive acts. It does not matter whether the performance is formal or informal — what matters is that the person is actively making a performance.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood playback singer performing live at a concert in Mumbai is a performer, and any unauthorized recording or broadcast of that concert requires the singer's consent under the Copyright Act.

A Bharatanatyam dancer performing at the Sangeet Natak Akademi festival in Delhi holds performer's rights in her live performance, protecting it from being recorded and commercially distributed without her permission.

A stand-up comedian performing at a comedy club in Bengaluru is a performer, meaning any unauthorized streaming or recording of his act on YouTube or OTT platforms would infringe his performer's right.

A classical Hindustani musician playing the sitar at the Dover Lane Music Conference in Kolkata is a performer, and a music label cannot record and sell the live performance as an album without obtaining the musician's consent.
A snake charmer performing a traditional act at a cultural fair in Rajasthan is explicitly covered under the definition, meaning even folk and traditional performers enjoy protection under the Act.

A professor delivering a keynote lecture at an IIT convocation is a performer, so broadcasting or commercially reproducing that lecture without consent could constitute infringement of performer's rights.
what_it_covers: Actors performing in theatrical productions, television serials, or films during live stage readings or performances.
Classical and contemporary musicians, singers, and instrumentalists performing live at concerts or public events.
Dancers, acrobats, jugglers, conjurers, and snake charmers presenting their acts before an audience.
Persons delivering lectures, speeches, or addresses in public, including academic or motivational speakers.
Stand-up comedians, mimics, and entertainers performing live acts before a gathered audience.
what_it_excludes: A film producer or director who does not personally perform before an audience — they are covered under the definition of 'author' as producer of a cinematograph film, not as a performer.
A composer or lyricist who only creates a musical work without performing it live — their rights are governed as authors of a literary or musical work, not as performers.
A sound engineer or technician who records or mixes a performance but does not himself make a performance is excluded from the definition of performer.
A broadcaster or broadcasting organisation that transmits a performance — they hold broadcast reproduction rights, not performer's rights.
A choreographer who only creates and notates a choreographic work without personally performing it may not qualify as a performer in respect of that work.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'performer' under the Act determines whether they hold statutory performer's rights under Sections 38, 38A, and 38B, which grant them the exclusive right to control reproduction, broadcasting, and communication of their performance to the public for fifty years. If this definition applies, unauthorized recording, reproduction, or broadcast of the performance constitutes infringement of performer's rights, triggering civil and criminal liability; if it does not apply, the person has no such independent rights under the Act.

definitions.definition: Where any performer appears or engages in any performance, he shall have a special right to be known as the 'performer's right' in relation to such performance. The performer's right shall subsist until fifty years from the beginning of the calendar year next following the year in which the performance is made.
definitions.plain_english: A performer's right is a special legal protection given to a person who performs — such as a singer, actor, dancer, or musician — over their live or recorded performance. It gives the performer control over how their performance is used, copied, or broadcast by others. This right lasts for 50 years from the year in which the performance took place. It exists independently from the copyright in the underlying work being performed.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood playback singer records a song for a film. If a streaming platform wants to use that recorded performance in an advertisement without permission, the singer can invoke their performer's right to prevent or seek compensation for such use.

A classical Bharatanatyam dancer performs at a cultural festival in Chennai. A television channel records and broadcasts the performance without her consent. She can claim infringement of her performer's right under Section 38.

A stand-up comedian performs a live show in Mumbai, which is recorded and uploaded to YouTube without permission by an audience member. The comedian can take down the video by asserting their performer's right over the performance.

A tabla maestro participates in a live concert in Varanasi. A music label wishes to commercially release a recording of the concert. The label must obtain the maestro's consent under his performer's right, even if the underlying compositions are in the public domain.

A Bollywood actor's dialogue delivery in a film is used in a remix video without permission. The actor can assert their performer's right to seek removal or royalties for such unauthorized use of their performance.
what_it_covers: Live performances by singers, musicians, dancers, actors, acrobats, and entertainers who physically appear and engage in the performance.
The right to control reproduction, broadcasting, and communication to the public of a performer's performance for a period of 50 years from the calendar year following the year of performance.
Rights enforceable against unauthorized sound recordings or visual recordings of a performance made for commercial exploitation.
Performances that are recorded and then later broadcast or streamed without the performer's consent, entitling the performer to take legal action.
The performer's right as it applies through provisions such as assignment, licensing, and enforcement mechanisms incorporated by Section 39A.
what_it_excludes: The making of a sound or visual recording of a performance for strictly private use by the person making the recording, which does not infringe the performer's right under Section 39.
Use of excerpts of a performance consistent with fair dealing for purposes such as reporting of current events, bona fide review, teaching, or research, which is expressly exempt under Section 39.
Any broadcast or performance that itself constitutes an infringement of copyright in the underlying work — no performer's right subsists in such a performance per Section 39A.
The performer's right does not override or merge with the separate copyright in the underlying literary, musical, or dramatic work being performed; it is a distinct, independent right.
Performances that have exceeded the 50-year subsistence period calculated from the beginning of the calendar year following the year in which the performance was made.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a performer's right applies determines whether consent and licensing from the performer are required before reproducing, broadcasting, or commercially exploiting a performance — failure to obtain such consent constitutes infringement attracting civil remedies and criminal liability under sections incorporated by reference through Section 39A, including Sections 55, 63, and 64. It also determines whether assignments or licences granted by the performer are legally valid and enforceable against third parties.

definitions.definition: A performing rights society means an association of persons that was functioning in the business of issuing or granting licences in respect of any work in which copyright subsists or in respect of any other rights conferred by this Act, in accordance with the provisions of section 33 on the date immediately before the coming into force of the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994 (38 of 1994), and which is deemed to be a copyright society for the purposes of Chapter VII upon such commencement.
definitions.plain_english: A performing rights society is an organisation that existed before 1994 and was already in the business of giving out licences for the use of copyrighted works — such as music or performances — on behalf of copyright owners. After the 1994 amendment to the Copyright Act, such societies were automatically treated as copyright societies and were required to re-register within one year. Essentially, it is the predecessor form of what is now called a 'copyright society' under Indian law.
real_world_examples: The Indian Performing Right Society (IPRS), which was issuing licences for the public performance and broadcast of musical and literary works before the 1994 amendment, was a classic performing rights society and was deemed a copyright society under the transitional provision of Section 33.

A radio broadcasting company in Mumbai seeking permission to play Bollywood songs on air before 1994 would have approached a performing rights society for a licence, rather than negotiating with each individual composer or lyricist.

A hotel chain in Delhi that played background music in its lobbies and restaurants before 1994 would have obtained a blanket licence from a performing rights society, which collected and distributed royalties to the original music creators.

An event management company organising live concerts across India before 1994 relied on performing rights societies to clear the rights for musical performances, avoiding the need to contact hundreds of individual copyright owners.

Doordarshan, before the 1994 amendment, paid licence fees to a performing rights society for broadcasting copyrighted musical works, with the society acting as a centralised body collecting and distributing those fees to authors and composers.
what_it_covers: An association of persons that was actively issuing or granting licences for copyrighted works immediately before the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994 came into force, and was operating in accordance with section 33 at that time.
Organisations like the Indian Performing Right Society (IPRS) that managed the collective licensing of musical, literary, and dramatic works on behalf of multiple copyright owners before 1994.

Any society transitionally deemed to be a copyright society under Chapter VII by virtue of the proviso to Section 33(1), pending its fresh registration within the prescribed one-year period after the 1994 amendment.
what_it_excludes: An individual copyright owner who grants licences in respect of his own works in his personal capacity, as the Act expressly preserves this as a separate and distinct right not requiring society registration.

Newly formed associations of persons constituted after the commencement of the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994, which must be registered as copyright societies from the outset and do not qualify as performing rights societies.

Film producers' organisations or associations dealing exclusively in licensing rights in respect of cinematograph films or sound recordings, as those are governed separately and must operate through a duly registered copyright society.

Foreign collecting societies or foreign organisations that issue licences for works outside India, as the performing rights society concept under Section 33 applies to bodies functioning within the Indian statutory framework.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an organisation qualifies as a performing rights society determines whether it is automatically deemed a registered copyright society under Chapter VII, thereby allowing it to continue issuing licences during the one-year transition period without fresh registration — failure to re-register within that period would render its licensing activities illegal under Section 33(1). The classification also triggers the obligations and protections applicable to copyright societies, including accountability to authors, renewal requirements, and the Central Government's power of suspension or cancellation.

definitions.definition: Persons with disability means individuals who have any disability as defined under the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995, or any other applicable law, including visual impairment, hearing impairment, or any other condition that prevents them from accessing or enjoying a work in its original published format; the term is used in the Copyright Act, 1957 to identify the class of beneficiaries for whom special access to copyrighted works is permitted without infringement under Section 52(1)(zb) and for whom compulsory licences may be granted under Section 31B.
definitions.plain_english: Persons with disability refers to individuals who have a physical, sensory, or cognitive condition — such as blindness, low vision, deafness, or dyslexia — that prevents them from reading or accessing a copyrighted work in the standard format it is published in. The Copyright Act gives these individuals and organisations working for them special rights to reproduce or convert works into accessible formats. This is to ensure that disability does not become a barrier to education, knowledge, and cultural participation.
real_world_examples: A visually impaired student in Mumbai requires a university textbook to be converted into Braille or an audio recording so they can study; under Section 52(1)(zb) this conversion is not a copyright infringement.

An NGO in Chennai working with persons having low vision converts bestselling Tamil novels into DAISY (Digital Accessible Information System) audio format for its beneficiaries without obtaining permission from the publisher.

A deaf individual in Delhi requires subtitled or sign-language-interpreted versions of a cinematograph film for educational purposes, which an organisation for the hearing-impaired produces under the disability exception.

A non-profit organisation in Pune working with dyslexic children converts school curriculum books into large-print or dyslexia-friendly digital formats and distributes them to enrolled students without seeking a licence from copyright owners.

A company in Bengaluru running a subscription-based accessible content service for blind users applies to the Appellate Board under Section 31B for a compulsory licence to convert and distribute copyrighted engineering reference books in accessible formats.
what_it_covers: Visually impaired or blind individuals who cannot access works in standard printed or visual formats.
Persons with hearing impairment who require sign-language interpretation or subtitling of audio-visual works.
Individuals with dyslexia, learning disabilities, or cognitive impairments that prevent them from using conventionally published works.
Persons with physical disabilities that prevent them from holding, turning pages of, or otherwise physically accessing a published work.
Organisations working on a non-profit or profit basis for the benefit of any of the above categories of individuals when seeking compulsory licences under Section 31B.
what_it_excludes: Persons who are temporarily ill or injured but do not have a recognised disability under applicable disability laws.
Individuals who simply prefer an alternative format for convenience rather than due to any genuine disability.
Organisations that claim to serve persons with disability but are found by the Appellate Board not to be acting in good faith or not actually serving disabled beneficiaries.
Commercial entities exploiting the disability exception for profit without demonstrating actual benefit to persons with disability as required under Section 31B.
Persons whose condition does not prevent them from accessing the work in its original published format.
