definitions.definition: The 'right of reproduction' refers to the exclusive right of the owner of copyright to reproduce or authorise the reproduction of a copyrighted work in printed or analogous forms, as contemplated under Section 32A of the Copyright Act, 1957, in the context of licences granted by the Appellate Board for the reproduction and publication of literary, scientific, or artistic works for systematic instructional activities where such works are unavailable or have not been put on sale in India at a reasonably related price.
definitions.plain_english: The right of reproduction is the exclusive power held by a copyright owner to make copies of their work or to allow others to do so. In the context of Section 32A, it specifically refers to the copyright owner's control over whether printed or similar copies of a published book or work are made available in India for educational purposes. If the copyright owner fails to make the work available in India at a reasonable price, the law allows someone else to apply for permission to reproduce it for educational use.
real_world_examples: A foreign academic publisher holds the right of reproduction for a university-level physics textbook first published in London. The book is not sold in India. An Indian educational trust applies to the Appellate Board under Section 32A for a licence to reproduce and publish the textbook at a price affordable to Indian students for use in systematic instructional activities.

A scientific journal publisher based in the United States holds the right of reproduction for a collection of research papers on biotechnology. After three years of non-availability in India, an Indian university press applies under Section 32A to reproduce and publish the collection for distribution to Indian science students at a subsidised price.

An Indian author's artistic work on classical dance forms is published abroad but not made available in India for over five years. A cultural education institute in Chennai applies to the Appellate Board for a licence to reproduce the work in printed form for use in its systematic instructional programmes.

A mathematics textbook authored by a European scholar and first published in Germany has not been put on sale in India for more than three years. An Indian publication house applies under Section 32A, demonstrating that the owner of the right of reproduction refused to authorise local reproduction, to obtain a compulsory licence to print and distribute affordable copies to Indian students.

A poetry anthology published in the UK is unavailable in India for over seven years. An Indian literary institute seeks a licence under Section 32A from the Appellate Board to reproduce the anthology in printed form for use in its instructional programmes, after showing that the owner of the right of reproduction could not be traced despite due diligence.
what_it_covers: The exclusive right of the copyright owner to authorise or deny the making of printed or analogous copies of a literary, scientific, or artistic work.

Reproduction of a work in printed or analogous forms by a person authorised by the owner of the right of reproduction for sale in India at a price reasonably related to that normally charged in India.

The right exercised by the owner or their authorised agent to put copies of a work on sale in India in connection with systematic instructional activities, the absence of which triggers the compulsory licence mechanism under Section 32A.
Reproduction of text incorporated in audio-visual fixations prepared and published solely for systematic instructional activities, as extended by the provisions of Section 32A.
what_it_excludes: The right of translation, which is separately governed and requires additional conditions under Section 32A — no licence to reproduce a translation is granted unless the translation has been published by the owner of the right of translation.

Export of reproduced copies outside India — a licence granted under Section 32A does not extend to the export of copies, meaning the right of reproduction as exercised under such licence is territorially restricted to India.
Reproduction for commercial rental or non-educational commercial purposes, as Section 32A licences are strictly limited to systematic instructional activities and not general commercial reproduction.

Reproduction of works where the author has withdrawn copies from circulation, which is a condition that bars the grant of a licence under Section 32A regardless of the availability status of the work.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether the owner of the right of reproduction has made a work available in India at a reasonable price is the central factual trigger for Section 32A — if they have done so, no compulsory licence can be granted; if they have not, an applicant may obtain a non-exclusive licence from the Appellate Board to reproduce the work for educational purposes. This directly determines whether the copyright owner retains exclusive control over Indian copies or whether a third party can lawfully reproduce and distribute the work in India without the owner's consent.

definitions.definition: Rights conferred by this Act refers to the full bundle of statutory rights granted under the Copyright Act, 1957, including copyright in original works, broadcast reproduction rights, performer's rights, moral rights, and any other rights specifically created or recognised by the provisions of this Act. These rights are not limited to copyright alone but extend to all legally enforceable entitlements arising from the Act in favour of authors, owners, performers, broadcasting organisations, and other rights-holders.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to all the different legal rights that the Copyright Act gives to creators and other rights-holders in India. It is broader than just copyright and includes things like a performer's right to control use of their performance, a broadcaster's right over their broadcast, and moral rights of authors. Essentially, if the Copyright Act says someone has a right, that right is a 'right conferred by this Act'.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music composer's copyright in a musical composition and the performer's right of the playback singer in the same song are both 'rights conferred by this Act'; a copyright society seeking to license both must be registered under Section 33.

A regional television channel's broadcast reproduction right under Section 37 prevents another channel from rebroadcasting its live cricket coverage without permission — this right is a right conferred by the Act, and any society licensing such rights must be a registered copyright society.

A classical dancer performing at a cultural festival in Chennai holds performer's rights under Section 38 of the Act; any attempt to circumvent technological protection measures used to protect a recording of that performance engages the rights conferred by this Act as referenced in Section 65A.

A Delhi-based software company owns copyright in its proprietary code under the Act; when a third party uses a technological lock to prevent reverse engineering beyond what the Act permits, the company's rights conferred by this Act are directly engaged.

An author of a Hindi novel who is a member of a copyright society retains the right under Section 33 to individually license her own work, as her copyright is a right conferred by this Act, distinct from the collective licensing administered by the society.

A Pune-based documentary filmmaker who encrypts her film with a digital rights management tool is protected under Section 65A against circumvention of that measure, since her copyright and related rights are rights conferred by this Act.
what_it_covers: Copyright in literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works as granted under Chapter IV of the Act.
Broadcast reproduction rights granted to broadcasting organisations under Section 37.
Performer's rights granted to performers under Sections 38 and 38A, including the right to receive royalties.
Moral rights of authors, including the right of paternity and integrity under Section 57.
The right of a copyright owner to communicate a work to the public under Section 14.
Rights of authors and composers to receive royalties in respect of sound recordings and cinematograph films under Section 18.
what_it_excludes: Rights arising purely from contract between private parties that are not grounded in any specific provision of the Copyright Act.
Intellectual property rights granted under other statutes, such as trademark rights under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 or patent rights under the Patents Act, 1970.
Rights that have lapsed or expired upon the expiry of the term of copyright or other rights prescribed under the Act.
Moral or equitable claims that are not codified in the Act, such as purely reputational claims governed by tort law outside the Act.
Rights of a foreign rights-holder whose work has not been extended protection under an order issued under Section 40 or 41 of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The scope of 'rights conferred by this Act' determines which rights must be collectively administered only through a registered copyright society under Section 33, making unlicensed licensing businesses illegal. Under Section 65A, circumvention of effective technological measures protecting any such right constitutes a criminal offence, meaning the breadth of this term directly defines the perimeter of criminal liability and the obligation to obtain or grant licences through authorised channels.

definitions.definition: Rights management information means any information which identifies the work, author, performer, or the owner of any right in the work, or information about the terms and conditions of use of the work, and any numbers or codes that represent such information, when any of these items is attached to a copy of the work or appears in connection with the communication of the work to the public.
definitions.plain_english: Rights management information is any electronic data attached to or accompanying a creative work — such as a song, film, book, or software — that identifies who created it, who owns it, and the rules for how it may be used. This could include digital watermarks, metadata embedded in an audio file, or licence terms encoded in an e-book. It helps copyright owners track and control how their works are distributed and used online and offline.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood production house embeds metadata in a digitally distributed film file containing the studio name, copyright year, and permitted streaming territories; removing this metadata before uploading the film to a piracy website would constitute tampering with rights management information under Section 65B.

A music label in Mumbai encodes ISRC (International Standard Recording Code) and licensing terms into an MP3 file released on a digital platform; a third party who strips this code and redistributes the track for commercial use without authorisation violates the protection of rights management information.

An Indian software company includes a digital licence key and ownership identifier in the header of its distributed software package; cracking or deleting this information to enable unauthorised copies is an infringement of rights management information protection.

A publishing house in Chennai embeds author attribution data and DRM (Digital Rights Management) licence conditions in an e-book sold through an online store; a user or aggregator who removes these embedded tags before republishing the e-book on another platform without permission breaches Section 65B.

A news photograph agency in Delhi watermarks its images with the photographer's name, copyright notice, and terms of use before licensing them to media outlets; a website that crops out the watermark and reposts the image without authorisation is tampering with rights management information.

An OTT platform in India embeds content fingerprinting and ownership metadata into each video stream; a person who intercepts the stream, strips the fingerprint data, and re-broadcasts the content without authority is liable under Section 65B.
what_it_covers: Digital watermarks embedded in photographs, films, or audio files identifying the copyright owner and usage conditions.
Metadata encoded in e-books, software, or music files that specifies the author, publisher, and permitted licensing terms.
Numeric codes or identifiers such as ISRC, ISWC, or ISBN attached to or accompanying a work that represent ownership or rights information.
Electronically attached copyright notices and terms-of-use statements that appear in connection with communication of a work to the public.
Content fingerprinting data used by broadcasting organisations and OTT platforms to identify and track works in digital distribution.
what_it_excludes: Physical labels or printed copyright notices on tangible media that are not in electronic form and are not attached to or embedded within the digital work.
General contractual agreements or licences between parties that are stored separately and are not attached to or encoded within the work itself.

Technical access-control measures (such as encryption or passwords) that restrict access to a work but do not carry identifying or terms-of-use information about the work — those are governed separately as effective technological measures.
Unrelated business metadata or file system properties (e.g., file creation timestamps added by an operating system) that do not identify the work, its author, or its rights conditions.
Oral or informal statements of ownership made in connection with a performance but not recorded electronically and attached to the work.

definitions.definition: Royalties means the periodic payments due to the author or owner of rights in a literary, musical, dramatic, or artistic work, or sound recording, in consideration of the exploitation or utilisation of such work, as determined or fixed under the provisions of this Act; such payments are to be shared on an equal basis between the author and the assignee of copyright where the work is utilised in any form beyond the originally assigned medium or mode.
definitions.plain_english: Royalties are the money that a creator (like a songwriter, author, or composer) earns every time their work is used, performed, sold, or broadcast by someone else. Think of it as an ongoing share of earnings that the original creator receives each time their creative work generates revenue. Under Indian copyright law, authors have a protected right to receive these payments that cannot be signed away except to their legal heirs or a registered copyright society.
real_world_examples: A Hindi film music composer like A.R. Rahman receives royalty payments every time one of his film songs is played on a radio station such as Radio Mirchi or streamed on Spotify India — these are collected and distributed by a copyright society like IPRS (Indian Performing Right Society).

A novelist whose book is published by Penguin India receives royalties — typically a percentage of the cover price — for every copy sold, whether in print, e-book, or audiobook format, as specified in the publishing assignment agreement.

When a Bollywood lyricist's song is used in a television advertisement by a company like Hindustan Unilever, the lyricist is entitled to receive royalties for that commercial utilisation, separate from any payment already made for the original film use, since this is a different mode of exploitation.

A music label that makes a cover version of an old Kishore Kumar song under Section 31C must pay advance royalties to the original rights holder at the rate fixed by the Appellate Board before manufacturing and selling copies of the new sound recording.

A Punjabi folk singer whose sound recordings are used on a digital streaming platform like JioSaavn is entitled to royalties to be shared equally with the record label (assignee of copyright), as the streaming constitutes utilisation beyond the original sound recording agreement.

An author of a textbook published by Oxford University Press India whose work is adapted for e-learning modules receives royalties for each such adaptation, separate from the original print publication royalties, since digital adaptation is a distinct mode of exploitation.
what_it_covers: Payments due to an author of a literary or musical work included in a cinematograph film for utilisation of that work in any form other than its communication to the public along with the film in a cinema hall (e.g., streaming, radio broadcast, ringtone use).
Advance royalties payable to the owner of rights in a work before a cover version sound recording is made and sold, at rates fixed by the Appellate Board under Section 31C.

The equal share of royalties an author of a literary or musical work included in a sound recording (not part of a cinematograph film) is entitled to receive for any utilisation of that work, regardless of any assignment agreement to the contrary.

Royalties collected and distributed by a copyright society or collecting society on behalf of authors who cannot individually track or enforce their royalty rights across multiple platforms and broadcasters.
Royalties payable under a statutory licence granted by the Copyright Board or Appellate Board where the parties cannot agree on terms, with the rate determined by the Board.
what_it_excludes: A one-time lump-sum assignment payment made to an author in full and final settlement of all rights — this is a consideration for assignment of copyright, not a royalty, though Section 19 requires both to be specified in the assignment deed.
Performance fees or sitting fees paid to a performer for a live performance, which relate to performer's rights rather than royalties arising from copyright ownership or authorship.
Damages or compensation awarded by a court for infringement of copyright — these are remedies for civil wrongs and are distinct from contractual or statutory royalty entitlements.

Licence fees paid under a tariff scheme by broadcasting organisations for general blanket use of a repertoire, to the extent these are treated as collective licensing fees rather than individual author royalty distributions.
Fees paid for the use of a work that is in the public domain (i.e., copyright has expired), since no copyright subsists in such work and no royalty obligation arises under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a payment as 'royalties' determines whether the author's entitlement is protected as a non-waivable right under Sections 18 and 19 — any assignment or agreement that purports to extinguish an author's equal share of royalties (other than to legal heirs or a copyright society) is void, making the assignee liable to pay despite the contractual clause. It also triggers the obligation of copyright societies under Section 35 to collect and equitably distribute such royalties, and governs the advance payment requirement for cover versions under Section 31C, non-compliance with which constitutes infringement.

definitions.definition: Royalty means the monetary consideration payable to the author or copyright owner or their legal heirs for the use, assignment, or licensing of a copyrighted work, as specified in the terms of an assignment or compulsory licence, including an equal share of royalties payable to an author in cases of utilisation of a work incorporated in a cinematograph film (other than communication to the public in a cinema hall) or in a sound recording.
definitions.plain_english: Royalty is the money paid to a creator (like a writer, composer, or lyricist) or their family whenever someone uses, publishes, or commercially exploits their creative work. It is like a usage fee that keeps flowing to the original creator even after they have handed over certain rights to another party. For example, a singer earns royalties every time their song is played on a streaming platform or used in a film.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music composer assigns the copyright in a film score to a music label; the label must pay the composer a share of royalties each time the songs are streamed on platforms like Spotify or JioSaavn, as mandated under Section 19(10).

A Hindi novelist assigns her novel to a publisher; the assignment deed specifies a royalty of 10% of the cover price for every copy sold, which the publisher must pay to the author or her legal heirs for the duration of the assignment.

A lyricist whose song was assigned to a film producer can claim an equal share of royalties whenever that song is used in a TV commercial, a ringtone, or a digital advertisement — separate from its screening in a cinema hall — as protected under Section 19(9).

Under Section 31A, where a work is withheld from the public and the copyright owner cannot be traced, the Appellate Board grants a compulsory licence to a publisher to publish the work, but directs the publisher to deposit the determined royalty amount in the public account of India so the owner or their heirs can claim it later.

A classical musician's composition is licensed by a copyright society (such as IPRS); the society collects royalties from radio stations and distributes them proportionally to the musician as per the tariff scheme.

An independent author files a complaint before the Appellate Board under Section 19A because the assignee has stopped paying royalties despite commercially exploiting the book; the Board passes an order for recovery of outstanding royalty payable.
what_it_covers: The share of revenue payable to an author or their legal heirs as specified in a copyright assignment agreement for commercial exploitation of the work.
The royalty determined and directed by the Appellate Board under a compulsory licence for publishing an unpublished or withheld work (Section 31A).
An author's equal share of royalties arising from utilisation of a literary or musical work embedded in a cinematograph film for purposes other than screening in a cinema hall (Section 19(9)).
An author's equal share of royalties for any utilisation of a work incorporated in a sound recording that does not form part of a cinematograph film (Section 19(10)).
Royalty ordered to be recovered by the Appellate Board upon a dispute arising from an assignment of copyright (Section 19A(2)).
what_it_excludes: A one-time flat fee paid to an author at the time of full and final assignment of copyright, where no recurring payment obligation is agreed upon, is not a royalty in the ongoing statutory sense.
Consideration paid purely for the right to screen a cinematograph film in a cinema hall — this is explicitly carved out as separate from the royalty-sharing right under Section 19(9).
Damages or compensation awarded in an infringement suit, which are remedies for violation of rights rather than agreed or determined royalty for authorised use.
Administrative fees or filing fees charged by the Copyright Office or Appellate Board, which are statutory charges and not royalties for use of a work.
Profits or dividends earned by a copyright society from investments; these are not royalties payable to the author for exploitation of their work.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a payment qualifies as royalty directly determines an author's or their legal heirs' entitlement to a share of proceeds from exploitation of the work, and failure by an assignee to pay royalty entitles the assignor to seek recovery through the Appellate Board under Section 19A or to have the assignment revoked. Royalty provisions also govern the terms of compulsory licences under Sections 31A, 31B, and 31C, without which a licensee cannot lawfully publish or communicate a work to the public.

definitions.definition: A work shall be deemed to be published simultaneously in India and in another country if the time between the publication in India and the publication in such other country does not exceed thirty days or such other period as the Central Government may, in relation to any specified country, determine.
definitions.plain_english: Simultaneous publication means releasing a work in India and in another country within 30 days of each other. When this happens, the work is treated as if it was first published in India, which gives it the full benefit of Indian copyright protection. The Central Government can change this 30-day window for specific countries by official notification.
real_world_examples: An Indian author publishes a novel in Mumbai on January 1st and the same novel is released in the United Kingdom on January 25th — since the gap is within 30 days, the work is deemed simultaneously published and treated as first published in India.

A Bollywood production house releases a Hindi film in India on March 10th and releases it in the United States on April 5th — the 26-day gap qualifies as simultaneous publication, securing the work's status as an Indian work under the Copyright Act.

A Delhi-based software company releases a computer programme in India on June 1st and in Canada on June 28th — the 27-day difference falls within 30 days, so the programme is deemed simultaneously published and enjoys Indian copyright protection as if first published in India.

A Chennai music label releases a sound recording in India and in Germany on the same day — this is a clear case of simultaneous publication, and since it is published in India, it is deemed first published in India for copyright purposes.

An Indian publisher releases a translated literary work in India on September 1st and in France on September 20th — the 19-day gap satisfies the 30-day simultaneous publication rule, ensuring the work is treated as first published in India regardless of the French publication.
what_it_covers: Publication of a work in India and another country within 30 days of each other, regardless of which country published first.
Cases where the Central Government has notified a different time period (other than 30 days) for a specified foreign country, and a work is released within that altered window.
Any type of copyrightable work — including literary, artistic, musical, cinematograph films, and sound recordings — released in India and abroad within the qualifying time gap.
Situations where an Indian work is published first abroad and then in India within 30 days, still allowing it to be treated as first published in India.
what_it_excludes: Publication in another country that occurs more than 30 days after the Indian publication date, which would not qualify as simultaneous and would not affect the first-publication status.
Cases where the foreign country in which the work is simultaneously published provides a shorter term of copyright for that work — in such cases, the work is not deemed first published in India.
Works where no publication occurs in India at all, regardless of how quickly they are published in another country, as there is no Indian publication to anchor the simultaneous publication rule.
Mere distribution, private circulation, or communication to a limited audience that does not constitute formal 'publication' as defined under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a work as simultaneously published determines whether it qualifies as 'first published in India,' directly affecting the duration of copyright protection it receives under Indian law and whether it is treated as an 'Indian work.' This has significant consequences for the applicability of Indian copyright term calculations, eligibility for compulsory licences, and the enforcement rights available to the copyright owner in Indian courts.

definitions.definition: 'sound recording' means a recording of sounds from which such sounds may be produced regardless of the medium on which such recording is made or the method by which the sounds are produced.
definitions.plain_english: A sound recording is any fixed capture of sounds — such as music, speech, or other audio — stored on any medium (like a CD, digital file, or vinyl record) in a way that allows those sounds to be played back. It does not matter what format or technology is used to store or reproduce the sounds. The person who produces the sound recording is treated as its author under copyright law.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood music album released by T-Series, where individual song tracks are recorded in a studio and pressed onto CDs or uploaded as digital files on platforms like Spotify or JioSaavn — each track constitutes a separate sound recording.

An audiobook of a Hindi novel recorded by a publisher such as Audible India, where a narrator reads the text aloud and the recording is distributed as an MP3 download, qualifies as a sound recording distinct from the underlying literary work.

A ghazal performance by a classical singer recorded live at the Sawai Gandharva Music Festival in Pune and later released on a cassette or digital platform is a sound recording, even though it is also a performer's performance.

A podcast produced by an independent Indian content creator and uploaded on Anchor or Spotify, capturing spoken commentary and interviews, constitutes a sound recording protected under the Copyright Act.

A devotional chant (bhajan) recorded by a religious institution in Varanasi and distributed as a free MP3 on their website is a sound recording, with the producer holding copyright independent of any underlying musical or literary work.

A ringtone created by a telecom company like Airtel by recording a customised musical jingle is a sound recording, and its commercial distribution requires a licence under Section 31D from the copyright owner.
what_it_covers: A studio-recorded music track stored on a digital file, CD, cassette, or vinyl record, regardless of the format.
A spoken-word recording such as an audiobook, podcast, or radio drama fixed on any medium.
A live concert recording made by a producer and released commercially, separate from the underlying musical composition.
A recorded jingle, advertisement voiceover, or sound effect produced for commercial use.
A devotional, folk, or classical music recording made by any producer and stored in any reproducible form.
what_it_excludes: A cinematograph film's soundtrack when it accompanies the visual recording — this falls within the definition of 'cinematograph film' rather than being treated solely as a sound recording.
A live, unrecorded performance of music or speech that has not been fixed in any medium and therefore cannot be reproduced.
The underlying musical work (composition and notation) or literary work (lyrics) embodied in the recording — these are separate works with independent copyright.
A visual recording or video film, even if it contains audio, as these are governed by the definitions of 'visual recording' or 'cinematograph film'.
Mere data files or signals that have not been fixed in a reproducible form from which sounds can actually be produced.

definitions.definition: Systematic instructional activities refers to organised, structured educational programmes conducted by recognised educational institutions or broadcasting authorities, wherein audio-visual fixations or texts are prepared and used solely for the purpose of formal teaching, dissemination of specialised, technical or scientific research results to experts, or structured instructional delivery — as contemplated under Section 32A of the Copyright Act, 1957.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to organised, formal teaching or training programmes — such as those run by schools, universities, or educational broadcasters — where copyrighted content is used specifically as part of a structured course or curriculum. It is not about casual or informal learning, but about purposeful, planned instruction delivered through recognised educational channels. The content must be prepared and used solely for the purpose of teaching or spreading specialised research knowledge.
real_world_examples: IGNOU (Indira Gandhi National Open University) preparing and broadcasting audio-visual lessons on Doordarshan as part of its distance education degree programmes, where copyrighted textbook content is translated and incorporated into telecasts for enrolled students.

An IIT broadcasting translated lectures of a foreign technical textbook over educational television channels under the EDUSAT programme specifically for engineering students enrolled in a certified course.

A State Government school education board producing translated video modules of a published scientific work for use in its Class 10 science curriculum broadcast over the state-run educational channel.

The National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) incorporating translated excerpts of a foreign-published literary or dramatic work into its structured audio-visual learning materials broadcast for secondary-level students appearing in board examinations.

A recognised medical college broadcasting translated summaries of a specialised foreign medical research publication to postgraduate medical students as part of a formal residency training programme curriculum.
what_it_covers: Organised degree or diploma programmes conducted by universities or recognised educational institutions where copyrighted works are translated and broadcast as part of the formal curriculum.

Audio-visual fixations prepared solely for structured teaching under a broadcasting authority's educational programming mandate, such as Doordarshan's educational channel broadcasts for enrolled students.
Broadcasting of translated texts to specialists for dissemination of specialised, technical or scientific research results as part of a structured expert training or academic programme.
Distance education programmes conducted by statutory open universities like IGNOU or NIOS where translated copyrighted content is embedded in formally prescribed study materials.
what_it_excludes: Casual, informal, or self-directed learning activities such as individuals watching educational YouTube videos or reading translated summaries without enrolment in a formal course.
Commercial online learning platforms (e.g., private EdTech companies) that sell courses to the general public without formal institutional affiliation or recognised curriculum structure.
General public broadcasting of translated works for entertainment or awareness purposes not tied to a specific structured instructional programme or enrolled student body.
Translation and publication of works for general scholarship or independent research not forming part of a formally organised instructional or teaching programme.
Works used in informal workshops, seminars, or public lectures that are not part of a recognised, structured educational curriculum or formal degree-granting activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an activity qualifies as 'systematic instructional activities' determines whether a broadcasting authority can invoke the compulsory licence provisions under Section 32A to translate and broadcast a copyrighted work without the owner's prior consent, subject to payment of royalties and compliance with prescribed conditions. If this definition does not apply, the broadcaster must obtain direct authorisation from the copyright owner and cannot rely on the statutory licence regime.

definitions.definition: A tariff scheme is the schedule of fees and rates published by a copyright society specifying the charges to be levied for the grant of licences in respect of the works in its repertoire, which every copyright society is required to publish in the prescribed manner, and which is subject to appeal before the Appellate Board by any aggrieved person on grounds of unreasonableness, anomaly, or inconsistency.
definitions.plain_english: A tariff scheme is essentially a price list published by a copyright society that tells users how much they must pay to legally use the songs, books, films, or other creative works managed by that society. Think of it as a rate card — for example, how much a radio station must pay to broadcast songs, or how much a hotel must pay to play music for guests. If someone thinks the rates are unfair or inconsistent, they can challenge the tariff scheme before a government appellate body.
real_world_examples: The Indian Performing Right Society (IPRS) publishes a tariff scheme specifying annual licence fees for commercial establishments such as restaurants, hotels, and shopping malls in Mumbai that play copyrighted music, with rates varying based on seating capacity or floor area.

Phonographic Performance Limited (PPL) publishes a tariff scheme listing fees payable by FM radio stations across India — such as Radio Mirchi or Big FM — for broadcasting sound recordings, calculated as a percentage of net advertising revenue.

A Bollywood film producer aggrieved by the tariff scheme of a copyright society charging excessively high synchronisation licence fees for background music appeals to the Appellate Board under Section 33A, seeking removal of the anomalous rate structure.

A copyright society managing literary works publishes a tariff scheme setting out per-page or per-copy reprography fees for educational institutions and public libraries in Delhi that wish to photocopy published books, prompting a university to challenge the rates before the Appellate Board.

A digital streaming platform such as JioSaavn negotiates with a copyright society but disputes the published tariff scheme for online streaming licences; pending resolution of the appeal before the Appellate Board, the platform continues paying the interim tariff fixed by the Board.

An event management company in Bengaluru organising live concerts receives the tariff scheme from a performing rights society and, finding the per-event fee disproportionate for small-scale cultural events, files an appeal before the Appellate Board while continuing to pay the prescribed fee as required.
what_it_covers: Schedules of fees published by copyright societies specifying licence charges for use of works in their repertoire across categories of users such as broadcasters, hotels, and event organisers.

Rate structures differentiated by type of use — such as public performance, broadcast, online streaming, or reprography — set out in the tariff scheme and subject to mandatory public disclosure in the prescribed manner.
An interim tariff fixed by the Appellate Board pending disposal of an appeal challenging the original tariff scheme, which binds the aggrieved party to make payments accordingly.
Fee anomalies, inconsistencies, or unreasonable elements embedded in a tariff scheme that an aggrieved person may specifically challenge before the Appellate Board under Section 33A.
what_it_excludes: Individually negotiated private licence agreements between a copyright owner and a user that are not published as part of a copyright society's standardised tariff schedule.

Royalty rates determined through compulsory licence proceedings under Sections 31, 31B, 31C, or 31D, which are fixed by the Appellate Board or the Central Government rather than published by a copyright society as a tariff scheme.

Fees or charges levied by the Copyright Office or the Registrar of Copyrights for registration or administrative purposes, which are governed by separate rules and are not part of any copyright society's tariff scheme.
Assignment or transfer consideration paid between a copyright owner and an assignee, which is a private contractual arrangement and not a published licensing tariff of a copyright society.
definitions.why_it_matters: A validly published tariff scheme is the legal basis upon which a copyright society can demand and collect licence fees from users; failure to publish or comply with it exposes the society to challenge, while an aggrieved user who does not continue paying prescribed fees pending appeal loses the right to seek relief from the Appellate Board. The tariff scheme directly determines the financial obligations of every commercial user of copyrighted works managed by a copyright society, and its validity or modification by the Appellate Board affects the enforceability of those obligations.

definitions.definition: The term 'trade or business' is not formally defined in the Copyright Act, 1957, but as used in Sections 63, 63A, and 63B, it denotes any commercial, mercantile, or professional activity undertaken with the motive of financial gain or profit, whether carried on regularly or as a one-time commercial venture. An infringement is considered to be made 'in the course of trade or business' when it is committed as part of, or in furtherance of, such a profit-oriented commercial undertaking.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to any activity done as part of running a business or making money — such as selling, distributing, or using copyrighted material to earn a profit. If someone infringes copyright just for personal, private, or non-commercial reasons (not to earn money), they fall outside this category. The distinction matters because courts can reduce the mandatory minimum punishment when the infringement was not done for financial gain in a commercial context.
real_world_examples: A street vendor in Delhi selling pirated DVDs of Bollywood films at a roadside stall is infringing copyright in the course of trade or business, as the activity is profit-driven and commercial in nature.

A small printing press in Mumbai reproducing and selling unauthorised copies of a popular NCERT textbook to coaching institutes for a fee is committing infringement in the course of trade or business.

A software reseller in Bengaluru knowingly installing unlicensed copies of accounting software on multiple client computers and charging clients for the installation service constitutes use in the course of trade or business under Section 63B.
A garment manufacturer in Surat printing copyrighted artistic designs on sarees without a licence and selling them wholesale to retailers is infringing copyright in the course of trade or business.

A music streaming startup in Chennai using sound recordings without obtaining licences from copyright owners, and monetising the platform through subscriptions and advertisements, is operating infringement in the course of trade or business.

A college student making a single unauthorised copy of a novel for personal reading, with no intent to sell or distribute, would likely fall outside the scope of 'trade or business' and could attract reduced penalties.
what_it_covers: Selling pirated copies of films, books, or software as part of a regular business operation for profit.
A printing enterprise reproducing and distributing copyrighted literary or artistic works to commercial clients for a fee.
A business entity deploying infringing copies of computer programmes across its operations to avoid paying licence fees, thereby gaining a commercial advantage.
An online marketplace or distributor knowingly trafficking in infringing copies of sound recordings or musical works as a commercial activity.
A cable operator or digital platform broadcasting copyrighted content without authorisation as part of a subscription-based commercial service.
what_it_excludes: A private individual making a single unauthorised copy of a work solely for personal use with no commercial purpose or distribution.
A student or researcher reproducing copyrighted material without gain for academic or non-commercial study purposes, not connected to any trade.
A non-profit organisation or charitable trust making limited copies of a work for educational or social welfare purposes without any intent of financial gain.
An individual gifting an infringing copy to a friend or family member without any monetary transaction or commercial motive.
Incidental personal use of an infringing copy of a computer programme where the user has no commercial relationship or business activity connected to the use.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an infringement is committed 'in the course of trade or business' is the critical threshold that determines the mandatory minimum sentence under Sections 63, 63A, and 63B — if the infringement is commercial, the court must impose the statutory minimum imprisonment and fine; if it is not, the court has discretion to impose lesser punishment or, in the case of Section 63B, even waive imprisonment entirely. This distinction thus directly governs the severity of criminal liability for copyright infringement under the Copyright Act, 1957.

definitions.definition: A 'translation' in the context of the Copyright Act means the conversion of a literary or dramatic work from one language into another language, and constitutes a distinct act in respect of which copyright subsists; the right to make any translation of the work is an exclusive right of the copyright owner under Section 14(a)(v), and a translation is also treated as a form of work in relation to which compulsory licences may be granted under Sections 31A, 32, and 32B.
definitions.plain_english: A translation is when someone takes a book, play, poem, or other written or dramatic work originally written in one language and rewrites or converts it into another language. For example, converting a Hindi novel into English or a Tamil play into Telugu would be a translation. The original author has the exclusive right to do this, and no one else can translate the work without permission unless a compulsory licence is granted by the Appellate Board.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based publisher translates a celebrated Bengali novel by a deceased author into Hindi for national distribution; since the author is dead and the copyright owner cannot be traced, the publisher applies to the Appellate Board under Section 31A for a compulsory licence to publish the Hindi translation.

An NGO working with rural communities in Maharashtra applies to the Appellate Board under Section 32 for a licence to translate and publish an English agricultural science textbook into Marathi after the seven-year period from first publication has elapsed, so that the material is accessible for educational purposes.

A Chennai-based film production company seeks permission to translate a popular French dramatic work into Tamil for stage performance in Tamil Nadu, acknowledging that making such a translation without the copyright owner's consent would infringe the exclusive right under Section 14(a)(v).

A Kolkata university press translates a German scientific treatise into Bengali under a voluntary licence obtained from the German copyright owner, paying agreed royalties, and publishes the translation for use in West Bengal universities.

An e-learning startup in Bengaluru translates a widely used English programming manual into Kannada and Odia to serve students in smaller towns; because the work is still within the protected period, the startup obtains a formal assignment of translation rights from the copyright holder before proceeding.
what_it_covers: Converting an English novel into any Indian regional language such as Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, or Marathi for publication in India.
Rendering a Hindi dramatic work into Urdu or any other scheduled language for performance or publication.
Translating a foreign literary or dramatic work (non-Indian) into any language in general use in India for educational or public benefit purposes under a compulsory licence.
Publishing a translated version of an unpublished manuscript in a different language where the original author is dead or untraceable, subject to Appellate Board approval.
Any reproduction, communication to the public, or issuance of copies of a translated text derived from the original literary or dramatic work.
what_it_excludes: Adaptation of a work, which involves recasting, abridging, or making other structural changes to the work beyond mere language conversion, and is treated as a separate exclusive right under Section 14(a)(vi).

Transliteration of a work, where the script is changed but the language itself remains the same (e.g., rendering Hindi written in Devanagari into Hindi written in Roman script), as this does not convert the work into a different language.

Translation of artistic works, cinematograph films, or sound recordings, as the exclusive translation right under Section 14 applies only to literary, dramatic, and musical works, not to these other categories.
Computer programmes, which are governed by a separate clause under Section 14(b) that does not expressly include a right of translation in the same manner as literary works.
Mere summarisation, critique, or commentary on a work in another language, which does not amount to a full or partial translation of the original work.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes a 'translation' determines whether the copyright owner's exclusive right under Section 14(a)(v) has been exercised or infringed, triggering liability for copyright infringement if done without consent or a valid licence. It also governs the eligibility to apply for compulsory licences under Sections 31A, 32, and 32B, and determines the royalty obligations and conditions that the Appellate Board may impose on the licensee.

definitions.plain_english: An 'unpublished' work is one that has never been made available or distributed to the general public by the person who owns the rights to it. This means the work exists — perhaps as a manuscript, a painting, a composition, or a recording — but has been kept private and not shared with the world in any formal way. Whether a work is unpublished affects how long copyright lasts and who qualifies for protection under Indian copyright law.
real_world_examples: A Hindi novelist in Mumbai writes a complete novel manuscript and stores it on her personal laptop without submitting it to any publisher or sharing it online — the manuscript is an unpublished literary work.

A classical Carnatic musician in Chennai composes a new raga and records it privately at home but never releases it commercially or performs it publicly — the sound recording and musical work remain unpublished.
A fine arts student in Kolkata creates a series of oil paintings for personal satisfaction and keeps them in her studio without exhibiting or selling them — these artistic works are unpublished.

A software developer in Bengaluru writes a proprietary computer programme for internal testing purposes and never distributes, sells, or communicates it to any external user — the programme is an unpublished work.

A documentary filmmaker in Delhi completes a short film about a social issue but never submits it to any film festival, broadcaster, or streaming platform — the cinematograph film remains unpublished.

A deceased poet's handwritten diaries and poems discovered by his family in Allahabad, which were never shared publicly during his lifetime, constitute unpublished literary works for copyright purposes.
what_it_covers: A manuscript of a novel or poem that the author has written but never submitted to a publisher or shared with any member of the public.
A musical composition recorded privately by the composer but never commercially released, broadcast, or performed in public.
An artistic work such as a painting, sketch, or sculpture created by an artist and retained in their private possession without exhibition or sale.
A computer programme developed by a programmer but kept strictly internal, never distributed or communicated outside the creator's personal control.
A cinematograph film or sound recording that has been produced but never screened, broadcast, or made available to any audience.
what_it_excludes: Any work that has been issued or distributed to the public in physical copies with the consent of the copyright owner, even if only a limited number of copies were distributed.
A work that has been communicated to the public through any broadcast, digital streaming, or public performance, since such communication constitutes publication under the Act.
A work that has been published abroad and simultaneously or subsequently published in India, as it would qualify as a published work under the simultaneous publication provisions of the Act.
A work that has been publicly exhibited at an art gallery, performed on a public stage, or read aloud at a public event with the owner's consent, as such acts may constitute publication.
A government work or official document that has been officially released, notified, or distributed under governmental authority, as it would no longer be unpublished.

definitions.definition: An 'unpublished work' refers to a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work that has not been published, i.e., copies of the work have not been issued to the public with the consent of the author or other copyright owner, and the work has not otherwise been made available to the public in any form. The term is used in contradistinction to a 'published work' and governs the nationality and domicile-based criteria for copyright protection under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An unpublished work is any creative work — such as a book, song, painting, or script — that has not yet been officially released or distributed to the public by the creator or with their permission. It could be a manuscript sitting in a drawer, a composition never performed, or a painting never exhibited for sale or public display. The law treats unpublished works differently from published ones, especially when determining who owns the copyright and which country's laws apply.
real_world_examples: A novelist in Mumbai writes a full manuscript of her debut Hindi novel but has not yet sent it to any publisher or shared copies with the public — this manuscript is an unpublished work protected under Indian copyright law.

A classical musician in Chennai composes a new raga and records it privately in a home studio but has not released it on any streaming platform or distributed physical copies — the sound recording and musical work remain unpublished.

A software engineer in Bengaluru writes original source code for a new application and stores it on a private server without licensing or distributing it — the computer programme qualifies as an unpublished literary work.

A documentary filmmaker in Delhi completes editing of a film about tribal communities but has not yet screened it at any festival or released it online — the cinematograph film is an unpublished work for copyright purposes.

A sculptor in Kolkata creates a clay model for a commissioned statue but has not yet publicly exhibited or reproduced it — the artistic work remains unpublished until copies are issued or it is displayed to the public with the artist's consent.
what_it_covers: A manuscript of a novel, poem, or academic paper written but not yet commercially printed or distributed to the public.
A musical composition or sound recording that has been created and fixed in notation or a recording medium but not released for public consumption.
An artistic work such as a painting, sculpture, or architectural drawing completed by the artist but not exhibited, reproduced, or offered for sale to the public.
A cinematograph film or video film that has been produced but not yet screened publicly or made available on any platform.
A computer programme written by a developer and stored privately without any distribution or licensing to third parties.
what_it_excludes: Any work of which copies have been issued to the public with the consent of the copyright owner, making it a 'published work' rather than an unpublished work.
A work that has been publicly performed or broadcast, as performance or broadcast may constitute publication depending on the context and issuance of copies.
A work in which copies have been distributed commercially, whether in print, digital download, or physical media, regardless of the scale of distribution.
Government works that have been officially released, notified, or published in the Official Gazette or similar public document.
Works uploaded to publicly accessible platforms such as websites, social media, or streaming services with the author's consent, as such acts may constitute publication by issuance to the public.

definitions.definition: Video film is included within the definition of 'cinematograph film' under Section 2(f) of the Copyright Act, 1957, which defines 'cinematograph film' as any work of visual recording and includes a sound recording accompanying such visual recording; 'cinematograph' is construed as including any work produced by any process analogous to cinematography including video films. Though not separately defined, a video film is a work of visual recording produced by a process analogous to cinematography, recorded and reproduced on a video medium.
definitions.plain_english: A video film is a recorded moving image production — like a movie, documentary, or TV serial — that is captured and stored on video format (such as VHS, DVD, digital file, etc.) rather than traditional celluloid film. It works just like a cinema film but uses video technology to record and play back visuals, usually accompanied by sound. Under Indian copyright law, it is treated as part of the broader category of cinematograph films and enjoys the same legal protections.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood film produced and released directly on a streaming platform like Amazon Prime Video in India, recorded entirely in digital video format, qualifies as a video film and must carry mandatory disclosures under Section 52A.

A regional Tamil or Telugu film distributed on DVD or Blu-ray in India is a video film; any person selling pirated copies of such a DVD without the producer's consent can be prosecuted under Section 68A of the Copyright Act.

A wedding videography production company in Mumbai that records and sells video films of ceremonies without proper agreements may infringe the copyright of the original producer of any background music or cinematographic content incorporated in the recording.

A news channel in India that records and broadcasts a documentary series about the 2023 Chandrayaan mission in video format is producing a video film, and unauthorised duplication of that recording for commercial sale would constitute infringement.

A Kannada devotional video film sold in cassette or pen-drive format at a temple fair without the producer's name and other particulars displayed as required under Section 52A would make the seller liable under the Act.
what_it_covers: Feature films, short films, and documentaries recorded and distributed in video format (VHS, DVD, Blu-ray, digital files) in India
Television serials, reality shows, and web series produced and distributed through video media including OTT platforms
Educational or instructional video recordings sold or distributed commercially in India
Regional language films distributed on video cassette, CD, or digital download formats across Indian markets
Corporate or promotional video productions reproduced and sold as video films for commercial purposes
what_it_excludes: Pure sound recordings that contain no accompanying visual content, such as music albums or audio books
Live performances or broadcasts that are not fixed or recorded in any video medium
Photographs or static images, even if compiled into a slideshow, as these do not constitute a moving visual recording
Written screenplays or scripts, which are literary or dramatic works and not video films
Computer-generated animations distributed solely as computer programmes without being fixed as a visual recording in video film format
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as a video film determines whether the mandatory display requirements under Section 52A (producer's name, address, and other particulars on every copy) apply, and whether unauthorised duplication for sale constitutes a criminal offence under Section 68A, which prescribes imprisonment and fines. Failure to comply with Section 52A obligations or engaging in unlicensed duplication of a video film triggers direct criminal and civil liability under the Copyright Act, 1957.

definitions.definition: "Visual recording" means the recording in any medium, by any method including the storing of it by electronic means, of moving visual images. It forms the basis of a "cinematograph film" which means any work of visual recording and includes a sound recording accompanying such visual recording.
definitions.plain_english: A visual recording is any captured sequence of moving images stored on any medium — such as film reels, digital files, magnetic tapes, or electronic storage — regardless of the technology used to create it. Think of it as the video portion of a movie, TV show, or any recorded footage. It is the foundational component of what the Copyright Act calls a 'cinematograph film', which additionally includes any accompanying audio track.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood production house records a feature film on digital cameras; the resulting stored video footage constitutes a 'visual recording', and together with its soundtrack it forms a 'cinematograph film' protected under the Act.
A YouTube content creator in Mumbai records a travel vlog saved as an MP4 file on a hard drive; that stored sequence of moving images is a visual recording attracting copyright protection.

Doordarshan records a live cricket match broadcast and stores it on magnetic tape for archival purposes; that stored footage is a visual recording, giving Doordarshan broadcast reproduction rights under Section 37.

A regional OTT platform in Chennai stores episodes of a Tamil web series in cloud servers; each episode stored electronically as a sequence of moving images qualifies as a visual recording under the Act.

A wedding videographer in Delhi records ceremony footage on a memory card; that recording of moving visual images constitutes a visual recording, and the producer (videographer or commissioning party) holds copyright in it.

A CCTV security company stores surveillance footage from a shopping mall on DVR; while the commercial rental provisions of Section 2 reference visual recordings, such stored moving image footage technically falls within the statutory meaning of visual recording.
what_it_covers: Feature films recorded on digital or analogue media and stored electronically, on celluloid, or magnetic tape.
Web series, short films, and video content stored as digital files on servers, hard drives, or cloud storage platforms.
Television broadcasts that are recorded and archived on any medium, including satellite or cable programme recordings.
Animation sequences comprising moving visual images rendered and stored electronically.
Documentary footage and news recordings captured and stored in any format by media organisations.
Video recordings accompanying a live performance stored on any medium, forming the basis of a performer's visual recording right under Section 38A.
what_it_excludes: Still photographs, which are single static images and not a sequence of moving visual images, falling instead under 'artistic work'.
Pure sound recordings that contain no visual element whatsoever, which are governed separately as 'sound recording' under Section 2.
Written scripts, screenplays, or literary works that describe a film but do not themselves embody moving visual images.
Live performances being played in real time that have not yet been captured or stored on any medium.
Graphical notations, diagrams, or charts, which are static representations covered under 'artistic work' rather than visual recording.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether content qualifies as a 'visual recording' determines whether it is protected as a 'cinematograph film' under the Act, triggering the producer's exclusive rights under Section 14(d), performer's rights under Sections 38 and 38A, and broadcast reproduction rights under Section 37; it also governs what constitutes an 'infringing copy' and what may or may not be commercially rented under Section 2's definition of 'commercial rental'.

definitions.definition: "Work" under the Copyright Act, 1957 refers to any of the following categories of intellectual creation in which copyright may subsist: a literary work, dramatic work, musical work, artistic work, cinematograph film, or sound recording, as those terms are defined in Section 2 of the Act. The term is used as the foundational subject-matter of copyright protection throughout the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'work' is any creative product that can be protected by copyright law in India — such as a book, a song, a painting, a film, or a computer programme. It is the thing that an author or creator makes, and which the law protects from being copied or used without permission. Only works falling into the specific categories recognised by the Act qualify for copyright protection.
real_world_examples: A Bollywood film produced by a Mumbai-based production house is a 'work' (cinematograph film) in which copyright subsists, protecting the producer's rights against unauthorised copying or streaming.
A novel written by an Indian author and published by Penguin India is a 'work' (literary work), giving the author the exclusive right to reproduce, translate, or adapt it.
A classical Carnatic composition recorded by a musician in Chennai is a 'work' (musical work and sound recording), protecting both the composer's and producer's rights separately.
A painting by a Delhi-based artist displayed at an art gallery is a 'work' (artistic work), granting the artist the right to control reproduction of the painting in posters or merchandise.
A mobile application developed by a Bengaluru startup contains a computer programme, which qualifies as a 'work' (literary work), protecting the code from being copied by competitors.
A choreographed dance piece fixed in writing by a Mumbai dance academy is a 'work' (dramatic work), entitling the creator to copyright protection against unauthorised public performance.
what_it_covers: Literary works including novels, poetry, computer programmes, tables, compilations, and computer databases authored by Indian or foreign creators.
Artistic works such as paintings, sculptures, drawings, maps, photographs, engravings, works of architecture, and works of artistic craftsmanship.
Dramatic works including plays, scripts, choreographic works, and entertainment in dumb show fixed in writing or otherwise.
Musical works consisting of music and graphical notation thereof, composed by any person regardless of whether it has been recorded.
Cinematograph films, including video films, produced by any process analogous to cinematography involving visual recording.
Sound recordings embodying any sequence of musical, spoken, or other sounds, irrespective of the medium on which the recording is made.
what_it_excludes: Mere ideas, concepts, themes, plots, or principles that have not been expressed or fixed in a tangible form — copyright protects expression, not the underlying idea.
News of the day and other miscellaneous facts having the character of mere items of press information, which are explicitly excluded from copyright protection.

Works not falling into the six enumerated categories (literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, cinematograph film, sound recording), such as a purely functional industrial design not possessing artistic character.
Performances or broadcasts in themselves, which are protected separately as neighbouring rights (performer's right, broadcast reproduction right) and are not 'works' in the copyright sense.
Any work in which the term of copyright has expired and which has entered the public domain, as no copyright 'work' protection subsists in it.
Words or actions intended to be sung, spoken, or performed with music, which are expressly excluded from the definition of 'musical work' and must instead qualify as literary or dramatic works.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as a 'work' under the Act is the threshold question for the entire statute — only a 'work' can be owned under Section 14, infringed under Section 51, assigned under Section 18, or licensed under Section 30, and criminal liability under Sections 63–65 is triggered only in respect of infringing copies of a 'work'; if a creation does not fall within the definition, none of these rights, obligations, or offences arise.

Only works falling into the specific categories recognised by the Act qualify for copyright protection.

Legal text: "Work" under the Copyright Act, 1957 refers to any of the following categories of intellectual creation in which copyright may subsist: a literary work, dramatic work, musical work, artistic work, cinematograph film, or sound recording, as those terms are defined in Section 2 of the Act. The term is used as the foundational subject-matter of copyright protection throughout the Act.

definitions.definition: 'work of architecture' means any building or structure having an artistic character or design, or any model for such building or structure.
definitions.plain_english: A 'work of architecture' refers to any building or structure that has an artistic quality or distinctive design, as well as any scale model made for such a building or structure. It is a special category of creative work that is protected under copyright law in India. This means the unique architectural design itself — not just the building materials — is treated as a creative work deserving legal protection.
real_world_examples: The iconic Lotus Temple in New Delhi, designed by architect Fariborz Sahba, qualifies as a work of architecture because of its distinctive petal-shaped artistic design.
A scale model prepared by an Indian architectural firm for a proposed luxury residential tower in Mumbai, showcasing its unique façade design, would be protected as a work of architecture.
The Vidhan Soudha in Bengaluru, with its neo-Dravidian architectural style and ornate design, constitutes a work of architecture under the Copyright Act.
A heritage bungalow in Ahmedabad designed with traditional Indo-Saracenic architectural elements and having artistic character would be covered as a work of architecture.

An architect's detailed physical model submitted for a smart city project tender in Pune, representing a creatively designed civic centre building, is protected as a model for a structure with artistic character.
what_it_covers: A uniquely designed residential or commercial building that embodies an artistic character, such as a sculptural façade or ornamental structural elements.
A physical or digital scale model created by an architect for a proposed building or structure that demonstrates artistic design intent.
A heritage or historic structure with distinct artistic architectural style, such as a colonial-era building with decorative arches and motifs.
A purpose-built public monument or civic structure designed with artistic intent, such as a specially designed memorial or cultural centre.
what_it_excludes: Purely functional or utilitarian structures lacking any artistic character or design, such as a plain industrial warehouse or a standard government boundary wall.
Engineering drawings, blueprints, or technical plans of a building, which may qualify separately as 'artistic works' under the drawing/diagram category rather than as works of architecture.
Temporary constructions or scaffolding arrangements that do not embody a building or structure with artistic character or design.
Interior decoration arrangements or furniture layouts within a building, which do not constitute a building or structure in themselves.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a structure qualifies as a 'work of architecture' determines if it attracts copyright protection under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, meaning unauthorised reproduction of its artistic design — including constructing a replica building or reproducing the model — constitutes infringement. It also governs the specific rules under the Act permitting incidental depiction of such works in public places without infringement liability.

definitions.definition: A 'work of joint authorship' means a work produced by the collaboration of two or more authors in which the contribution of one author is not distinct from the contribution of the other author or authors.
definitions.plain_english: A work of joint authorship is a creative work made together by two or more people, where their individual contributions are so blended that you cannot separate out who wrote or created which specific part. For example, if two writers co-write a novel and their writing is completely merged, it is a work of joint authorship. The key idea is that the contributions are inseparable, not that they simply worked on the same project at the same time.
real_world_examples: Two Bollywood lyricists jointly compose song lyrics where both contribute lines and verses that are so intertwined that neither person's individual portion can be independently identified — this constitutes a work of joint authorship under the Copyright Act.

Two software engineers in a Bengaluru startup co-write a computer programme together, editing each other's code throughout development until the final codebase cannot be attributed to one person alone — the resulting programme is a work of joint authorship.

A pair of authors from Mumbai jointly write a legal commentary textbook, each contributing to every chapter and revising each other's content so extensively that no chapter can be attributed solely to one author — the textbook qualifies as a work of joint authorship.

Two choreographers in Chennai collaboratively create a classical Bharatanatyam performance piece, with their artistic contributions to the choreography being deeply intermingled and indistinguishable — the dramatic choreographic work is a work of joint authorship.

Two music composers jointly score the background music for a Tamil film, with both contributing melodic and harmonic elements throughout the score in a way that cannot be separated — the resulting musical work is a work of joint authorship.

Two graphic designers in Delhi jointly create an artistic illustration for a national magazine cover, where each designer's visual contribution is blended seamlessly into the final artwork — the illustration is a work of joint authorship.
what_it_covers: A novel co-written by two authors where each author's prose is so thoroughly revised and merged with the other's that individual contributions cannot be identified.
A musical composition jointly created by two composers whose melodic and harmonic contributions are blended throughout the piece without clear demarcation.
A software programme co-developed by two programmers who continuously edited and integrated each other's code such that individual contributions are indistinguishable.
A jointly authored screenplay where two writers collaborated on every scene and dialogue, making it impossible to attribute specific portions to either writer alone.
A choreographic dramatic work created by two choreographers working in tandem, with no identifiable distinct sections attributable to each independently.
what_it_excludes: Works where each author's contribution is clearly distinct and separable, such as an anthology where different chapters are solely written by different identified authors — these are compilations, not works of joint authorship.

A cinematograph film, even though it involves multiple creative contributors, because the producer is specifically designated as the 'author' under the Act and contributions are typically distinct by role.
A work produced under a contract of service or employment where one person directed the creation and another merely executed instructions, as there is no genuine collaborative authorship.
Works where one person made a trivial or negligible contribution that does not rise to the level of co-authorship, as co-authorship requires meaningful creative collaboration.

A musical work where a lyricist and composer collaborate — under Indian copyright law, words and music may be treated as separate works, and the lyricist's and composer's contributions are typically considered distinct.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a work as a 'work of joint authorship' directly determines how copyright duration is calculated under Section 22 (term of copyright runs from the death of the author who dies last) and governs how all joint authors must consent before copyright can be assigned or licensed, preventing any single co-author from unilaterally exercising or transferring the rights; failure to secure all co-authors' consent can render a licence or assignment legally invalid.
