definitions.definition: A 'work of sculpture' is not separately defined in the Copyright Act, 1957, but it is included within the definition of 'artistic work' under Section 2(c), which states that 'artistic work' means a painting, a sculpture, a drawing (including a diagram, map, chart or plan), an engraving or a photograph, whether or not any such work possesses artistic quality. A work of sculpture is thus a three-dimensional artistic creation shaped or fashioned by hand or tool from any material, enjoying copyright protection as an artistic work regardless of its artistic merit.
definitions.plain_english: A work of sculpture is a three-dimensional object created by an artist by shaping, carving, casting, or modelling materials such as stone, wood, metal, clay, or any other substance. It is protected under copyright law in India as a type of artistic work, meaning the creator has the exclusive right to reproduce, display, or make copies of it. Importantly, it does not need to be considered 'fine art' or of high artistic quality to receive this protection.
real_world_examples: A sculptor in Jaipur hand-carves a decorative marble statue of a deity for a temple — the finished three-dimensional figure is a work of sculpture protected by copyright.

A Mumbai-based contemporary artist creates a large bronze installation displayed at the Kochi-Muziris Biennale — this installation qualifies as a work of sculpture and the artist holds copyright over it.

A craftsman in Chandigarh creates a plaster-of-Paris model replica of the famous Rock Garden figures designed by Nek Chand — reproduction of this model without permission would infringe the copyright in the original works of sculpture.

An art student in Chennai casts a terracotta figurine as part of a college project — even this student work qualifies as a work of sculpture under the Act and copyright vests in the student automatically upon creation.

A toy manufacturer in Agra mass-produces miniature replicas of the Taj Mahal in the style of a well-known sculptor's artistic interpretation — if the original sculptural design is still within the copyright term, manufacturing the replicas without a licence would constitute infringement.
what_it_covers: A hand-carved wooden figurine made by a craftsman in Rajasthan, regardless of whether it is considered fine art.
A large-scale bronze or stone statue created by a professional sculptor for a public monument or private commission.
A clay or plaster model made as a preparatory or final work by an artist, including student projects.
A cast-metal industrial-style sculpture created using modern fabrication techniques by a contemporary artist.
A traditional religious idol crafted by a shilpi (traditional sculptor) where the artistic expression is original to that creator.
what_it_excludes: A building or structure with artistic character, which is separately covered as a 'work of architecture' under Section 2(b) of the Act.
A two-dimensional painting, drawing, diagram, or engraving, which are distinct categories of artistic work under Section 2(c) and do not qualify as works of sculpture.
A photograph, which is expressly listed as a separate sub-category of 'artistic work' and is governed by its own considerations under the Act.

A purely functional three-dimensional object (such as a standard manufactured product) that has no element of original artistic expression and is governed by the Designs Act, 2000 once applied industrially.
A cinematograph film or sound recording, which are entirely separate categories of works under the Copyright Act and are not treated as sculptural works.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a three-dimensional object qualifies as a 'work of sculpture' determines whether it attracts copyright protection under the Copyright Act, 1957, giving the creator exclusive rights to reproduce, publish, communicate, or adapt the work and entitling them to remedies for infringement including injunctions and damages. If the object instead qualifies only as a registered design under the Designs Act, 2000, copyright protection ceases upon industrial application, making this classification critical to the scope and duration of the creator's legal rights.

definitions.definition: Works first published in India refers to literary, artistic, musical, dramatic, or other works that were first brought out or released to the public within the territory of India, thereby qualifying for copyright protection under the Act. Such works attract the full suite of copyright provisions under this Act, subject to the Central Government's power under Section 42 to restrict those protections in cases where the author is a subject or citizen of a foreign country that does not afford adequate protection to works of Indian authors.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to any creative work — such as a book, song, painting, or film — that was first officially released or published in India. If a work is first published in India, Indian copyright law normally gives it full protection. However, if the author is a citizen of a foreign country that does not protect Indian authors' works adequately, the Indian government can withdraw those protections for new works by citizens of that country, even if those works are first published in India.
real_world_examples: A French novelist publishes her debut novel for the first time through a Mumbai-based publisher; since France is deemed not to adequately protect Indian authors' works, the Central Government issues an order and her novel, though first published in India, does not receive Indian copyright protection.

A German music composer releases an album for the first time via a Chennai record label; if Germany has not undertaken to give adequate protection to Indian authors, the Central Government may direct that copyright provisions shall not apply to that album.

An American screenwriter who is not domiciled in India submits a screenplay first published by a Delhi production house; upon a Central Government order regarding the USA, the copyright provisions that would otherwise protect works first published in India would not apply to this screenplay.

A Japanese manga artist publishes a graphic novel exclusively and for the first time through a Kolkata-based publisher; if Japan is listed in an Official Gazette order as not providing adequate protection to Indian authors, the copyright protections applicable to works first published in India would be withheld for this work.

An Australian poet whose first collection is published by a Bengaluru literary press would normally benefit from Indian copyright law as a work first published in India, but if Australia were subject to a Central Government restriction order, those protections would not apply to works published after the specified date.
what_it_covers: A work by a foreign author that is published for the very first time in India, before being published anywhere else in the world, thereby qualifying as first published in India.
Works by authors of any nationality (including foreign nationals not domiciled in India) that are initially released to the public within India's territory through an Indian publisher or distributor.

Creative works across all categories — literary, artistic, dramatic, musical, cinematographic — so long as their first public release occurred in India, making them eligible for the copyright protections ordinarily conferred by the Act.
Works simultaneously published in India and another country where the simultaneous publication qualifies as 'first published in India' under the Act's provisions on simultaneous publication.
what_it_excludes: Works first published outside India, even if subsequently published or widely distributed in India — these do not qualify as 'works first published in India'.

Works by foreign authors who are subjects or citizens of a country against which the Central Government has issued a restriction order under Section 42, published after the date specified in that order — these are explicitly excluded from the copyright provisions applicable to works first published in India.
Unpublished works that have never been released or made available to the public in India, as the concept of 'first published in India' inherently requires an act of publication.

Works by foreign authors not domiciled in India where the Central Government has directed that copyright provisions shall not apply, regardless of the fact that such works may have been physically produced or printed in India.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a work qualifies as 'first published in India' determines whether it is entitled to the full suite of copyright protections under the Act; if it does qualify, copyright subsists in it and infringement provisions, moral rights, and licensing obligations are triggered. Conversely, where the Central Government invokes Section 42 and restricts these provisions for works of foreign nationals whose home country does not protect Indian authors, those works lose copyright protection in India entirely, meaning no infringement action can be brought and no royalties are owed.

definitions.definition: In sub-section (1) of Section 12, 'zone' means a zone specified in section 15 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (37 of 1956), and is used to determine the territorial jurisdiction within which the Appellate Board shall ordinarily hear any proceeding instituted before it under the Copyright Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'zone' refers to one of the large regional groupings of Indian states as defined under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. It is used to decide which bench of the Appellate Board should hear a copyright dispute — ordinarily, the bench covering the zone where the person who filed the case actually lives or runs their business. This ensures that people do not have to travel across the entire country to attend hearings.
real_world_examples: A film producer based in Mumbai (Maharashtra, falling in the Western Zone) files a copyright infringement complaint before the Appellate Board; the Board's bench responsible for the Western Zone would ordinarily hear the matter.

A music composer residing in Chennai (Tamil Nadu, Southern Zone) seeks a compulsory licence before the Appellate Board; the Southern Zone bench would ordinarily be the appropriate forum to hear his petition.

A software company with its registered office in Bengaluru (Karnataka, Southern Zone) institutes proceedings against unauthorized reproduction of its computer programme; the case would ordinarily be listed before the Southern Zone bench of the Appellate Board.

A literary author who voluntarily resides in Kolkata (West Bengal, Eastern Zone) challenges a refusal by the Registrar of Copyrights; the Eastern Zone bench of the Appellate Board would ordinarily have jurisdiction to hear the appeal.

A Delhi-based (Northern Zone) collecting society disputes a tariff scheme before the Appellate Board; the Northern Zone bench would ordinarily conduct the proceedings since the society carries on its principal business there.
what_it_covers: The five zones specified under section 15 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, namely Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western, and Central zones.
The zone in which the petitioner or applicant actually and voluntarily resides at the time of instituting proceedings before the Appellate Board.
The zone in which the person instituting the proceeding carries on business or personally works for gain, as an alternative basis for determining the appropriate zone.
what_it_excludes: Zones or territorial divisions defined under any other statute, such as revenue zones, police zones, or administrative zones created by state governments — only the zones under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 apply.
The location of the respondent or the place where the infringement occurred, as these are not the determinative factors for identifying the 'zone' under Section 12.
Union Territories that may not fall neatly within a specified zone under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, where special bench allocation by the Chairman may be required.
Purely temporary or incidental residence of the petitioner — only actual and voluntary residence at the time of institution of proceedings is relevant.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'zone' directly determines which regional bench of the Appellate Board has ordinary jurisdiction to hear a copyright proceeding; filing before the wrong bench or in an incorrect zone could result in procedural objections, delay, or transfer of the case, affecting the efficiency of enforcing copyright remedies under the Act.

zone: A 'zone' refers to one of the large regional groupings of Indian states as defined under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. It is used to decide which bench of the Appellate Board should hear a copyright dispute — ordinarily, the bench covering the zone where the person who filed the case actually lives or runs their business. This ensures that people do not have to travel across the entire country to attend hearings.

Legal text: In sub-section (1) of Section 12, 'zone' means a zone specified in section 15 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (37 of 1956), and is used to determine the territorial jurisdiction within which the Appellate Board shall ordinarily hear any proceeding instituted before it under the Copyright Act.
